# Elci documentation

Elci 0.1.0-dev (Julc 0.1.0-pre20-ebaf028-SNAPSHOT). Every page of https://elci-lang.dev, in reading order.

---

# Why Elci

> What Elci is, who it is for, how it turns Elm-syntax source into Plutus V3 scripts, and what you get from it today.

Source: https://elci-lang.dev/start/introduction/

Elci (pronounced "el-see") is a small functional language for writing Cardano smart contracts. You write
Elm-syntax `.elm` files, and Elci compiles them to Plutus V3 scripts that run on the Cardano ledger.
This page explains what Elci is, who it is for, how the compiler works, and where the project stands today.

## What Elci is

A Cardano smart contract is a **validator**: a function that the ledger runs when a transaction tries to
spend locked funds, mint tokens, withdraw rewards or take part in governance. It receives the data involved
and the whole transaction, and it either approves or rejects.

Elci lets you write those functions in the syntax of [Elm](https://elm-lang.org), a language known for
readable code and helpful compile errors:

```elm title="src/Treasury.elm"
module Treasury exposing (Action(..), Payout, spend)

import Julc.Ledger exposing (PubKeyHash, ScriptContext)

type alias Payout =
    { beneficiary : PubKeyHash
    , amount : Int
    }

type Action
    = Release
    | Cancel

spend : PubKeyHash -> Payout -> Action -> ScriptContext -> Bool
spend admin payout action ctx =
    case action of
        Release ->
            payout.amount > 0 && signedBy payout.beneficiary ctx

        Cancel ->
            signedBy admin ctx

signedBy : PubKeyHash -> ScriptContext -> Bool
signedBy key ctx =
    List.any (\signer -> signer == key) ctx.txInfo.signatories
```

The `Payout` record is the datum stored with the locked funds, `Action` is the redeemer the spender sends,
and `admin` is a deployment parameter. You declare how the function is deployed in `elci.toml`, not in the source:

```toml title="elci.toml"
[project]
source-directories = ["src"]
target = "plutus-v3-pv11-uplc-1.1.0"
julc-version = "0.1.0-pre20-ebaf028-SNAPSHOT"

[validators.treasury]
boundary = "julc-strict-v1"
parameters = ["admin"]
spend = "Treasury.spend"
```

A test runs the compiled script against a real transaction context:

```elm title="tests/TreasuryTest.elm"
module TreasuryTest exposing (beneficiaryReleases, strangerCannotRelease)

import Julc.Data as Data
import Julc.Ledger exposing (PubKeyHash)
import Scenario exposing (Scenario)
import Treasury exposing (Action(..))

admin : PubKeyHash
admin =
    Scenario.key "admin"

beneficiary : PubKeyHash
beneficiary =
    Scenario.key "beneficiary"

release : Scenario
release =
    Scenario.spend "treasury" (Scenario.outRef "treasury" 0) (Data.encode { beneficiary = beneficiary, amount = 50 })
        |> Scenario.parameters [ Data.encode admin ]
        |> Scenario.redeemer (Data.encode Release)

beneficiaryReleases : Scenario
beneficiaryReleases =
    release
        |> Scenario.signedBy beneficiary

strangerCannotRelease : Scenario
strangerCannotRelease =
    release
        |> Scenario.signedBy (Scenario.key "stranger")
        |> Scenario.expectFailure
```

```text
$ elci test .
PASS TreasuryTest.beneficiaryReleases (cpu 11698810, mem 46679)
PASS TreasuryTest.strangerCannotRelease (cpu 12077243, mem 48611)
2 passed, 0 failed
$ elci build .
validator treasury (spend): checked; 458 FLAT bytes; plutus-v3-pv11-uplc-1.1.0
```

## Who it is for

- **Developers who like typed functional programming.** If you know Elm, Haskell, F# or OCaml, most of the
  syntax will be familiar. If you don't, it is a small language, and the Learn pages cover all of it.
- **Newcomers to Cardano.** The compiler rejects whole classes of mistakes before anything reaches the
  chain, and the test runner runs your script in a realistic ledger context.
- **Java and Cardano Client Lib teams.** Elci is built on Julc, the Java toolchain for Cardano smart
  contracts. It writes Julc's artifact format, can call Julc's on-chain Java libraries, and its scripts can
  be tested from JUnit.

## How it works

Elci is a compiler frontend. It owns the language (parsing, modules, types) and hands a typed program to
Julc's backend, which produces the script:

```text
 .elm source ──► parse and resolve modules ──► type inference and checks
                                                      │
       ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
       ▼
 specialization ──► typed PIR ──► Julc backend ──► Plutus V3 UPLC
                                  (wrapper, strict      (validator.plutus.json,
                                   decoding, optimizer)  abi.json, .flat, .plutus)
```

1. **Source.** Your modules under `src/`, written in Elm 0.19 syntax.
2. **Type inference.** Hindley–Milner style inference checks every expression. It also checks that
   every `case` covers all possibilities and that `==` is used only on types that support it.
3. **Typed PIR.** Generic functions are specialized for each type they are used at, and the program is
   lowered to PIR, the typed intermediate language that Julc also uses for its Java validators.
4. **Julc backend.** Julc wraps each validator so that it checks the purpose (spend, mint and so on)
   and strictly decodes the datum and redeemer before calling your handler. Then it optimizes and
   serializes the script.
5. **Plutus V3 UPLC.** The result is a Plutus V3 script, plus an `abi.json` that records exactly how your
   types are encoded as on-chain data.

## What you get

- **Elm syntax with type inference.** Records, custom types, pattern matching, pipelines and lambdas.
  Types are inferred inside functions. Every top-level declaration needs a signature, so its types are
  written where the reader can see them.
- **Exhaustive pattern matching.** A `case` that misses a constructor is a compile error, and so is an
  unreachable branch. Adding a redeemer action means the compiler shows you every place that must handle it.
- **Strict data boundaries.** Datums and redeemers are decoded strictly before your code runs. Wrong
  constructor tags, wrong field counts and wrong kinds of data fail the script instead of reaching your
  logic. `elci apply` checks deployment parameters against their types before applying them.
- **Named, multi-purpose validators with parameters.** Each `[validators.<name>]` table is one script with
  one hash. It can combine `spend`, `mint`, `withdraw`, `certify`, `vote` and `propose` handlers, take
  deployment parameters, and have them applied with `elci apply`.
- **Built-in testing.** `elci test` runs unit tests, transaction scenarios against the same script that
  `elci build` writes, and property-based tests with shrinking. Every test reports its CPU and memory budget.
- **Julc libraries and Java interop.** Map a Julc on-chain Java library (math, cryptography, byte strings and
  more) in `elci.toml` and import it like an Elm module. Elci compiles the library's Java source to
  on-chain code. It doesn't run that Java on your machine.
- **Typed collections, values and bytes.** `Dict k v` is Elm's `Dict`, stored as a sorted Plutus map,
  `Map k v` holds the ledger's own maps, `Array a` gives constant-time indexed reads, `Value` handles
  multi-asset values with exact `==` on the protocol's value builtins, and `Bytes` exposes the Plutus
  byte-string builtins, including hashes and bitwise operations.
- **Transaction helpers.** `Tx` answers the questions validators ask about a transaction: who signed, what
  it spends and pays, which outputs stay at the script, what it mints and which datum an output carries.
  `Interval` checks deadlines against the validity range.
- **A native CLI.** Build `elci` as a GraalVM native executable that starts fast and needs no Java at
  runtime, or run the JVM version.

## Current status

:::caution[Development preview]
Elci is a development preview, not a production-ready contract toolchain, and its own test suite is not
a security audit. Test your contracts thoroughly, and don't lock real value with them yet.
:::

Be aware of these limits before you start:

- **You build it from source.** Elci depends on a development build of Julc that you publish to your local
  Maven repository. [Installation](https://elci-lang.dev/start/installation/) walks you through it.
- **It is not browser Elm.** There is no `Html`, no ports, no commands or subscriptions, and no `Float`.
  A contract is a pure function that returns `Bool`.
- **No Elm packages.** Elci has Elm's core modules (`Basics`, `List`, `Maybe`, `Result`, `Tuple`, `Dict` and
  part of `String`), its own `Map`, `Array`, `Value`, `Interval`, `Tx`, `Bytes` and `Julc.Data` modules, and
  Julc's Java libraries. `elm.json` and the Elm package registry are not used.
- **Some tooling is missing.** There is no language server, and no CIP-57 blueprint generation yet. The
  build writes Julc's `validator.plutus.json` format and Elci's own `abi.json`.

[Coming from Elm](https://elci-lang.dev/learn/coming-from-elm/) lists every difference in detail.

## Next steps

  - [Installation](https://elci-lang.dev/start/installation/): Build the elci CLI and put it on your PATH.
  - [Your first validator](https://elci-lang.dev/start/first-validator/): Create, test, build and change a validator in a few minutes.
  - [Learn the language](https://elci-lang.dev/learn/basics/): Values, functions and types, with examples you can run.
  - [Coming from Elm](https://elci-lang.dev/learn/coming-from-elm/): What stays the same and what changes on-chain.

# Installation

> Build the elci compiler from source with Java 25, optionally as a native executable, and put it on your PATH.

Source: https://elci-lang.dev/start/installation/

On this page you build the `elci` command-line compiler from source and put it on your `PATH`. You need
Java 25. GraalVM is only needed if you also want the native executable.

:::note[Development preview]
Elci depends on a development snapshot of [Julc](https://github.com/bloxbean/julc) that is not on Maven
Central. Gradle downloads that exact version from the BloxBean Maven repository
(`https://repo.bloxbean.org/maven/snapshots`), so you don't need to build Julc yourself.
:::

## Prerequisites

| Tool | Needed for | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| JDK 25 | Building Elci and running the JVM `elci` | Set `JAVA_HOME` to it |
| Git | Cloning Elci | |
| GraalVM 25 with `native-image` | Only the native `elci` executable | Also needs your platform's C toolchain |
| Node.js and npm | Only formatting with elm-format | Optional |

You don't need to install Gradle: the project includes the Gradle wrapper (`./gradlew`). The commands
below are for macOS and Linux shells.

## Build from source

1. **Check your Java version.** Gradle builds Elci with Java 25:

   ```sh
   java -version
   ```

   The first line of the output should report version 25. If it doesn't, install a JDK 25 and point
   `JAVA_HOME` at it.

2. **Clone Elci.**

   ```sh
   git clone https://github.com/bloxbean/elci-lang.git
   ```

3. **Check the pinned Julc version.** Elci's `gradle.properties` names the Julc snapshot it was built
   and tested with, and the Julc commit it was built from:

   ```sh
   grep '^julc' elci-lang/gradle.properties
   ```

   ```text
   julcVersion=0.1.0-pre20-ebaf028-SNAPSHOT
   julcRevision=ebaf028c982479906a1f9449b9fef68fa7836301
   ```

   The first build downloads that version from the BloxBean Maven repository.

4. **Build the Elci CLI.**

   ```sh
   cd elci-lang
   ./gradlew installDist
   ```

   This creates `build/install/elci/bin/elci`, a launcher script that runs the compiler on your Java 25.
   To run Elci's own test suite first, use `./gradlew test installDist`.

5. **Optional: build the native executable.** Point `GRAALVM_HOME` at a GraalVM 25 installation that
   contains `bin/native-image`, then run:

   ```sh
   export GRAALVM_HOME=/path/to/graalvm
   ./gradlew nativeCompile
   ```

   This creates `build/native/elci`. It starts fast and doesn't need Java at runtime, but it only runs on
   the platform you built it on.

6. **Put `elci` on your `PATH`.** From the `elci-lang` directory, add one of the two builds:

   ```sh
   # The JVM build
   export PATH="$PWD/build/install/elci/bin:$PATH"

   # Or the native build
   export PATH="$PWD/build/native:$PATH"
   ```

   Add the same line, with the absolute path, to your shell profile (for example `~/.zshrc` or
   `~/.bashrc`) to keep it in new terminals.

7. **Check the installation.**

   ```sh
   elci --version
   ```

   ```text
   elci 0.1.0-dev / julc 0.1.0-pre20-ebaf028-SNAPSHOT
   ```

   The first part is the Elci version and the second is the Julc version the compiler is pinned to.

:::tip[Prebuilt binaries]
Elci's release workflow builds native archives for Linux (x64 and arm64) and macOS (Apple Silicon) from
version tags. When a release is published for your platform, you can download the archive, check it
against `SHA256SUMS`, and put the `elci` executable on your `PATH` without installing Java or Julc.
:::

## The Julc version in your projects

Every project's `elci.toml` records the Julc version it expects:

```toml
julc-version = "0.1.0-pre20-ebaf028-SNAPSHOT"
```

It must equal the version that `elci --version` prints. `elci init` writes the right value for you. If they
differ, for example after you upgrade Elci, every command stops with:

```text
elci: ELCI4001: Julc version does not match this compiler; expected julc-version = "0.1.0-pre20-ebaf028-SNAPSHOT"
```

Update `julc-version` in `elci.toml`, then rebuild and re-run your tests. A new Julc version can change
the generated scripts and their hashes.

## Editor setup

- **Syntax highlighting:** Elci source files use the `.elm` extension, so any Elm syntax-highlighting
  extension works.
- **Formatting:** Elci code follows [elm-format](https://github.com/avh4/elm-format) 0.8.8 style. To check your
  files without installing anything globally:

  ```sh
  npm exec --yes --package elm-format@0.8.8 -- elm-format src tests --validate
  ```

- **Diagnostics:** the Elm language server doesn't know Elci's modules (`Julc.Ledger`, `Map`, `Array`,
  `Bytes`, your Java library imports), so its errors aren't reliable for Elci code. Use `elci check`, which
  reports every error as `file:line:column: ELCIxxxx: message`, followed by the source line and any hints.
  With `--report=json` it prints each error as one JSON object on its own line instead, for editor
  integrations. `elci explain <code>` explains a code.

:::caution
elm-format silently changes integer literals larger than about 9.2 × 10¹⁸, because it stores them as 64-bit
numbers. See [Coming from Elm](https://elci-lang.dev/learn/coming-from-elm/).
:::

## Troubleshooting

- **Could not resolve `org.julclang:...` while building Elci.** Gradle could not download the pinned Julc
  snapshot. Check that `https://repo.bloxbean.org/maven/snapshots` is reachable from your machine (a proxy or
  firewall can block it), and that `julcVersion` in `gradle.properties` is unchanged.
- **Gradle reports a Java toolchain problem.** Elci and Julc need Java 25. Check `java -version` and
  `JAVA_HOME`.
- **`GRAALVM_HOME must point to a GraalVM installation containing native-image`.** `nativeCompile` needs
  `GRAALVM_HOME` set to a GraalVM installation that contains `bin/native-image`.
- **`elci: command not found`.** The build directory is not on your `PATH`. Run the binary by its full path
  to confirm the build worked, then fix your `PATH`.

Next, create your first project: [Your first validator](https://elci-lang.dev/start/first-validator/).

---

# Your first validator

> Create a validator with elci init, read every generated file, check, test and build it, then change it to require a second signature.

Source: https://elci-lang.dev/start/first-validator/

In this tutorial you create a small validator, read every file that `elci init` generates, and check, test
and build it. Then you change it to require a second signature and update its tests. You need `elci` on your
`PATH` (see [Installation](https://elci-lang.dev/start/installation/)).

## What a validator does

On Cardano, funds can be locked at a script address. Whenever a transaction tries to spend them, the
ledger runs the script, called a **validator**, and the spend only happens if the validator approves. A
spending validator receives four things:

- **Parameters** that you fix when you deploy the script, such as the owner's key.
- The **datum**: data stored with the locked output when it was created.
- The **redeemer**: data that the spending transaction supplies.
- The **script context**: the whole transaction being validated, including who signed it.

It returns `True` to approve the transaction. Returning `False`, or failing during evaluation, rejects it.
Validators can also control minting, reward withdrawals and governance actions; this tutorial sticks to
spending.

## Create the project

```sh
elci init my-contract
cd my-contract
```

```text
Created Elci project at .../my-contract with initial spend handler in validator main.
Run: elci check .../my-contract
```

`elci init` creates this layout:

- my-contract/
  - elci.toml project configuration
  - README.md
  - .gitignore ignores build/
  - src/
    - Main.elm the validator
  - tests/
    - MainTest.elm two transaction scenarios

## The configuration

```toml title="elci.toml"
[project]
source-directories = ["src"]
target = "plutus-v3-pv11-uplc-1.1.0"
julc-version = "0.1.0-pre20-ebaf028-SNAPSHOT"

# One deployed script. Add handler keys (spend, mint, withdraw, certify, vote,
# propose) to let this script serve more purposes; add more [validators.<name>]
# tables for independent scripts.
[validators.main]
boundary = "julc-strict-v1"
parameters = ["owner"]
spend = "Main.spend"
```

- `[project]` says where your modules live, which on-chain target to compile for (Plutus V3), and which Julc
  version the compiler must match.
- `[validators.main]` declares one script called `main`. Its `spend` handler is the function `spend` in module
  `Main`, and it takes one deployment parameter called `owner`.
- `boundary = "julc-strict-v1"` selects strict decoding of the data the script receives. It is currently the
  only boundary policy.

The source code doesn't say how it is deployed. The configuration does, so the same function could be
reused in another validator.

## The validator

```elm title="src/Main.elm"
module Main exposing (spend)

import Julc.Ledger exposing (PubKeyHash, ScriptContext)

{-| Accept only transactions signed by the owner, a deployment parameter.
-}
spend : PubKeyHash -> () -> () -> ScriptContext -> Bool
spend owner _ _ ctx =
    List.any (\signer -> signer == owner) ctx.txInfo.signatories
```

Line by line:

- `module Main exposing (spend)` names the module (it must match the file path `src/Main.elm`) and makes
  `spend` visible to the configuration and to tests.
- `import Julc.Ledger exposing (PubKeyHash, ScriptContext)` brings in two Cardano ledger types.
- The signature lists the arguments in the order the handler receives them:

  | Argument | Type | Meaning |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `owner` | `PubKeyHash` | The `owner` parameter: the hash of the owner's public key |
  | `_` | `()` | The datum. `()` (unit) means "no information" |
  | `_` | `()` | The redeemer, also unit |
  | `ctx` | `ScriptContext` | The transaction being validated |

- The body reads `ctx.txInfo.signatories`, the key hashes that signed the transaction, and uses `List.any`
  to check whether one of them is the owner. `\signer -> signer == owner` is an anonymous function (a lambda).
  The core `Tx` module has the same check as `Tx.signedBy owner ctx`, after `import Tx`.

The `_` pattern ignores an argument. The datum and redeemer are still decoded strictly before `spend` runs,
so they must be unit data.

## Check it

`elci check` compiles every validator all the way through the backend, without writing any files:

```sh
elci check .
```

```text
validator main (spend): checked; 300 FLAT bytes; plutus-v3-pv11-uplc-1.1.0
```

The line names the validator and its purposes, then gives the size of the compiled script in bytes and
the target. Script size matters on Cardano, because the transaction that uses a script pays for its bytes.

## The tests

```elm title="tests/MainTest.elm"
module MainTest exposing (othersAreRejected, ownerSigns)

import Julc.Data as Data
import Julc.Ledger as Ledger exposing (PubKeyHash)
import Scenario exposing (Scenario)

owner : PubKeyHash
owner =
    Scenario.key "owner"

transaction : Scenario
transaction =
    Scenario.spend "main" (Scenario.outRef "main" 0) Scenario.unit
        |> Scenario.parameters [ Data.encode owner ]

ownerSigns : Scenario
ownerSigns =
    transaction
        |> Scenario.signedBy owner

othersAreRejected : Scenario
othersAreRejected =
    transaction
        |> Scenario.signedBy (Scenario.key "someone else")
        |> Scenario.expectFailure
```

A `Scenario` describes one transaction against a validator of your project:

- `Scenario.key "owner"` derives a deterministic test key hash from a name.
- `Scenario.spend "main" (Scenario.outRef "main" 0) Scenario.unit` spends an output locked at validator
  `main`'s address, with a unit datum.
- `Scenario.parameters [ Data.encode owner ]` supplies the deployment parameters, in the order declared in
  `elci.toml`. `Data.encode` turns an Elci value into on-chain data.
- `Scenario.signedBy` adds a signer, and `Scenario.expectFailure` says the validator must reject the
  transaction.

Only the exposed declarations of type `Scenario` are tests. `owner` and `transaction` are helpers.

## Run the tests

```sh
elci test .
```

```text
PASS MainTest.ownerSigns (cpu 7675163, mem 29990)
PASS MainTest.othersAreRejected (cpu 8053596, mem 31922)
2 passed, 0 failed
```

Each scenario compiles the validator exactly as `elci build` does, applies the parameters, builds a complete
ledger context for the transaction and runs the script. `cpu` and `mem` are the execution budget the script
used. The ledger charges fees for these units and limits how many a transaction may use.

## Build it

```sh
elci build .
```

```text
validator main (spend): checked; 300 FLAT bytes; plutus-v3-pv11-uplc-1.1.0
```

The build writes one directory per validator:

- build/
  - validators/
    - elci-outputs.json the files Elci owns
    - main/
      - abi.json how your types are encoded
      - validator.flat the script in FLAT encoding
      - validator.plutus a Plutus V3 text envelope
      - validator.plutus.json the Julc artifact for Cardano Client Lib

`validator.plutus.json` is the file your off-chain code loads (the `cborHex` value is shortened here):

```json title="build/validators/main/validator.plutus.json"
{
  "type": "PlutusScriptV3",
  "purpose": "spending",
  "description": "main",
  "cborHex": "59012f59012c010100323232322322323232323293370e...",
  "hash": "",
  "params": "owner:PubKeyHash",
  "sizeBytes": 300
}
```

The `hash` is empty because the script still needs its `owner` parameter. The hash of a script changes
when you apply parameters to it.

## Make it your own

Now change the validator so that spending needs two signatures: the owner's and a guardian's.

1. **Change the handler.** Add a `guardian` parameter, and move the signature check into a helper function
   so you can use it twice:

   ```elm title="src/Main.elm" ins={6,8-10,13-15}
   module Main exposing (spend)

   import Julc.Ledger exposing (PubKeyHash, ScriptContext)

   {-| Accept only transactions signed by both the owner and the guardian.
   -}
   spend : PubKeyHash -> PubKeyHash -> () -> () -> ScriptContext -> Bool
   spend owner guardian _ _ ctx =
       signedBy owner ctx && signedBy guardian ctx

   signedBy : PubKeyHash -> ScriptContext -> Bool
   signedBy key ctx =
       List.any (\signer -> signer == key) ctx.txInfo.signatories
   ```

   `signedBy` isn't exposed, so it stays private to the module.

2. **Check it.** The compiler notices that the handler no longer matches its configuration:

   ```sh
   elci check .
   ```

   ```text
   .../my-contract/src/Main.elm:8:1: ELCI2014: Handler Main.spend does not have the spend signature owner -> datum -> redeemer -> ScriptContext -> Bool that [validators.main] needs (1 parameter); its type is PubKeyHash -> PubKeyHash -> () -> () -> ScriptContext -> Bool; it has `()` where the configuration needs `ScriptContext`

   8| spend : PubKeyHash -> PubKeyHash -> () -> () -> ScriptContext -> Bool
      ^^^^^

   In .../my-contract/elci.toml:9: [validators.main]

   For more on ELCI2014, run `elci explain ELCI2014`.
   ```

   The table still declares one parameter, so the handler must take one parameter, then the datum, the
   redeemer and the context. `spend` now takes two parameters, so its arguments no longer line up.
   `ELCI2014` always means that a handler and its `elci.toml` table disagree; `elci explain ELCI2014`
   says more.

3. **Declare the new parameter.** Parameters are listed in the order the handler receives them:

   ```toml title="elci.toml" ins={3}
   [validators.main]
   boundary = "julc-strict-v1"
   parameters = ["owner", "guardian"]
   spend = "Main.spend"
   ```

   ```sh
   elci check .
   ```

   ```text
   validator main (spend): checked; 323 FLAT bytes; plutus-v3-pv11-uplc-1.1.0
   ```

4. **Run the old tests.** They still supply only one parameter:

   ```sh
   elci test .
   ```

   ```text
   FAIL MainTest.ownerSigns
       cannot prepare validator 'main': it takes 2 parameters [owner, guardian], but the scenario gives 1; set them with Scenario.parameters
   FAIL MainTest.othersAreRejected
       cannot prepare validator 'main': it takes 2 parameters [owner, guardian], but the scenario gives 1; set them with Scenario.parameters
   0 passed, 2 failed
   ```

   Both scenarios fail before the script even runs, and that includes `othersAreRejected`, which expects the
   validator to reject its transaction. Without this check it could pass for the wrong reason: the script
   would fail on the missing parameter, not on the missing signature. A scenario with `expectFailure` only
   proves something when the transaction is otherwise valid, so pair each one with a similar scenario that
   must succeed.

5. **Update the tests.** Supply both parameters, and cover each way the transaction can be signed:

   ```elm title="tests/MainTest.elm"
   module MainTest exposing (bothSign, guardianAloneIsRejected, othersAreRejected, ownerAloneIsRejected)

   import Julc.Data as Data
   import Julc.Ledger as Ledger exposing (PubKeyHash)
   import Scenario exposing (Scenario)

   owner : PubKeyHash
   owner =
       Scenario.key "owner"

   guardian : PubKeyHash
   guardian =
       Scenario.key "guardian"

   transaction : Scenario
   transaction =
       Scenario.spend "main" (Scenario.outRef "main" 0) Scenario.unit
           |> Scenario.parameters [ Data.encode owner, Data.encode guardian ]

   bothSign : Scenario
   bothSign =
       transaction
           |> Scenario.signedBy owner
           |> Scenario.signedBy guardian

   ownerAloneIsRejected : Scenario
   ownerAloneIsRejected =
       transaction
           |> Scenario.signedBy owner
           |> Scenario.expectFailure

   guardianAloneIsRejected : Scenario
   guardianAloneIsRejected =
       transaction
           |> Scenario.signedBy guardian
           |> Scenario.expectFailure

   othersAreRejected : Scenario
   othersAreRejected =
       transaction
           |> Scenario.signedBy (Scenario.key "someone else")
           |> Scenario.expectFailure
   ```

6. **Run the tests again.**

   ```sh
   elci test .
   ```

   ```text
   PASS MainTest.bothSign (cpu 11441262, mem 45132)
   PASS MainTest.ownerAloneIsRejected (cpu 11088065, mem 43199)
   PASS MainTest.guardianAloneIsRejected (cpu 8425738, mem 34154)
   PASS MainTest.othersAreRejected (cpu 8425738, mem 34154)
   4 passed, 0 failed
   ```

   To run only some tests, pass part of their name with `--match`:

   ```sh
   elci test . --match alone
   ```

   ```text
   PASS MainTest.ownerAloneIsRejected (cpu 11088065, mem 43199)
   PASS MainTest.guardianAloneIsRejected (cpu 8425738, mem 34154)
   2 passed, 0 failed
   ```

7. **Build the new script.**

   ```sh
   elci build .
   ```

   ```text
   validator main (spend): checked; 323 FLAT bytes; plutus-v3-pv11-uplc-1.1.0
   ```

   `validator.plutus.json` now lists both parameters: `"params": "owner:PubKeyHash,guardian:PubKeyHash"`.

## Apply the parameters

Before you deploy, you apply the real parameter values. `elci apply` takes each value as Plutus Data in
cardano-cli's JSON format. A `PubKeyHash` is 28 bytes, written as hex. These two keys are placeholders:

```sh
elci apply . --validator main \
  --param 'owner={"bytes": "01000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000"}' \
  --param 'guardian={"bytes": "02000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000"}'
```

```text
validator main: applied 2 parameters; hash 7cf11fa222b171e7a3102db8f51aac3f4815ee8256ed47bde39cc6a6; wrote .../my-contract/build/validators/main/applied.plutus.json
```

`apply` first checks each value against the parameter's type. The applied script has its own hash, which
determines its address on-chain. [Parameterized validators](https://elci-lang.dev/contracts/parameters/) explains the format.

## What you learned

- `elci.toml` decides how functions are deployed: `[validators.<name>]`, handler keys and `parameters`.
- A spend handler receives parameters, datum, redeemer and context, and returns `Bool`.
- `elci check` catches mistakes, including a handler that doesn't match its configuration.
- `elci test` runs transaction scenarios against the exact script that `elci build` writes.

## Next steps

  - [Anatomy of a project](https://elci-lang.dev/start/project-tour/): Every file and directory in an Elci project.
  - [Learn the language](https://elci-lang.dev/learn/basics/): Values, functions and types, with runnable examples.
  - [Validators and purposes](https://elci-lang.dev/contracts/validators/): Handlers for spending, minting, withdrawing and governance.
  - [Transaction scenarios](https://elci-lang.dev/testing/scenarios/): Everything a scenario can describe.

# Anatomy of a project

> What each file and directory in an Elci project is for, from elci.toml and src/ to tests/ and the build outputs.

Source: https://elci-lang.dev/start/project-tour/

This page walks through the files in an Elci project and what each one does, so you know where new code,
tests and configuration belong.

## Two kinds of project

Every project has an `elci.toml` that makes it one of two kinds:

| Kind | Created with | Configured by | Commands |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Validator project | `elci init <dir>` | One or more `[validators.<name>]` tables | `check`, `test`, `build`, `apply` |
| Function project | `elci init <dir> --purpose function` | One `[entrypoint]` table | `check`, `test`, `build`, `eval` |

A **validator project** holds scripts you deploy. A **function project** names one function or value for
`elci eval` to run. It is not a validator, which makes it a good playground for learning the language, and
the [Learn](https://elci-lang.dev/learn/basics/) pages use one. A project can't be both:

```text
elci: ELCI4001: elci.toml mixes [entrypoint] with [validators.*]; use one form
```

## The layout

Here is a validator project with two validators, a shared helper module and a test module, after `elci build`:

- treasury/
  - elci.toml configuration
  - README.md
  - .gitignore contains build/
  - src/ your modules
    - Auth.elm shared helper
    - Badge.elm the badge minting policy
    - Treasury.elm the treasury validator
  - tests/ test modules, never deployed
    - TreasuryTest.elm
  - build/ generated by elci build
    - validators/
      - elci-outputs.json
      - badge/
        - abi.json
        - validator.flat
        - validator.plutus
        - validator.plutus.json
      - treasury/
        - abi.json
        - validator.flat
        - validator.plutus
        - validator.plutus.json

## elci.toml

The configuration for that project:

```toml title="elci.toml"
[project]
source-directories = ["src"]
target = "plutus-v3-pv11-uplc-1.1.0"
julc-version = "0.1.0-pre20-ebaf028-SNAPSHOT"

# The treasury script: holds payouts until a beneficiary claims them.
[validators.treasury]
boundary = "julc-strict-v1"
parameters = ["admin"]
spend = "Treasury.spend"

# A separate script: a minting policy for badges.
[validators.badge]
boundary = "julc-strict-v1"
parameters = ["admin"]
mint = "Badge.mint"

# Julc Java libraries, imported in Elci as `import Julc.Math as Math`.
[java-modules]
"Julc.Math" = "org.julclang.stdlib.lib.MathLib"

[tests]
source-directories = ["tests"]
```

| Section | What it configures |
| --- | --- |
| `[project]` | `source-directories`, the on-chain `target` and the `julc-version` the compiler must match. Optionally `library-jars` for custom Java libraries. |
| `[validators.<name>]` | One deployed script with its own hash: `boundary`, handler keys (`spend`, `mint`, `withdraw`, `certify`, `vote`, `propose`), and optionally `parameters`, `spend-datum` and `expected-abi`. |
| `[entrypoint]` | A function project: `module`, `function` and `purpose = "function"`. |
| `[java-modules]` | Maps an Elm-style module name to a Julc on-chain Java library class. The core modules, such as `Tx` and `Interval`, need no mapping. |
| `[tests]` | Where test modules live. The default is `["tests"]`. |

Validator names use lowercase letters, digits, `-` and `_`, and start with a letter. The name becomes the
directory under `build/validators/`, and tests refer to the validator by that name.

The file uses a strict subset of TOML: section headers, `key = "value"` with quoted strings (no escapes), and
arrays of quoted strings. Full-line `#` comments are fine, but a comment at the end of a line is not:

```text
elci: ELCI4001: Expected a quoted string without escapes: "Main.spend" # the handler
```

Unknown or duplicate keys are errors too, which catches typos:

```text
elci: ELCI4001: Unknown configuration key: [validators.main] boundry
```

[elci.toml reference](https://elci-lang.dev/reference/configuration/) lists every key.

## src/: your modules

Each module lives at the path that matches its name under a source directory. `Treasury` is
`src/Treasury.elm`, and `Market.Pricing` would be `src/Market/Pricing.elm`. Handler keys in `elci.toml`
point at exposed functions as `Module.function`.

Put code shared by several validators in its own module, such as `Auth.elm` above, and import it where you
need it. Each validator only includes the code its handlers use.

:::note
`elci check` compiles the modules that your handlers (or your entrypoint) import, directly or indirectly. A
module that nothing imports isn't compiled, so its errors don't show up until you use it.
:::

To share Elci code between projects, keep it in its own directory and add that directory to
`source-directories`. See [Modules and imports](https://elci-lang.dev/learn/modules/).

## tests/: test modules

Test modules live under `tests/` and are compiled only by `elci test`. They are never part of `check`,
`build` or the published scripts. A test is an exposed, zero-argument declaration of type `Bool`,
`Expectation`, `Scenario` or `Property` (or an exposed function that returns a `Property`). Other declarations
are helpers:

```text
PASS TreasuryTest.beneficiaryReleases (cpu 11698810, mem 46679)
PASS TreasuryTest.strangerCannotRelease (cpu 12077243, mem 48611)
2 passed, 0 failed
```

See [Unit tests](https://elci-lang.dev/testing/unit-tests/) for the details.

## build/: generated files

`elci build` writes everything under `build/`, and `.gitignore` keeps it out of version control. For each
validator it writes a directory under `build/validators/`:

| File | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `validator.plutus.json` | Julc's validator artifact (`type`, `purpose`, `cborHex`, `hash`, `params`, `sizeBytes`), which Cardano Client Lib applications load |
| `validator.plutus` | A Plutus V3 text envelope |
| `validator.flat` | The script's UPLC in FLAT encoding |
| `abi.json` | Parameters, handlers, and how every datum and redeemer type is encoded |
| `applied.plutus.json` | Written by `elci apply`: the script with its parameters applied, and its hash |

`build/validators/elci-outputs.json` records which files Elci wrote. When you remove a validator from
`elci.toml`, the next full build deletes that validator's files. Any other files in those directories are
left alone. `elci build . --validator treasury` builds only the named validator and removes nothing else.
Every selected validator compiles before anything is written, so a failed build leaves the previous outputs
untouched.

A function project writes `build/validator.flat`, `build/validator.plutus` and `build/abi.json`. It writes no
`validator.plutus.json`, because a function isn't deployed.

:::tip
To guard against accidental changes to your on-chain data format, keep a copy of a validator's `abi.json`
outside `build/` and point `expected-abi` at it. The build then fails if the encoding drifts. See
[Build and deploy](https://elci-lang.dev/contracts/build-and-deploy/).
:::

## Where things go

| You want to… | Put it in |
| --- | --- |
| Write a validator | A module in `src/`, plus a handler key in a `[validators.<name>]` table |
| Share helpers between validators | Another module in `src/`, imported where needed |
| Reuse Elci code across projects | A separate source directory, added to `source-directories` |
| Use a Julc Java library | A `[java-modules]` entry, then `import` it |
| Use your own Java library | `library-jars` in `[project]`, plus a `[java-modules]` entry |
| Test a validator or function | A module under `tests/` |
| Pin the on-chain data format | A committed copy of `abi.json`, referenced by `expected-abi` |
| Experiment with the language | A separate function project (`elci init playground --purpose function`) |

---

# Build with AI

> Point Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot or any coding agent at Elci's AI resources, and let it write, check and test Elci contracts.

Source: https://elci-lang.dev/ai/

Elci is new, so AI models have seen little or none of it. Without context, an agent writes code that looks
like Elm but doesn't compile in Elci. Typical mistakes are `Float`, `Set`, `Debug.log`, `String.length`,
`Html` and helpers Elci doesn't have. The resources on this page give an agent the exact language, APIs and workflow in
one read. The `elci` CLI then lets it check its own work.

## The short version

Install Elci first ([Installation](https://elci-lang.dev/start/installation/)). Then start your agent with this prompt:

```text wrap
You are writing Cardano smart contracts in Elci, an Elm-syntax language that compiles to Plutus V3.
Before writing any code, read https://elci-lang.dev/ai/starter-pack.md and follow it strictly.
Use https://elci-lang.dev/llms.txt to find other pages when you need them.
After every change, run `elci check .` and `elci test .` and fix every ELCI error before continuing.
Only use functions and modules that the starter pack or https://elci-lang.dev/ai/catalog.json lists.
```

## Resources for agents

| Resource | What it is | Use it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Starter pack](https://elci-lang.dev/ai/starter-pack.md) | The language subset, encodings, handler signatures, APIs, error fixes and complete examples, written for agents | Read it first, every session |
| [Agent instructions](https://elci-lang.dev/ai/agent-instructions.md) | The must-follow rules in about a hundred lines | Save it as `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md` or a rules file |
| [llms.txt](https://elci-lang.dev/llms.txt) | An index of every page, following the [llms.txt](https://llmstxt.org) convention | To find the right page |
| [llms-full.txt](https://elci-lang.dev/llms-full.txt) | All documentation in one Markdown file | Attach it for long sessions |
| `/ai/pages/…` | Each page as plain Markdown, such as [transaction scenarios](https://elci-lang.dev/ai/pages/testing/scenarios.md) | To read one topic |
| [catalog.json](https://elci-lang.dev/ai/catalog.json) | Signatures of the bundled modules, compiler-provided modules and Java libraries | To check that a function exists |
| [diagnostics.json](https://elci-lang.dev/ai/diagnostics.json) | Every ELCI error code and its meaning, the error format and the `--report=json` fields | To explain a compiler error |
| [examples.json](https://elci-lang.dev/ai/examples.json) | The example projects, with every source file | To copy a working pattern |
| [manifest.json](https://elci-lang.dev/ai/manifest.json) | The Elci and Julc versions the docs describe, and checksums of all of the above | To match your installed version |

The pages and the catalog are generated from the same sources as this site. Every code sample in them was
compiled with the Elci version named in the manifest. Check that `elci --version` reports the same version.

## Set up your agent

Save the agent instructions where your tool reads them. They point the agent to the starter pack and the
rest of these resources.

**Claude Code**

Claude Code reads `CLAUDE.md` at the start of every session. An `@path` line in it imports another file, so
the whole starter pack is loaded too:

```sh
curl -o CLAUDE.md https://elci-lang.dev/ai/agent-instructions.md
curl --create-dirs -o docs/elci/starter-pack.md https://elci-lang.dev/ai/starter-pack.md
echo '@docs/elci/starter-pack.md' >> CLAUDE.md
```

**Codex and AGENTS.md**

Codex and other tools that follow the `AGENTS.md` convention read it from the project root:

```sh
curl -o AGENTS.md https://elci-lang.dev/ai/agent-instructions.md
```

**Cursor**

Cursor applies the rules in `.cursor/rules/`. This rule is active for Elci sources and `elci.toml`:

```sh
mkdir -p .cursor/rules
{ printf -- '---\ndescription: Elci smart contract rules\nglobs: ["**/*.elm", "elci.toml"]\nalwaysApply: true\n---\n\n'
  curl -s https://elci-lang.dev/ai/agent-instructions.md; } > .cursor/rules/elci.mdc
```

**GitHub Copilot**

Copilot reads repository instructions from `.github/copilot-instructions.md`:

```sh
mkdir -p .github
curl -o .github/copilot-instructions.md https://elci-lang.dev/ai/agent-instructions.md
```

**Chat on the web**

For ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini in the browser, paste [the prompt above](#the-short-version). For a longer
project, attach [llms-full.txt](https://elci-lang.dev/llms-full.txt) or the [starter pack](https://elci-lang.dev/ai/starter-pack.md) as a file.
A chat can't run the compiler, so paste `elci check` and `elci test` output back into the conversation.

## Let the agent check its own work

The CLI is the agent's feedback loop. Every command is non-interactive and exits with status 1 on failure.
Errors are printed as `path:line:column: ELCIxxxx: message`, followed by the source line and any hints
with the likely fix. A run reports every error it finds, one per top-level declaration, so the agent can fix
several at once. With `--report=json`, `check`, `build`, `eval` and `test` print each error as one JSON
object on its own line instead. `elci explain <code>` prints the long-form explanation of a code, with an
example and its fix.

| Command | What the agent uses it for |
| --- | --- |
| `elci check .` | Type-check and compile every validator, without writing files |
| `elci test .` | Run unit tests, transaction scenarios and property tests. `--match` selects tests, and `--seed` reproduces a property run |
| `elci eval .` | Evaluate a function project's value and print it with its cost; handy for checking an expression |
| `elci build .` | Write the deployable artifacts once everything passes |
| `elci explain <code>` | Explain an error code, such as `ELCI2002`, with an example and its fix |
| `elci --help` | Every command and option |

A loop that works well:

1. Write the types (datum, redeemer, parameters) and the handler signature, then run `elci check .`.
2. Write the logic, and run `elci check .` until it passes.
3. Add scenarios for every way the transaction should succeed or fail, plus a property, and run `elci test .`.
4. When a test fails, read the reason and the counterexample, then fix the code rather than the test.
5. Run `elci build .`.

The native `elci` binary starts in milliseconds, which suits agents that run the compiler many times.

## Prompts to try

```text wrap
Create an Elci validator in this project for a time-locked escrow: the datum holds the
beneficiary and a deadline; the beneficiary may claim at or after the deadline; the depositor
may reclaim before it. Add scenarios for every case and a property over the validity start.
Follow the starter pack, and run elci check and elci test until everything passes.
```

```text wrap
Explain this Elci error and fix the code, using https://elci-lang.dev/ai/diagnostics.json and
the starter pack: <paste the elci output>
```

```text wrap
Add property tests to tests/ for the validator in src/, covering every branch of the redeemer.
Run elci test --seed 1 and show me any counterexample you find before changing code.
```

## What to review yourself

Agents write plausible code quickly. On-chain mistakes are costly, so review what matters before
deploying:

- **Authorization:** every path that releases funds or mints checks the right signatures, inputs or
  validity range.
- **Types at the boundary:** the datum, redeemer and parameter types. `abi.json` records exactly how they are
  encoded.
- **What leaves the script:** outputs, amounts and minted tokens, not only the redeemer's claims.
- **Tests that prove something:** every `expectFailure` scenario has a matching success scenario, so a
  failure isn't caused by something unrelated.

Elci is a development preview. Tests are not a security audit.

There is no Elci MCP server yet. The CLI is the tool interface, and every agent that can run shell
commands can use it.

## Next steps

  - [AI starter pack](https://elci-lang.dev/ai/starter-pack/): What an agent needs to write correct Elci.
  - [Agent instructions](https://elci-lang.dev/ai/agent-instructions/): The compact rules file for your project.
  - [Your first validator](https://elci-lang.dev/start/first-validator/): The hands-on tutorial, for you or your agent.
  - [Transaction scenarios](https://elci-lang.dev/testing/scenarios/): How to test validators against full transactions.

# Elci AI starter pack

> Everything an AI agent needs to write correct Elci on the first try. Ingest this page before generating Elci code.

Source: https://elci-lang.dev/ai/starter-pack/

> **Read this entire page before generating any Elci code.** It states the Elci subset of Elm, the
> project format, the on-chain rules and the mistakes agents make most often. Every rule, signature
> and message here was checked with the Elci CLI (`elci 0.1.0-dev / julc 0.1.0-pre20-ebaf028-SNAPSHOT`).

This page is optimized for AI ingestion, not for humans. For the tutorial, see
[your first validator](https://elci-lang.dev/start/first-validator/). Sections are numbered so you can cite them.

---

## 1. What Elci is, and what it is not

- **Elci** compiles `.elm` source written in an **Elm 0.19 syntax subset** into **Plutus V3** scripts
  for Cardano. It lowers to typed PIR and uses Julc's backend (validator wrapper, UPLC optimizer,
  evaluator). The only target is `plutus-v3-pv11-uplc-1.1.0`.
- **On-chain only.** Elci code is validator logic. Building transactions is done off-chain with other
  tools (for example Cardano Client Lib, reading `validator.plutus.json`).
- **Not browser Elm.** There is no `Html`, `Browser`, `Cmd`, `Sub`, `port`, JSON decoders or runtime.
- **No Elm packages.** `elm.json` is not used. There is no package manager.
- **Elm's core library, partly.** `Basics`, `List`, `Maybe`, `Result`, `Tuple`, `String` and `Debug` are
  imported by default, as in Elm, with Elm's names and argument orders, but `String` has only five
  functions and `Debug` only `trace`. `Dict` exists with Elm's API (`import Dict exposing (Dict)`); `Set`,
  `Char` and `Float` **do not exist** (section 3.3). A `Value` module (`import Value exposing (Value)`)
  handles the ledger's multi-asset values (section 7). `Tx` and `Interval` answer questions about the
  transaction and its validity range (section 8); prefer them to hand-written list walks and to Julc's
  `ContextsLib` and `IntervalLib`.
- **Strict, not lazy.** Every `let` value and every function argument is evaluated (section 4).
- **Configuration decides deployment.** Handlers are ordinary functions; `elci.toml` says which
  function serves which ledger purpose (section 2).
- **Development preview.** Not production-ready. No CIP-57 blueprints, no language server.

## 2. Project layout and `elci.toml`

`elci init my-project` creates a validator project; `elci init my-project --purpose function` creates a
function project for `elci eval`.

```text
my-project/
  elci.toml            project configuration (strict TOML subset)
  src/Main.elm         source modules; module A.B lives at src/A/B.elm
  tests/MainTest.elm   test modules (validator projects only)
  build/               outputs of elci build (git-ignored)
```

A complete `elci.toml` using every validator setting:

```toml title="elci.toml"
# Settings for the whole project.
[project]
source-directories = ["src", "lib"]
target = "plutus-v3-pv11-uplc-1.1.0"
julc-version = "0.1.0-pre20-ebaf028-SNAPSHOT"
library-jars = ["libs/pricing.jar"]

# One script with two purposes and a deployment parameter.
[validators.treasury]
boundary = "julc-strict-v1"
parameters = ["admin"]
spend = "Treasury.spend"
withdraw = "Treasury.withdraw"
spend-datum = "optional"
expected-abi = "abi/treasury.json"

# A second, independent script.
[validators.badge]
boundary = "julc-strict-v1"
parameters = ["admin"]
mint = "Badge.mint"

[java-modules]
"Julc.Math" = "org.julclang.stdlib.lib.MathLib"
"Acme.Pricing" = "acme.Pricing"

[tests]
source-directories = ["spec"]
```

A function project instead has:

```toml title="elci.toml"
[project]
source-directories = ["src"]
target = "plutus-v3-pv11-uplc-1.1.0"
julc-version = "0.1.0-pre20-ebaf028-SNAPSHOT"

[entrypoint]
module = "Main"
function = "main"
purpose = "function"
```

### 2.1 Rules

1. `[project]` requires `source-directories`, `target = "plutus-v3-pv11-uplc-1.1.0"` and
   `julc-version = "0.1.0-pre20-ebaf028-SNAPSHOT"` (must equal the compiler's pinned version; `elci --version` prints it).
   Optional: `library-jars`; `expected-abi` only in function projects.
2. A project has **either** one or more `[validators.<name>]` tables **or** one `[entrypoint]`, never both.
3. `[validators.<name>]`: name is 1–64 chars of `a-z`, `0-9`, `-`, `_`, starting with a letter. `boundary =
   "julc-strict-v1"` is required. At least one handler key: `spend`, `mint`, `withdraw`, `certify`,
   `vote`, `propose`, each `"Module.function"` naming an **exposed** function. One table = one script = one hash.
4. `parameters = ["a", "b"]`: deployment parameters in application order; names match `[a-z][A-Za-z0-9_]*`.
   Every handler of the table receives all of them as leading arguments, with the same types.
5. `spend-datum = "required"` (default), `"optional"` or `"absent"`; requires a `spend` handler.
6. `expected-abi = "path"`: `check`, `build` and `apply` fail if the ABI (`abi.json`) differs.
7. `[java-modules]`: `"Module.Name" = "fully.qualified.Class"`. You choose the module name. `Julc.TypedMap`
   and `Julc.TypedArray` are reserved, and so are the core module names (`Basics`, `List`, `Maybe`,
   `Result`, `String`, `Tuple`, `Map`, `Dict`, `Array`, `Set`, `Value`, `Interval`, `Tx`, `Elci`) and names
   starting with `Elci.`.
8. `[tests]`: `source-directories`, default `["tests"]`.
9. TOML subset: one `key = value` per line; values are quoted strings without escapes or single-line
   arrays of quoted strings; comments are whole lines starting with `#` (no trailing comments); unknown
   tables and keys are errors.

## 3. The language subset

### 3.1 Allowed

- Modules: `module A.B exposing (f, T, U(..))` or `exposing (..)`; `import M as N exposing (x, T(..))`.
  Imports must be acyclic. Every module has Elm's default imports (section 8). Own declarations shadow
  imports; a name two imports expose is ambiguous where used, except that a name listed in `exposing`
  beats a default import.
- **Every top-level declaration needs a type signature.** Local (`let`) definitions may have one.
- Functions, lambdas `\a b -> ...`, currying, partial application, `|>`, `<|`, `>>`, `<<`. Operators as
  functions: `(+)`, `(::)`, `(<)`, as in `List.foldl (+) 0 xs`. `^` is integer power.
- Rank-1 generics (`a -> a`), specialized per concrete use. Local helpers may be used at several types.
  Elm's constrained variables: a signature variable compared with `<`/`compare` must be named
  `comparable…`, one appended with `++` `appendable…`, both `compappend…`.
- Types nothing determines need no annotation (`[] == []`, `List.length []`, `Data.encode Nothing`),
  except where a value is created: `Data.decode` and generic Java functions (`ELCI3001`).
- Self-recursion and mutually recursive functions (top-level or local).
- Types: `Int` (arbitrary precision), `Bool`, `String`, `()`, `Bytes`, `Data`, `List a`, `Maybe a`,
  `Result error value`, `Order`, `Dict k v` (comparable keys), `Map k v`, `Array a`, `Value`, tuples of 2
  or 3, closed records, custom types (generic, recursive).
- `type alias R = { x : Int }` (also a constructor `R 1`); `type T a = A a | B`.
- Records: `{ x = 1 }`, `r.x`, `{ r | x = 2 }`, destructuring `{ x, y }` in parameters and `let`.
  Accessor functions as in Elm: `.x` is `\r -> r.x`, so `List.map .amount payouts` works. A field of a
  qualified value: `Config.settings.fee`. Write qualified names without spaces.
- `case` with nested patterns: constructors, `[]`, `[ a, b ]`, `a :: rest`, tuples, record fields, `as`,
  `_`, `()`, `True`/`False`, Int and String literals. Exhaustive and no unreachable branches.
- `if c then a else b` (else required), `let ... in`, `++` on `String` and `List`, `::`.
- `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, `compare`, `min`, `max`, `List.sort` on **comparable** types: `Int`, `String`
  (UTF-8 byte order), `Bytes`, ledger hashes (`PubKeyHash`, `ScriptHash`, `PolicyId`, `TokenName`,
  `TxId`, …), and lists and tuples of these.
- Comments `--`, `{- nested {- ok -} -}`, doc comments `{-| -}`.

### 3.2 Rejected by the compiler

| Construct | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `Float`, `1.5`, `/` | `ELCI1001`/`ELCI2001`; use scaled `Int` and `//` |
| `number` in a signature | `ELCI2003`; write `Int` |
| `a > b` or `a ++ b` on a signature variable not named `comparable…`/`appendable…` | `ELCI2003`; rename it |
| Extensible records `{ r \| x : Int }` | `ELCI1002` |
| Refutable patterns in function or lambda arguments (`f (x :: _) = ...`) | `ELCI1002`; use `case` |
| Chained comparisons `a < b < c` | `ELCI1002`; use `a < b && b < c` |
| Tuples of 4 or more | `ELCI1002` |
| `(/)` | `ELCI2001`; use `(//)` |
| Char literals `'a'`, `%`, hex `0xFF`, `1_000` | `ELCI1001` |
| `port module`, `import Html` | `ELCI1002` / `ELCI2101` |
| Polymorphic recursion, recursive values (`a = b + 1`, `b = a + 1`) | `ELCI2002` / `ELCI2008` |
| `==` on functions, `Map`, `Array`, `TxOut`, `TxInInfo`, `TxInfo` (`Data` and `Value` do have `==`) | `ELCI2003` |
| `<`, `compare`, `List.sort` on `Bool`, records, custom types, `Maybe`, `Dict`, `Map`, `Value`, `Data`, `TxOutRef` | `ELCI2003`; use `List.sortBy` with a key; compare values with `Value.geq` |
| `Dict` keys that are not comparable (`Dict.get` on a `Dict Credential Int`; a `Dict Bool Int` in a datum or `Data.decode`) | `ELCI2003`; use a `Map` |
| A Java library generic at a type containing a `Dict` | `ELCI3003`; pass a `Map` or `List`, then `Dict.fromList` |
| A Java export whose result can hold a `Value` (`ValuesLib.add`, `ValuesLib.singleton`, a Java record with a `Value` field, …); `ContextsLib` and `OutputLib` are exempt | `ELCI2105`; use the core `Value` module |
| A Java library generic at a type holding a `Value` (`Lists.filter values f`) | `ELCI3003`; use `List` and the `Value` module |
| `Value` in a datum, redeemer or parameter type | `ELCI2013`; store `List ( PolicyId, TokenName, Int )`, rebuild with `Value.fromList` |
| Module named `Basics`, `List`, `Maybe`, `Result`, `String`, `Tuple`, `Map`, `Dict`, `Array`, `Set`, `Value`, `Interval`, `Tx`, `Elci` or `Elci.*`; alias named after a default import (`Basics`, `List`, `Maybe`, `Result`, `String`, `Tuple`, `Debug`) | `ELCI2104` |
| Constructors named `Just`, `Nothing`, `True`, `False`; types named `Int`, `Bool`, `String`, `Bytes`, `Data`, `List`, `Maybe`, `Dict`, `Map`, `Array`, `Float` | `ELCI2011` |
| `f <\| x \|> g`, `f << g >> h` (opposite associativity mixed) | `ELCI1002`; add parentheses |
| `Tuple a b`, `Unit` as type names | `ELCI2012`; write `( a, b )`, `()` |

### 3.3 Elm idioms that do NOT exist in Elci, and what to write instead

| Elm | Elci |
| --- | --- |
| `String.length s` | `Bytes.length (Bytes.fromString s)` (UTF-8 byte count) |
| `String.toInt`, `split`, `slice`, `toUpper` and other `String.*` | none; keep numbers as `Int` and bytes as `Bytes`. `String` has only `fromInt`, `isEmpty`, `append`, `concat`, `join` |
| `String.fromFloat`, `toFloat`, `round`, `sqrt`, `pi` | none; no `Float`: use scaled `Int` |
| `Set` | `Dict k Bool` or a `List` (`Dict k ()` is rejected: `()` has no Data encoding) |
| `Char`, `'a'` | none |
| `List.map4`, `Maybe.map4`, `Result.map5`, … | nest `map3`, or `case` |
| `Debug.log`, `Debug.toString`, `Debug.todo` | `Debug.trace : String -> a -> a`; `String.fromInt` for numbers |
| `Bytes.lessThan` (removed) | `a < b` |

Everything else in Elm's `Basics`, `List`, `Maybe`, `Result`, `Tuple` exists with Elm's signature
(section 8). This program uses them; it compiles and runs:

```elm title="src/Main.elm"
module Main exposing (main)

type alias Payout =
    { beneficiary : String
    , amount : Int
    }

payouts : List Payout
payouts =
    [ Payout "carol" 30, Payout "alice" 50, Payout "bob" 30 ]

main : ( ( Int, Maybe Int, List String ), ( String, Int, Result String Int ) )
main =
    ( ( List.sum (List.map (\p -> p.amount) payouts)
      , List.maximum (List.map (\p -> p.amount) payouts)
      , List.map (\p -> p.beneficiary) (List.sortBy (\p -> p.amount) payouts)
      )
    , ( String.join ", " (List.map (\p -> p.beneficiary ++ "=" ++ String.fromInt p.amount) payouts)
      , Maybe.withDefault 0 (List.head (List.range 5 9))
      , Result.fromMaybe "no payouts" (Maybe.map (\p -> p.amount) (List.head payouts))
      )
    )
```

```text
$ elci eval
( ( 110, Just 50, ["carol", "bob", "alice"] ), ( "carol=30, alice=50, bob=30", 5, Ok 30 ) )
cpu 65205046, mem 276517
```

## 4. Evaluation rules

1. **Strict.** Every `let` binding is evaluated before the body, even if unused. An unused
   `let bad = 10 // 0` fails the script.
2. **Selective forms only:** `if`, `case`, `&&`, `||` evaluate just the taken branch/operand. Put cheap,
   likely-false checks first **inline**; a check bound in `let` is always paid for.
3. **Order:** function, then arguments left to right; `let` bindings in dependency order, ties in source
   order; record fields, list and tuple elements in source order; record update: base, then new fields.
   Arguments are always evaluated: `Maybe.withDefault expensive m` computes `expensive` even for a
   `Just`, and `(&&) a b` as a function evaluates `b`. Use `case` or the `&&` operator to skip work.
4. **Top-level values** (zero-argument declarations) reachable from any handler run once per script
   execution **before** purpose dispatch, so every purpose pays for them. Make expensive ones functions
   (`limit : () -> Int`).
5. **Negation** follows Elm 0.19: `f -1` passes `-1`; `scale -x 10` passes `-x`; `x - 1` and `x-1`
   subtract; `x -1` is an application of `x`.
6. **Integers:** `//` truncates towards zero (`-7 // 2` is `-3`). `modBy d v` has the divisor's sign
   (`modBy 3 -7` is `2`); `remainderBy d v` has the value's sign (`remainderBy 3 -7` is `-1`). Division by
   zero fails the script.
7. **Failure:** a runtime failure (division by zero, out-of-range byte, failed decode) or a handler result
   of `False` rejects the transaction. There are no exceptions to catch.
8. **Equality** (`==`, `/=`): Int, Bool, String, `()`, Bytes, ledger hashes of the same type, `Value`
   (exact), `Data` (exact structure), lists, tuples, records, `Maybe`, `Dict` (same bindings) and custom
   types of these; imported types with approved equality. Not `Map`, functions, `Array`, `TxOut`,
   `TxInInfo`, `TxInfo`. Both operands are evaluated once, left to right.
9. **Ordering** (`<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, `compare`, `min`, `max`, `List.sort`): Int numerically; String by
   UTF-8 bytes (`"Zebra" < "apple"`); Bytes and ledger hashes lexicographically by unsigned byte, a
   proper prefix first (`#ff` > `#0001`); lists lexicographically; tuples by component. Every order agrees
   with `==`.
10. **Integer power:** `2 ^ 10` is `1024`; `^` binds tighter than `*` and groups right; a negative
    exponent fails the script.

## 5. Data encoding and `Julc.Data`

Datums, redeemers and parameters cross the script boundary as Plutus Data and are **decoded strictly**
(tags, arity, field kinds checked; malformed data fails the script, never `Nothing`).

| Elci value | Plutus Data |
| --- | --- |
| `Int` | integer |
| `Bytes`, ledger hashes | byte string |
| `String` | byte string (UTF-8) |
| `Bool` | `False` = constructor 0, `True` = constructor 1, no fields |
| `()` | constructor 0, no fields (as datum/redeemer; `Julc.Data.encode ()` is rejected) |
| record | constructor 0, fields **sorted by field name** (not declaration order) |
| tuple | constructor 0, fields in position order |
| custom type | constructor tag = variant's declaration position from 0, fields in order |
| `Maybe a` | `Nothing` = constructor 0; `Just x` = constructor 1 `[x]` |
| `Result e a` | `Ok x` = constructor 0 `[x]`; `Err e` = constructor 1 `[e]` (the **reverse** of PlutusTx `Either`) |
| `Order` | `LT`, `EQ`, `GT` = constructors 0, 1, 2 |
| `JulcOptional a` (Java `Optional`) | `Some x` = constructor 0 `[x]`; `None` = constructor 1 |
| `List a` / `Map k v` | list / map (in the map's order) |
| `Dict k v` | map with **strictly ascending keys**; unsorted or repeated keys fail to decode (datum, redeemer, parameter, `Data.decode`) |
| `Array a`, functions | **no encoding**; cannot be stored in data (`ELCI2013`) |

```elm
type Action
    = Buy Int
    | Cancel

type alias Payout =
    { beneficiary : Int, amount : Int }

main : List Data
main =
    [ Data.encode (Just 5)
    , Data.encode Cancel
    , Data.encode (Buy 3)
    , Data.encode { beneficiary = 1, amount = 2 }
    , Data.encode ( 1, True )
    , Data.encode [ 1, 2 ]
    , Data.encode (Data.toOptional (Just 5))
    , Data.encode "hi"
    ]
```

```text
$ elci eval
[Constr 1 [5], Constr 1, Constr 0 [3], Constr 0 [2, 1], Constr 0 [1, Constr 1], [1, 2], Constr 0 [5], #6869]
cpu 5878521, mem 25242
```

`Julc.Data` (`import Julc.Data as Data`): `decode : Data -> a`, `encode : a -> Data`,
`fromOptional : JulcOptional a -> Maybe a`, `toOptional : Maybe a -> JulcOptional a`. The decoded type
must be known where `decode` is used; annotate otherwise
(`ELCI3001: Cannot determine the type converted by Julc.Data.decode; add a type annotation`).
`==` on `Data` compares structure exactly, so a datum check needs no decoding:
`Tx.inlineDatum out == Just (Data.encode expected)`. Elci's encodings are deterministic, except that a
`Map`'s encoding follows its insertion order: `Data.encode` of two maps with the same bindings may differ,
so compare their sorted `toList` or use a `Dict`. Tests build datums and redeemers with `Data.encode`.

## 6. Handler signatures

`parameters` come first, in the order listed in `elci.toml`. The last argument is always `ScriptContext`
(`import Julc.Ledger exposing (ScriptContext)`). The result is `Bool`. Handlers must be exposed and have
concrete types.

| Handler key | Required type |
| --- | --- |
| `spend` | `params -> datum -> redeemer -> ScriptContext -> Bool` |
| `spend` + `spend-datum = "optional"` | `params -> Maybe datum -> redeemer -> ScriptContext -> Bool` |
| `spend` + `spend-datum = "absent"` | `params -> redeemer -> ScriptContext -> Bool` |
| `mint`, `withdraw`, `certify`, `vote`, `propose` | `params -> redeemer -> ScriptContext -> Bool` |

- Datum, redeemer and parameter types need a strict Data boundary: your records and custom types, `Int`,
  `Bool`, `String`, `Bytes`, `()`, tuples, lists, `Dict`, `Map`, `Maybe`, and ledger types such as
  `PubKeyHash`, `TxOutRef`, `Credential`, `PolicyId`, `TokenName`. Not: functions, `Array`, `ScriptContext`,
  `TxOut`, `TxInfo`, `Value` (for an amount of tokens, store `List ( PolicyId, TokenName, Int )` and call
  `Value.fromList`).
- Use `()` for an unused redeemer or datum. Only the selected handler's datum and redeemer are decoded.
- A validator always checks the purpose; purposes without a handler are rejected.
- Parameters are decoded but **not validated on-chain**; `elci apply` validates them off-chain. Exception:
  the key order of a `Dict` (in a datum, redeemer or parameter) is checked on every run.

## 7. The script context and ledger types

`import Julc.Ledger exposing (ScriptContext, PubKeyHash)` exposes types. To match or build a sum type's
constructors unqualified, expose them with `(..)`: `Credential(..)`, `ScriptInfo(..)`, `OutputDatum(..)`,
`IntervalBoundType(..)`. `exposing (..)` exposes types only, not constructors (a `PubKeyCredential`
pattern then fails with `ELCI2001`). Fields are read with `.field`.

| Expression | Type |
| --- | --- |
| `ctx.txInfo` | `TxInfo` |
| `ctx.scriptInfo` | `ScriptInfo` |
| `ctx.redeemer` | `Data` (raw; the handler already gets it decoded) |
| `tx.inputs`, `tx.referenceInputs` | `List TxInInfo` |
| `tx.outputs` | `List TxOut` |
| `tx.fee` | `Int` (lovelace) |
| `tx.mint` | `Value` |
| `tx.certificates` | `List TxCert` |
| `tx.withdrawals` | `Map Credential Int` |
| `tx.validRange` | `Interval` (POSIX milliseconds) |
| `tx.signatories` | `List PubKeyHash` |
| `tx.redeemers` | `Map ScriptPurpose Data` |
| `tx.datums` | `Map DatumHash Data` |
| `tx.id` | `TxId` |
| `tx.proposalProcedures` | `List ProposalProcedure` |
| `input.outRef` / `input.resolved` | `TxOutRef` / `TxOut` |
| `out.address`, `out.value`, `out.datum`, `out.referenceScript` | `Address`, `Value`, `OutputDatum`, `JulcOptional ScriptHash` |
| `ref.txId`, `ref.index` | `TxId`, `Int` |
| `addr.credential`, `addr.stakingCredential` | `Credential`, `JulcOptional StakingCredential` |
| `range.from`, `range.to` | `IntervalBound` |
| `bound.boundType`, `bound.isInclusive` | `IntervalBoundType`, `Bool` |
| `pkh.hash`, `txId.hash`, `policy.hash`, `token.hash` (a `TokenName`; it has no `.name`), `scriptHash.hash` | `Bytes` |

Sum types: `Credential = PubKeyCredential PubKeyHash | ScriptCredential ScriptHash`;
`OutputDatum = NoOutputDatum | OutputDatumHash DatumHash | OutputDatumInline Data`;
`IntervalBoundType = NegInf | Finite Int | PosInf`;
`ScriptInfo = MintingScript PolicyId | SpendingScript TxOutRef (JulcOptional Data) | RewardingScript Credential | CertifyingScript Int TxCert | VotingScript Voter | ProposingScript Int ProposalProcedure`.

```elm
keyOf : Credential -> Bytes
keyOf cred =
    case cred of
        PubKeyCredential pkh ->
            pkh.hash

        ScriptCredential sh ->
            sh.hash
```

For datums, use `Tx.inlineDatum out` or `Tx.datumOf out ctx` (section 8) rather than matching
`OutputDatum` yourself.

Rules:

- `PubKeyHash`, `ScriptHash`, `PolicyId`, `TokenName`, `TxId`, `DatumHash` are **distinct from `Bytes`**;
  compare like with like, or use `.hash`. `key == Bytes.fromString "k"` with `key : PubKeyHash` is
  `` ELCI2002: The two sides of == have different types: the left is `PubKeyHash`, but the right is `Bytes` ``,
  with a hint to wrap the bytes with the constructor. `token.name` is
  `ELCI2010: Unknown field 'name' of TokenName`; write `token.hash`.
- Signature check: `Tx.signedBy key ctx`.
- Ledger hashes order like bytes: `List.sort` sorts a `List PubKeyHash`. `TxOutRef` and other ledger
  records are not comparable.
- Construct ledger values qualified: `import Julc.Ledger as Ledger` then `Ledger.PubKeyHash bytes`,
  `Ledger.TxOutRef (Ledger.TxId bytes) 0`.
- `Value` (`out.value`, `tx.mint`) is the core `Value` type: read it with the `Value` module (section 8),
  `Value.lovelaceOf value`, `Value.quantityOf policy tokenName value`. Build asset ids with
  `import Julc.Ledger exposing (PolicyId(..), TokenName(..))`: `PolicyId bytes`, `TokenName (Bytes.fromString "BADGE")`.
  Ada is `PolicyId Bytes.empty` with `TokenName Bytes.empty`; use `Value.lovelace` and `Value.lovelaceOf`.
- Every `Value` is canonical (policies and token names ascending, no zero quantity), so `==` on values is
  exact. `TxOut`, `TxInInfo` and `TxInfo`, which contain a `Value`, have no equality. A `Value` cannot
  cross the boundary yet. In `tx.mint`, burns are negative quantities.
- `JulcOptional` has no equality; convert with `Data.fromOptional`.

## 8. Core modules and test library (exact signatures)

Every source and test module implicitly has, as in Elm:

```elm
import Basics exposing (..)
import List
import Maybe exposing (Maybe(..))
import Result exposing (Result(..))
import String
import Tuple
import Debug
```

`Bytes`, `Dict`, `Map`, `Array`, `Value`, `Interval`, `Tx` and `Julc.Data` need explicit imports. Using one without its import is
`` ELCI2104: Bytes.fromString needs the Bytes module; add `import Bytes` ``. Machine-readable signatures of
every module are in `/ai/catalog.json`.

**Basics** (unqualified everywhere):

```text
negate : Int -> Int
abs : Int -> Int
min : comparable -> comparable -> comparable
max : comparable -> comparable -> comparable
clamp : Int -> Int -> Int -> Int                -- clamp low high x
compare : comparable -> comparable -> Order     -- type Order = LT | EQ | GT
identity : a -> a
always : a -> b -> a
not : Bool -> Bool
xor : Bool -> Bool -> Bool
modBy : Int -> Int -> Int                        -- modBy divisor value; divisor's sign
remainderBy : Int -> Int -> Int                  -- value's sign
(^) : Int -> Int -> Int                          -- negative exponent fails
```

Built-in constructors: `Just`, `Nothing`, `True`, `False`. Every binary operator is also a function:
`(+)`, `(::)`, `(<)`, `(++)`.

**List** (element first, accumulator second in folds; `map2`/`map3` stop at the shortest list; sorts are
stable):

```text
singleton : a -> List a
repeat : Int -> a -> List a                      -- [] when n <= 0
range : Int -> Int -> List Int                   -- range 1 3 == [ 1, 2, 3 ]; range 5 1 == []
map : (a -> b) -> List a -> List b
indexedMap : (Int -> a -> b) -> List a -> List b
filter : (a -> Bool) -> List a -> List a
filterMap : (a -> Maybe b) -> List a -> List b
foldl : (a -> b -> b) -> b -> List a -> b
foldr : (a -> b -> b) -> b -> List a -> b
concat : List (List a) -> List a
concatMap : (a -> List b) -> List a -> List b
intersperse : a -> List a -> List a
map2 : (a -> b -> result) -> List a -> List b -> List result
map3 : (a -> b -> c -> result) -> List a -> List b -> List c -> List result
length : List a -> Int
reverse : List a -> List a
member : a -> List a -> Bool
all : (a -> Bool) -> List a -> Bool
any : (a -> Bool) -> List a -> Bool
maximum : List comparable -> Maybe comparable
minimum : List comparable -> Maybe comparable
sum : List Int -> Int
product : List Int -> Int
append : List a -> List a -> List a
isEmpty : List a -> Bool
head : List a -> Maybe a
tail : List a -> Maybe (List a)
take : Int -> List a -> List a                   -- [] when n <= 0
drop : Int -> List a -> List a                   -- unchanged when n <= 0
partition : (a -> Bool) -> List a -> ( List a, List a )   -- ( passing, failing )
unzip : List ( a, b ) -> ( List a, List b )
sort : List comparable -> List comparable
sortBy : (a -> comparable) -> List a -> List a
sortWith : (a -> a -> Order) -> List a -> List a
```

**Maybe** (`Maybe`, `Just`, `Nothing` built in):

```text
withDefault : a -> Maybe a -> a                  -- evaluates the default even for Just
map : (a -> b) -> Maybe a -> Maybe b
map2 : (a -> b -> value) -> Maybe a -> Maybe b -> Maybe value
map3 : (a -> b -> c -> value) -> Maybe a -> Maybe b -> Maybe c -> Maybe value
andThen : (a -> Maybe b) -> Maybe a -> Maybe b
```

**Result** (`type Result error value = Ok value | Err error`):

```text
map : (a -> value) -> Result x a -> Result x value
map2 : (a -> b -> value) -> Result x a -> Result x b -> Result x value     -- first Err wins
map3 : (a -> b -> c -> value) -> Result x a -> Result x b -> Result x c -> Result x value
andThen : (a -> Result x b) -> Result x a -> Result x b
withDefault : a -> Result x a -> a
toMaybe : Result x a -> Maybe a
fromMaybe : x -> Maybe a -> Result x a
mapError : (x -> y) -> Result x a -> Result y a
```

**Tuple** (pairs only):

```text
pair : a -> b -> ( a, b )
first : ( a, b ) -> a
second : ( a, b ) -> b
mapFirst : (a -> x) -> ( a, b ) -> ( x, b )
mapSecond : (b -> y) -> ( a, b ) -> ( a, y )
mapBoth : (a -> x) -> (b -> y) -> ( a, b ) -> ( x, y )
```

**String** (UTF-8 text; these five only):

```text
fromInt : Int -> String                          -- fromInt -42 == "-42"
isEmpty : String -> Bool
append : String -> String -> String
concat : List String -> String
join : String -> List String -> String           -- join ", " [ "a", "b" ] == "a, b"
```

**Dict** (`import Dict exposing (Dict)`; Elm's API; a Plutus map with keys strictly ascending; keys must be
comparable; `keys`/`toList`/folds in ascending key order; `get`/`member`/`insert`/`remove` O(n), stopping at
the first key not smaller; `fromList` O(n log n), last binding wins; `union` prefers the left; `==` compares
bindings):

```text
empty : Dict k v
singleton : comparable -> v -> Dict comparable v
insert : comparable -> v -> Dict comparable v -> Dict comparable v
update : comparable -> (Maybe v -> Maybe v) -> Dict comparable v -> Dict comparable v
remove : comparable -> Dict comparable v -> Dict comparable v
isEmpty : Dict k v -> Bool
member : comparable -> Dict comparable v -> Bool
get : comparable -> Dict comparable v -> Maybe v
size : Dict k v -> Int
keys : Dict k v -> List k
values : Dict k v -> List v
toList : Dict k v -> List ( k, v )
fromList : List ( comparable, v ) -> Dict comparable v
map : (k -> a -> b) -> Dict k a -> Dict k b
foldl : (k -> v -> b -> b) -> b -> Dict k v -> b          -- smallest key first
foldr : (k -> v -> b -> b) -> b -> Dict k v -> b          -- largest key first
filter : (comparable -> v -> Bool) -> Dict comparable v -> Dict comparable v
partition : (comparable -> v -> Bool) -> Dict comparable v -> ( Dict comparable v, Dict comparable v )
union : Dict comparable v -> Dict comparable v -> Dict comparable v
intersect : Dict comparable v -> Dict comparable v -> Dict comparable v
diff : Dict comparable a -> Dict comparable b -> Dict comparable a
merge : (comparable -> a -> result -> result) -> (comparable -> a -> b -> result -> result) -> (comparable -> b -> result -> result) -> Dict comparable a -> Dict comparable b -> result -> result
```

**Map** (`import Map` or `import Map exposing (Map)`; the ledger's association list, keys compared by Data
encoding, any Data-encodable key; O(n) lookups; `insert` puts the binding first; `fromList` is O(n²);
`filter`/`map` are O(n) and keep order; no `==`. A map decoded from Data may repeat a key: `get` returns
the first binding, `remove`/`insert` drop every binding of it. Use it for ledger maps such as
`txInfo.withdrawals` and for keys that are not comparable; use `Dict` otherwise):

```text
empty : Map k v
singleton : k -> v -> Map k v
get : k -> Map k v -> Maybe v
member : k -> Map k v -> Bool
insert : k -> v -> Map k v -> Map k v
remove : k -> Map k v -> Map k v
update : k -> (Maybe v -> Maybe v) -> Map k v -> Map k v
size : Map k v -> Int
isEmpty : Map k v -> Bool
keys : Map k v -> List k
values : Map k v -> List v
toList : Map k v -> List ( k, v )
fromList : List ( k, v ) -> Map k v
foldl : (k -> v -> b -> b) -> b -> Map k v -> b
foldr : (k -> v -> b -> b) -> b -> Map k v -> b
filter : (k -> v -> Bool) -> Map k v -> Map k v
map : (k -> a -> b) -> Map k a -> Map k b
```

**Array** (`import Array`; O(1) `get`/`length`; no Data encoding; no `set`/`push`):

```text
empty : Array a
fromList : List a -> Array a
toList : Array a -> List a
toIndexedList : Array a -> List ( Int, a )
length : Array a -> Int
isEmpty : Array a -> Bool
get : Int -> Array a -> Maybe a
initialize : Int -> (Int -> a) -> Array a
repeat : Int -> a -> Array a
foldl : (a -> b -> b) -> b -> Array a -> b
foldr : (a -> b -> b) -> b -> Array a -> b
map : (a -> b) -> Array a -> Array b
indexedMap : (Int -> a -> b) -> Array a -> Array b
filter : (a -> Bool) -> Array a -> Array a
slice : Int -> Int -> Array a -> Array a
```

**Value** (`import Value exposing (Value)`; the ledger's multi-asset value, as in `out.value` and
`tx.mint`; `PolicyId` and `TokenName` from `Julc.Ledger`; always canonical, so `==` is exact; quantities may
be negative, as for burns in a mint; `lovelaceOf` and `isZero` read the Data directly, the filters
(`positive`, `negative`, `restrictedTo`, `withoutLovelace`) walk it, the rest convert through the CIP-153
builtins, about 1M CPU for a few assets; a policy id or token name over 32 bytes, or a quantity outside
signed 128 bits, fails the script. `Data.encode` of a `Value` is free and `Data.decode`
accepts only canonical values, but a `Value` cannot be a datum, redeemer or parameter, and a type that
contains one cannot be decoded):

```text
zero : Value
lovelace : Int -> Value
singleton : PolicyId -> TokenName -> Int -> Value
insert : PolicyId -> TokenName -> Int -> Value -> Value      -- sets the quantity; 0 removes the token
fromList : List ( PolicyId, TokenName, Int ) -> Value        -- repeated tokens add up
lovelaceOf : Value -> Int                                    -- ada's token only; 0 when none, as in a mint
quantityOf : PolicyId -> TokenName -> Value -> Int           -- 0 when none
isZero : Value -> Bool
policies : Value -> List PolicyId                            -- ascending; ada's is the empty policy
tokens : PolicyId -> Value -> Dict TokenName Int
toList : Value -> List ( PolicyId, TokenName, Int )          -- ascending
add : Value -> Value -> Value
subtract : Value -> Value -> Value                           -- first minus second
negate : Value -> Value
scale : Int -> Value -> Value
sum : List Value -> Value
geq : Value -> Value -> Bool          -- geq a b: a holds at least as much of every token as b; total, also with negatives
leq : Value -> Value -> Bool
withoutLovelace : Value -> Value
restrictedTo : List PolicyId -> Value -> Value
positive : Value -> Value             -- in a mint: what is minted
negative : Value -> Value             -- in a mint: what is burned, still negative
```

**Interval** (`import Interval`; the ledger's time range, as in `tx.validRange`; POSIX milliseconds; name the
type with `import Interval exposing (Interval)`; build ranges by hand with `Interval`, `IntervalBound`,
`Finite`, `NegInf`, `PosInf` from `Julc.Ledger`; about 3M CPU per check):

```text
isEntirelyAfter : Int -> Interval -> Bool     -- the range has a finite start and every time in it is > t
isEntirelyBefore : Int -> Interval -> Bool    -- the range has a finite end and every time in it is < t
contains : Int -> Interval -> Bool            -- honors inclusive and exclusive bounds
start : Interval -> Maybe Int                 -- Nothing for an infinite start; ignores inclusiveness
```
