The core modules cover what Julc's `ContextsLib`, `IntervalLib` and most of `OutputLib` are used for. Julc's
libraries still help in a few cases. Map a class under `[java-modules]` and import it with the alias you
chose:

| Class under `org.julclang.stdlib.lib` | Still useful for |
| --- | --- |
| `OutputLib` | matching outputs by whole address, staking part included: `outputsAt`, `lovelacePaidTo`, `paidAtLeast` |
| `AddressLib` | classifying an address: `isPubKeyAddress`, `isScriptAddress`, `paymentCredential`, `credentialHash` |

Prefer the `Interval` module to `IntervalLib`: `IntervalLib.finiteLowerBound` and `finiteUpperBound` return
`-1` for an infinite bound, a sentinel that makes "no end" look like "ends at -1". Don't alias a Java module
as `Interval` or `Tx`; those names belong to the core modules. Functions that return a Java `Optional`, such
as `ContextsLib.findOwnInput`, give you a `JulcOptional`; convert it with `Julc.Data.fromOptional`.
`ContextsLib` and `OutputLib` may return the ledger's own values, as `valuePaid` does, but no other Java
library may hand Elci a `Value`: `ValuesLib.add` and the other exports that build one are rejected
(`ELCI2105`), because Java libraries don't keep values in the ledger's order. Use the `Value` module for
those. The [standard library](https://elci-lang.dev/advanced/standard-library/) page lists every verified export.

Next, see how your own datum and redeemer types cross the boundary in [Datums and redeemers](https://elci-lang.dev/contracts/datums-and-redeemers/).

---

# Datums and redeemers

> Which types can be datums, redeemers and parameters, how strict decoding protects a validator, the three spending-datum profiles, and exactly how Elci values are encoded as Plutus Data.

Source: https://elci-lang.dev/contracts/datums-and-redeemers/

A validator receives its datum and redeemer as Plutus **Data**, the ledger's universal format, and Elci decodes them into your types before your handler runs. This page covers which types you can use, how strict decoding behaves, how to accept outputs with or without a datum, and how each Elci type is encoded.

## Datum, redeemer and parameters

- The **datum** is stored with an output when it is locked at a script address. It records the state of that output: who may claim it, a price, a deadline.
- The **redeemer** is supplied by the transaction that runs the script. It says what the transaction wants to do: claim, cancel, refund.
- **Parameters** are fixed once per deployed script. See [Parameterized validators](https://elci-lang.dev/contracts/parameters/).

All three use the same types and the same encoding. The difference is when they are checked: the script checks the datum and redeemer on every run, while parameters are checked once, off-chain, when you apply them. The key order of a `Dict` is the exception: the script checks it in parameters too.

## Types you can use

| Type | At the boundary |
| --- | --- |
| `Int`, `Bool`, `String`, `Bytes` | yes |
| `()` | yes, as a whole datum or redeemer; not yet inside records, lists or other containers (`ELCI2013`) |
| Records and custom types | yes, when their fields are allowed types |
| `Maybe a`, tuples, `List a`, `Dict k v`, `Map k v` | yes, when their contents are allowed types |
| Ledger types such as `PubKeyHash`, `TxOutRef`, `Credential`, `Address` | yes |
| `Data` | yes: any data is accepted unchecked; decode it yourself with `Julc.Data.decode` |
| `Value` | not yet (`ELCI2013`): store a `List ( PolicyId, TokenName, Int )` and rebuild the value with `Value.fromList` |
| `TxOut`, `TxInInfo`, `TxInfo` | no: the compiler can't check their layout (`ELCI2013`) |
| `ScriptContext`, functions | no (`ELCI2013`) |
| `Array a` | no: arrays have no Data encoding (`ELCI2013`); keep a `List` and convert it with `Array.fromList` |

The compiler checks this when it compiles a handler, so an unsupported type is a compile error, never a runtime surprise.

## Strict decoding

Decoding is **strict**. Before your handler runs, the script checks the whole datum and redeemer: every constructor tag, every field count and every field's kind, even the fields your handler never reads. Data of the wrong shape fails the script.

This escrow shows the effect. The datum is a record and the redeemer a custom type:

```toml title="elci.toml"
[project]
source-directories = ["src"]
target = "plutus-v3-pv11-uplc-1.1.0"
julc-version = "0.1.0-pre20-ebaf028-SNAPSHOT"

[validators.escrow]
boundary = "julc-strict-v1"
spend = "Escrow.spend"

[validators.locker]
boundary = "julc-strict-v1"
parameters = ["admin"]
spend-datum = "optional"
spend = "Locker.spend"

[validators.donations]
boundary = "julc-strict-v1"
parameters = ["admin"]
spend-datum = "absent"
spend = "Donations.spend"

[validators.ballot]
boundary = "julc-strict-v1"
spend = "Ballot.spend"
```

```elm title="src/Auth.elm"
module Auth exposing (signedBy)

import Julc.Ledger exposing (PubKeyHash, ScriptContext)

signedBy : PubKeyHash -> ScriptContext -> Bool
signedBy key ctx =
    List.any (\signer -> signer == key) ctx.txInfo.signatories
```

```elm title="src/Escrow.elm"
module Escrow exposing (Action(..), Deal, spend)

import Auth exposing (signedBy)
import Julc.Ledger exposing (PubKeyHash, ScriptContext)

type alias Deal =
    { seller : PubKeyHash
    , buyer : PubKeyHash
    , price : Int
    }

type Action
    = Complete
    | Refund Int

spend : Deal -> Action -> ScriptContext -> Bool
spend deal action ctx =
    case action of
        Complete ->
            signedBy deal.buyer ctx

        Refund amount ->
            amount <= deal.price && signedBy deal.seller ctx
```

The tests lock outputs with good and bad datums. Scenarios take the datum and redeemer as `Data`, so each value goes through `Data.encode`:

```elm title="tests/EscrowTest.elm"
module EscrowTest exposing (buyerCompletes, dealsRoundTrip, incompleteDealsAreRejected, missingDatumsAreRejected, sellerRefunds, wrongRedeemersAreRejected)

import Escrow exposing (Action(..), Deal)
import Expect exposing (Expectation)
import Julc.Data as Data
import Julc.Ledger exposing (PubKeyHash)
import Property exposing (Property)
import Scenario exposing (Scenario)

seller : PubKeyHash
seller =
    Scenario.key "seller"

buyer : PubKeyHash
buyer =
    Scenario.key "buyer"

deal : Deal
deal =
    { seller = seller, buyer = buyer, price = 100 }

spendDeal : Data -> Scenario
spendDeal datum =
    Scenario.spend "escrow" (Scenario.outRef "escrow" 0) datum

buyerCompletes : Scenario
buyerCompletes =
    spendDeal (Data.encode deal)
        |> Scenario.redeemer (Data.encode Complete)
        |> Scenario.signedBy buyer

sellerRefunds : Scenario
sellerRefunds =
    spendDeal (Data.encode deal)
        |> Scenario.redeemer (Data.encode (Refund 30))
        |> Scenario.signedBy seller

{-| `Complete` never reads `price`, but the whole datum is still decoded.
-}
incompleteDealsAreRejected : Scenario
incompleteDealsAreRejected =
    spendDeal (Data.encode { seller = seller, buyer = buyer })
        |> Scenario.redeemer (Data.encode Complete)
        |> Scenario.signedBy buyer
        |> Scenario.expectFailure

missingDatumsAreRejected : Scenario
missingDatumsAreRejected =
    Scenario.spendWithoutDatum "escrow" (Scenario.outRef "escrow" 0)
        |> Scenario.redeemer (Data.encode Complete)
        |> Scenario.signedBy buyer
        |> Scenario.expectFailure

wrongRedeemersAreRejected : Scenario
wrongRedeemersAreRejected =
    spendDeal (Data.encode deal)
        |> Scenario.redeemer (Data.encode 0)
        |> Scenario.signedBy buyer
        |> Scenario.expectFailure

dealsRoundTrip : Deal -> Property
dealsRoundTrip generated =
    Property.expect (Expect.equal generated (Data.decode (Data.encode generated)))
```

```sh
elci test . --match escrow --seed 42
```

```text
PASS EscrowTest.buyerCompletes (cpu 12087950, mem 48649)
PASS EscrowTest.sellerRefunds (cpu 15076849, mem 59803)
PASS EscrowTest.incompleteDealsAreRejected (cpu 5999806, mem 24913)
PASS EscrowTest.missingDatumsAreRejected (cpu 3001320, mem 10881)
PASS EscrowTest.wrongRedeemersAreRejected (cpu 7930169, mem 33878)
PASS EscrowTest.dealsRoundTrip (100 runs, max cpu 11543229, mem 46989)
6 passed, 0 failed (seed 42)
```

`incompleteDealsAreRejected` deserves a closer look. The buyer signs and the redeemer is `Complete`, which only checks the buyer's signature, yet the script rejects the transaction. Without `expectFailure` you would see why:

```text
FAIL EscrowTest.incompleteDealsAreRejected (cpu 5999806, mem 24913)
    validator escrow rejected the transaction: UnIData: not IntData
```

The datum has two fields where `Deal` has three, so decoding fails before `spend` is called. Strictness means your handler only ever sees well-formed values, and an attacker can't slip in data of an unexpected shape.

:::caution[A bad datum locks funds]
Strictness also applies to the outputs you create. If an output is locked at the escrow address with a datum that isn't a valid `Deal`, **no** transaction can ever spend it. Encode datums from the same types the validator uses (`Data.encode` in Elci, or the layout in `abi.json` off-chain), and test them.
:::

### Dictionaries in data

A `Dict` crosses the boundary as a Plutus map with its keys in ascending order, and decoding checks that order. The check matters because `Dict.member` and `Dict.get` stop at the first key that isn't smaller than the one they look for: in a map whose keys are out of order, they could stop before a key that is there. This ballot, the `ballot` validator in the `elci.toml` above, lets each key holder vote once:

```elm title="src/Ballot.elm"
module Ballot exposing (Ballot, spend)

import Dict exposing (Dict)
import Julc.Ledger exposing (PubKeyHash, ScriptContext)

type alias Ballot =
    { votes : Dict PubKeyHash Int
    }

{-| The redeemer names the voter, who must sign and must not have voted yet.
-}
spend : Ballot -> PubKeyHash -> ScriptContext -> Bool
spend ballot voter ctx =
    not (Dict.member voter ballot.votes)
        && List.member voter ctx.txInfo.signatories
```

The scenarios vote with a fresh key, vote twice, and try to vote twice with a forged datum:

```elm title="tests/BallotTest.elm"
module BallotTest exposing (forgedOrderIsRejected, keysAscend, newVotersVote, votersVoteOnce)

import Ballot exposing (Ballot)
import Dict
import Julc.Data as Data
import Julc.Ledger exposing (PubKeyHash)
import Map exposing (Map)
import Scenario exposing (Scenario)

alice : PubKeyHash
alice =
    Scenario.key "alice"

bob : PubKeyHash
bob =
    Scenario.key "bob"

carol : PubKeyHash
carol =
    Scenario.key "carol"

keysAscend : Bool
keysAscend =
    Dict.keys (Dict.fromList [ ( carol, 1 ), ( alice, 1 ), ( bob, 1 ) ]) == [ alice, bob, carol ]

vote : Data -> PubKeyHash -> Scenario
vote ballot voter =
    Scenario.spend "ballot" (Scenario.outRef "ballot" 0) ballot
        |> Scenario.redeemer (Data.encode voter)
        |> Scenario.signedBy voter

newVotersVote : Scenario
newVotersVote =
    vote (Data.encode (Ballot (Dict.fromList [ ( alice, 1 ) ]))) bob

votersVoteOnce : Scenario
votersVoteOnce =
    vote (Data.encode (Ballot (Dict.fromList [ ( alice, 1 ), ( bob, 1 ) ]))) bob
        |> Scenario.expectFailure

{-| `Ballot`'s layout, but a `Map` keeps its own order: the newest key first.
-}
type alias Forged =
    { votes : Map PubKeyHash Int
    }

{-| Bob has voted, but his key comes after Carol's larger one.
-}
forgedOrderIsRejected : Scenario
forgedOrderIsRejected =
    vote (Data.encode (Forged (Map.fromList [ ( bob, 1 ), ( carol, 1 ) ]))) bob
        |> Scenario.expectFailure
```

```sh
elci test . --match ballot
```

```text
PASS BallotTest.keysAscend (cpu 35117763, mem 132891)
PASS BallotTest.newVotersVote (cpu 15827728, mem 64830)
PASS BallotTest.votersVoteOnce (cpu 18258644, mem 76709)
PASS BallotTest.forgedOrderIsRejected (cpu 14523407, mem 60626)
4 passed, 0 failed
```

`keysAscend` shows that the test keys order as Alice, Bob, Carol. `Forged` has `Ballot`'s layout, but a `Map` keeps its own order, so the forged datum lists Carol's key before Bob's. Bob has already voted, yet `Dict.member` would stop at Carol's key, the first that isn't smaller than his, and answer `False`. The script never gets that far: a datum whose keys are out of order or repeated fails to decode, whatever the handler would have decided. The check reads each key once, at about 1.1 million CPU units per entry.

When you build such a datum off-chain, write the keys in Elci's order: integers numerically, byte strings and strings by their bytes with a proper prefix first, lists and tuples element by element. This is not CBOR's canonical key order, which puts shorter byte strings first and negative integers after positive ones. Build test datums with `Dict.fromList` and `Data.encode`, which always produce the right order.

## Spending-datum profiles

By default a spending handler requires a datum, and an output without one can't be spent (`missingDatumsAreRejected` above). Set `spend-datum` in the validator's table to change that. It changes the handler's signature:

| `spend-datum` | Handler type | An output without a datum |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `"required"` (default) | `params -> datum -> redeemer -> ScriptContext -> Bool` | is rejected |
| `"optional"` | `params -> Maybe datum -> redeemer -> ScriptContext -> Bool` | arrives as `Nothing` |
| `"absent"` | `params -> redeemer -> ScriptContext -> Bool` | is accepted; no datum is ever read |

### Optional

With `"optional"`, the handler receives `Just datum` or `Nothing`. A datum that is present is still decoded strictly. This locker lets each output name its owner, and lets the admin recover outputs sent without a datum:

```elm title="src/Locker.elm"
module Locker exposing (spend)

import Auth exposing (signedBy)
import Julc.Ledger exposing (PubKeyHash, ScriptContext)

{-| An output's datum names its owner. Outputs sent without a datum can be recovered by the admin.
-}
spend : PubKeyHash -> Maybe PubKeyHash -> () -> ScriptContext -> Bool
spend admin datum _ ctx =
    case datum of
        Just owner ->
            signedBy owner ctx

        Nothing ->
            signedBy admin ctx
```

```elm title="tests/LockerTest.elm"
module LockerTest exposing (adminCannotTakeOwnedOutputs, adminRecoversUnlabelled, malformedDatumsAreRejected, ownerSpends)

import Julc.Data as Data
import Julc.Ledger exposing (PubKeyHash, TxOutRef)
import Scenario exposing (Scenario)

admin : PubKeyHash
admin =
    Scenario.key "admin"

owner : PubKeyHash
owner =
    Scenario.key "owner"

ref : TxOutRef
ref =
    Scenario.outRef "locker" 0

ownerSpends : Scenario
ownerSpends =
    Scenario.spend "locker" ref (Data.encode owner)
        |> Scenario.parameters [ Data.encode admin ]
        |> Scenario.signedBy owner

adminCannotTakeOwnedOutputs : Scenario
adminCannotTakeOwnedOutputs =
    Scenario.spend "locker" ref (Data.encode owner)
        |> Scenario.parameters [ Data.encode admin ]
        |> Scenario.signedBy admin
        |> Scenario.expectFailure

adminRecoversUnlabelled : Scenario
adminRecoversUnlabelled =
    Scenario.spendWithoutDatum "locker" ref
        |> Scenario.parameters [ Data.encode admin ]
        |> Scenario.signedBy admin

malformedDatumsAreRejected : Scenario
malformedDatumsAreRejected =
    Scenario.spend "locker" ref (Data.encode 42)
        |> Scenario.parameters [ Data.encode admin ]
        |> Scenario.signedBy admin
        |> Scenario.expectFailure
```

```sh
elci test . --match locker
```

```text
PASS LockerTest.ownerSpends (cpu 10898424, mem 43407)
PASS LockerTest.adminCannotTakeOwnedOutputs (cpu 11276857, mem 45339)
PASS LockerTest.adminRecoversUnlabelled (cpu 9203608, mem 36654)
PASS LockerTest.malformedDatumsAreRejected (cpu 4502607, mem 19149)
4 passed, 0 failed
```

`malformedDatumsAreRejected` shows that "optional" doesn't mean "anything goes": the integer `42` is not a `PubKeyHash`, so it is not treated as a missing datum.

### Absent

With `"absent"`, the handler has no datum argument and the datum is never inspected. Use it when outputs may arrive from wallets that attach no datum, or any datum:

```elm title="src/Donations.elm"
module Donations exposing (spend)

import Auth exposing (signedBy)
import Julc.Ledger exposing (PubKeyHash, ScriptContext)

{-| Anyone can donate, with or without a datum; only the admin can spend.
-}
spend : PubKeyHash -> () -> ScriptContext -> Bool
spend admin _ ctx =
    signedBy admin ctx
```

```elm title="tests/DonationsTest.elm"
module DonationsTest exposing (adminSpendsAnyDatum, adminSpendsWithoutDatum, strangersCannotSpend)

import Julc.Data as Data
import Julc.Ledger exposing (PubKeyHash, TxOutRef)
import Scenario exposing (Scenario)

admin : PubKeyHash
admin =
    Scenario.key "admin"

ref : TxOutRef
ref =
    Scenario.outRef "donations" 0

adminSpendsWithoutDatum : Scenario
adminSpendsWithoutDatum =
    Scenario.spendWithoutDatum "donations" ref
        |> Scenario.parameters [ Data.encode admin ]
        |> Scenario.signedBy admin

adminSpendsAnyDatum : Scenario
adminSpendsAnyDatum =
    Scenario.spend "donations" ref (Data.encode "thank you")
        |> Scenario.parameters [ Data.encode admin ]
        |> Scenario.signedBy admin

strangersCannotSpend : Scenario
strangersCannotSpend =
    Scenario.spendWithoutDatum "donations" ref
        |> Scenario.parameters [ Data.encode admin ]
        |> Scenario.signedBy (Scenario.key "stranger")
        |> Scenario.expectFailure
```

```sh
elci test . --match donations
```

```text
PASS DonationsTest.adminSpendsWithoutDatum (cpu 5906941, mem 23432)
PASS DonationsTest.adminSpendsAnyDatum (cpu 5906941, mem 23432)
PASS DonationsTest.strangersCannotSpend (cpu 6285374, mem 25364)
3 passed, 0 failed
```

## How Elci values are encoded

Every boundary type has one fixed Data encoding. You need it whenever off-chain code builds a datum, redeemer or parameter, and whenever you decode data that another contract wrote.

| Elci type | Plutus Data |
| --- | --- |
| `Int` | integer |
| `Bytes`, and hashes such as `PubKeyHash` | byte string |
| `String` | byte string holding the UTF-8 text |
| `Bool` | `False` is constructor 0, `True` is constructor 1, both with no fields |
| `()` | constructor 0 with no fields |
| Record | constructor 0; fields **sorted by name**, not in declaration order |
| Custom type | constructor tag = position in the declaration (first is 0); fields in argument order |
| `Maybe a` | `Nothing` is constructor 0; `Just x` is constructor 1 with one field |
| Tuple | constructor 0; components in order |
| `List a` | list |
| `Dict k v` | map, with its keys in strictly ascending order |
| `Map k v` | map, in the map's order |
| `TxOutRef` | constructor 0 with the transaction id bytes and the index |

Three rules cause most surprises:

- **Record fields are sorted by name.** `Deal` is declared as seller, buyer, price but encoded as buyer, price, seller. Reordering a record's declaration never changes its encoding.
- **Constructor order is the encoding.** Reordering the constructors of a custom type changes their tags, and existing on-chain data no longer decodes as intended. Add new constructors at the end.
- **`Maybe` is not Julc's optional.** Julc's Java `Optional` uses different tags, so the two are not interchangeable. Convert with `Julc.Data.fromOptional` and `toOptional`.

You can see these rules in action by encoding a value and decoding it as a different type with the same layout:

```elm title="tests/EncodingTest.elm"
module EncodingTest exposing (boolsAreConstructors, maybeIsNothingThenJust, recordsAreSortedByFieldName)

import Escrow exposing (Deal)
import Expect exposing (Expectation)
import Julc.Data as Data
import Julc.Ledger exposing (PubKeyHash)
import Scenario

type Switch
    = Off
    | On

type Option
    = None
    | Some Int

seller : PubKeyHash
seller =
    Scenario.key "seller"

buyer : PubKeyHash
buyer =
    Scenario.key "buyer"

{-| `Deal` declares seller, buyer, price; it is encoded as buyer, price, seller.
-}
recordsAreSortedByFieldName : Expectation
recordsAreSortedByFieldName =
    let
        deal : Deal
        deal =
            { seller = seller, buyer = buyer, price = 100 }
    in
    Expect.equal ( buyer, 100, seller ) (Data.decode (Data.encode deal))

{-| `False` is constructor 0 and `True` is constructor 1.
-}
boolsAreConstructors : Expectation
boolsAreConstructors =
    Expect.equal [ Off, On ] (Data.decode (Data.encode [ False, True ]))

{-| `Nothing` is constructor 0; `Just x` is constructor 1 with one field.
-}
maybeIsNothingThenJust : Expectation
maybeIsNothingThenJust =
    Expect.equal [ None, Some 5 ] (Data.decode (Data.encode [ Nothing, Just 5 ]))
```

```sh
elci test . --match encoding
```

```text
PASS EncodingTest.recordsAreSortedByFieldName (cpu 9149529, mem 33661)
PASS EncodingTest.boolsAreConstructors (cpu 7559553, mem 29633)
PASS EncodingTest.maybeIsNothingThenJust (cpu 9322159, mem 36461)
3 passed, 0 failed
```

The build records every layout in `abi.json`, so off-chain code doesn't have to guess. This is the escrow's datum, extracted with `jq`:

```sh
jq '.handlers[0].datum' build/validators/escrow/abi.json
```

```json
{
  "profile": "required",
  "schema": {
    "fields": [
      {
        "name": "buyer",
        "schema": {
          "encoding": "B",
          "kind": "bytes"
        }
      },
      {
        "name": "price",
        "schema": {
          "encoding": "I",
          "kind": "integer"
        }
      },
      {
        "name": "seller",
        "schema": {
          "encoding": "B",
          "kind": "bytes"
        }
      }
    ],
    "identity": "elci.Record:buyer,price,seller [org.julclang.ledger.PubKeyHash, Int, org.julclang.ledger.PubKeyHash]",
    "kind": "record",
    "tag": 0
  },
  "sourceType": "Record:buyer,price,seller [org.julclang.ledger.PubKeyHash, Int, org.julclang.ledger.PubKeyHash]"
}
```

## Converting with `Julc.Data`

`Julc.Data` is a compiler-provided module of explicit conversions. Import it with `import Julc.Data as Data`.

| Function | Type | Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Data.encode` | `a -> Data` | The Data encoding of a value |
| `Data.decode` | `Data -> a` | Strict decoding; malformed data fails the script |
| `Data.fromOptional` | `JulcOptional a -> Maybe a` | Re-tags a Julc optional (a ledger field or a library result) as `Maybe` |
| `Data.toOptional` | `Maybe a -> JulcOptional a` | The reverse |

The type `a` must be known where you convert. Usually the context fixes it, as in the tests above; otherwise add a type annotation. Where you use them:

- **In tests**, to build the `Data` a scenario needs: `Data.encode deal`, `Data.encode (Refund 30)`.
- **In contracts**, to read data the handler doesn't receive directly, such as the inline datum of another output (see [Reading the transaction](https://elci-lang.dev/contracts/reading-the-transaction/)).
- **In properties**, to check that a type survives a round trip, like `dealsRoundTrip` above.

`decode` never returns a `Maybe` on bad input: a failed decode fails the transaction. In a unit test that decodes a string as an `Int`:

```elm
decodingIsStrict : Bool
decodingIsStrict =
    Data.decode (Data.encode "five") == 5
```

```text
FAIL EncodingTest.decodingIsStrict (cpu 928281, mem 5171)
    evaluation failed: UnIData: not IntData
```

A `Value` converts on its own: `Data.encode ctx.txInfo.mint` costs nothing, and `Data.decode` accepts only a canonical value (see [`Value`](https://elci-lang.dev/reference/core-modules/#value)). A type that contains a `Value` can't be decoded yet, a list or tuple of values can't be encoded either, and a ledger record without a checkable layout, such as `TxOut`, can't be decoded. Each is rejected at compile time. For `Data.encode [ Value.lovelace 5 ]`:

```text
ELCI3003: No encoder for List [org.julclang.ledger.Value]: The library provider cannot supply encode List record Value: [JULC0051] Library request encode List record Value is not supported: org.julclang.ledger.Value does not approve ENCODE
```

Convert the values with `Value.toList` first, and back with `Value.fromList`.

---

# Parameterized validators

> Declare deployment parameters, test them with scenarios, and apply them to a built script with elci apply and cardano-cli's detailed Data JSON.

Source: https://elci-lang.dev/contracts/parameters/

A parameter is a value baked into a script when you deploy it, such as an admin's key or a limit. This page shows how to declare parameters, test them, and apply them to the built script with `elci apply`.

## Why parameters

A datum belongs to one output; a parameter belongs to the whole script. Two deployments of the same code with different parameters are different scripts, with different hashes, addresses and policy ids. That is exactly what you want when the value decides who controls the script: someone who deploys your policy with their own admin key gets their own policy id, not yours.

## Declaring parameters

List the names under `parameters` in the validator's table. The handlers receive them as leading arguments, in that order. This minting policy lets an admin mint between a minimum and a maximum quantity per transaction:

```toml title="elci.toml"
[project]
source-directories = ["src"]
target = "plutus-v3-pv11-uplc-1.1.0"
julc-version = "0.1.0-pre20-ebaf028-SNAPSHOT"

[validators.drop]
boundary = "julc-strict-v1"
parameters = ["admin", "limits"]
mint = "Drop.mint"
```

```elm title="src/Drop.elm"
module Drop exposing (Limits, mint)

import Julc.Ledger exposing (PubKeyHash, ScriptContext)

type alias Limits =
    { minimum : Int
    , maximum : Int
    }

mint : PubKeyHash -> Limits -> Int -> ScriptContext -> Bool
mint admin limits quantity ctx =
    (quantity >= limits.minimum)
        && (quantity <= limits.maximum)
        && List.any (\signer -> signer == admin) ctx.txInfo.signatories
```

`admin` and `limits` come first, then the redeemer (here the quantity the transaction claims to mint), then the context.

The rules:

- **Order matters.** Parameters are applied in the listed order, and every handler of the validator receives all of them, in that order.
- **Types must agree.** Each parameter must have the same type in every handler. If `Treasury.spend` takes `admin : PubKeyHash` but `Treasury.withdraw` declares and uses it as an `Int`, the check fails:

  ```text
  .../treasury/src/Treasury.elm:11:1: ELCI2014: Handler Treasury.withdraw does not have the withdraw signature admin -> redeemer -> ScriptContext -> Bool that [validators.treasury] needs (1 parameter); its type is Int -> () -> ScriptContext -> Bool; it has `Int` where the configuration needs `PubKeyHash`

  11| withdraw : Int -> () -> ScriptContext -> Bool
      ^^^^^^^^

  In .../treasury/elci.toml:6: [validators.treasury]
  ```

- **Boundary types only.** Parameters follow the same rules as datums and redeemers: records, custom types, lists, dictionaries, maps and ledger types such as `PubKeyHash` or `TxOutRef` are fine; functions, arrays and `Value` are not. To parameterize a script by an amount of tokens, take a `List ( PolicyId, TokenName, Int )` and build the value with `Value.fromList`. See [Datums and redeemers](https://elci-lang.dev/contracts/datums-and-redeemers/).
- **Names** start with a lowercase letter and use letters, digits and `_`.

Parameters are decoded when the script is applied, but the script doesn't validate them on-chain. `elci apply` checks them off-chain instead, as shown below. The one exception is a `Dict`: the script checks its key order on every run, as it does in a datum.

## Testing with parameters

A scenario supplies parameters as `Data`, in the declared order, with `Scenario.parameters`:

```elm title="tests/DropTest.elm"
module DropTest exposing (adminMintsWithinLimits, onlyQuantitiesWithinLimits, tooManyAreRejected)

import Bytes
import Drop exposing (Limits)
import Julc.Data as Data
import Julc.Ledger exposing (PubKeyHash)
import Property exposing (Property)
import Scenario exposing (Scenario)

admin : PubKeyHash
admin =
    Scenario.key "admin"

limits : Limits
limits =
    { minimum = 1, maximum = 10 }

drop : Int -> Scenario
drop quantity =
    Scenario.mint "drop"
        |> Scenario.parameters [ Data.encode admin, Data.encode limits ]
        |> Scenario.minting (Bytes.fromString "DROP") quantity
        |> Scenario.redeemer (Data.encode quantity)
        |> Scenario.signedBy admin

adminMintsWithinLimits : Scenario
adminMintsWithinLimits =
    drop 10

tooManyAreRejected : Scenario
tooManyAreRejected =
    drop 11
        |> Scenario.expectFailure

onlyQuantitiesWithinLimits : Int -> Property
onlyQuantitiesWithinLimits quantity =
    if quantity >= 1 && quantity <= 10 then
        Property.scenario (drop quantity)

    else
        Property.scenario (Scenario.expectFailure (drop quantity))
```

```sh
elci test . --seed 42
```

```text
PASS DropTest.adminMintsWithinLimits (cpu 6369489, mem 23925)
PASS DropTest.tooManyAreRejected (cpu 3787162, mem 15380)
PASS DropTest.onlyQuantitiesWithinLimits (100 runs, max cpu 6369489, mem 23925)
3 passed, 0 failed (seed 42)
```

The test runner applies the parameters to the compiled script before it builds the transaction, so the script's address and policy id in each scenario are those of the applied script. A scenario must supply every parameter. If `drop` passed only `[ Data.encode admin ]`, its scenarios would fail before running:

```text
FAIL DropTest.adminMintsWithinLimits
    cannot prepare validator 'drop': it takes 2 parameters [admin, limits], but the scenario gives 1; set them with Scenario.parameters
0 passed, 1 failed
```

:::note
This example trusts the redeemer to tell the truth about the quantity, which keeps it short. A real policy should read the minted quantity from `ctx.txInfo.mint` with `Value.quantityOf`, as the [treasury tutorial](https://elci-lang.dev/tutorials/treasury/) does.
:::

## The built script

`elci build` writes the script **before** parameters are applied. Its `validator.plutus.json` lists the parameters and leaves the hash empty, because the hash only exists once the parameters are known:

```json title="build/validators/drop/validator.plutus.json"
{
  "type": "PlutusScriptV3",
  "purpose": "minting",
  "description": "drop",
  "cborHex": "...",
  "hash": "",
  "params": "admin:PubKeyHash,limits:Record",
  "sizeBytes": 218
}
```

`params` shows records as `Record`. The full layout of each parameter is in `abi.json`:

```sh
jq '.parameters' build/validators/drop/abi.json
```

```json
[
  {
    "name": "admin",
    "schema": {
      "encoding": "B",
      "kind": "bytes"
    },
    "sourceType": "org.julclang.ledger.PubKeyHash"
  },
  {
    "name": "limits",
    "schema": {
      "fields": [
        {
          "name": "maximum",
          "schema": {
            "encoding": "I",
            "kind": "integer"
          }
        },
        {
          "name": "minimum",
          "schema": {
            "encoding": "I",
            "kind": "integer"
          }
        }
      ],
      "identity": "elci.Record:maximum,minimum [Int, Int]",
      "kind": "record",
      "tag": 0
    },
    "sourceType": "Record:maximum,minimum [Int, Int]"
  }
]
```

Note the field order: `maximum` before `minimum`, because record fields are encoded sorted by name.

## Applying parameters with `elci apply`

`elci apply` compiles the validator, checks each value and writes the applied script. Pass every parameter with `--param name=value`, where the value is Plutus Data in cardano-cli's detailed JSON schema:

```sh
elci apply . --validator drop \
  --param 'admin={"bytes": "887d8fbb82ce756a9dac9210c3d1235e9d3ff2457a667d311d318142"}' \
  --param 'limits={"constructor": 0, "fields": [{"int": 10}, {"int": 1}]}'
```

```text
validator drop: applied 2 parameters; hash 4ba1e0d80a5891c79032b5eccdf0514392f90e90278ce6567a7d3d76; wrote .../token-drop/build/validators/drop/applied.plutus.json
```

The applied artifact has the same format as `validator.plutus.json`, now with a hash and no remaining parameters:

```json title="build/validators/drop/applied.plutus.json"
{
  "type": "PlutusScriptV3",
  "purpose": "minting",
  "description": "drop",
  "cborHex": "59010a590107010100333232323223222323232323293370e...",
  "hash": "4ba1e0d80a5891c79032b5eccdf0514392f90e90278ce6567a7d3d76",
  "params": "",
  "sizeBytes": 263
}
```

For a minting policy, this hash is the policy id. For a spending validator, the script address is derived from it.

### Plutus Data JSON

Each value is one JSON object in the detailed schema:

| JSON | Data | For Elci types |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `{"int": 42}` | integer | `Int` |
| `{"bytes": "0a1b"}` | byte string, as hex | `Bytes`, hashes, `String` (the UTF-8 bytes) |
| `{"list": [ ... ]}` | list | `List a` |
| `{"map": [{"k": ..., "v": ...}]}` | map | `Dict k v` (keys in ascending order), `Map k v` |
| `{"constructor": 0, "fields": [ ... ]}` | constructor | records, custom types, `Bool`, `Maybe`, tuples, `()`, `TxOutRef` |

Build values with the [encoding rules](https://elci-lang.dev/contracts/datums-and-redeemers/): a record is constructor 0 with its fields sorted by name, `True` is `{"constructor": 1, "fields": []}`, and a `TxOutRef` is `{"constructor": 0, "fields": [{"bytes": "<transaction id>"}, {"int": <index>}]}`. The parser accepts integers, hex strings, arrays and objects; strings with escape sequences are not supported.

### What `apply` checks

Before applying anything, `apply` runs Julc's strict decoder for each parameter's type against the value you gave. Wrong kinds, constructor tags and field counts are rejected, and nothing is written:

```text
elci: ELCI4001: parameter limits is not a well-formed Record:maximum,minimum [Int, Int] value
```

(from `{"constructor": 0, "fields": [{"int": 10}]}`, which has one field too few), and:

```text
elci: ELCI4001: parameter admin is not a well-formed org.julclang.ledger.PubKeyHash value
```

(from `{"int": 42}`). A `Dict` must list its keys in ascending order, each once, so `apply` also rejects

```json
{"map": [{"k": {"int": 2}, "v": {"int": 10}}, {"k": {"int": 1}, "v": {"int": 5}}]}
```

for a parameter `caps : Dict Int Int`:

```text
elci: ELCI4001: parameter caps has a Dict whose keys are not strictly ascending; write its keys sorted and without repeats
```

Other mistakes are reported the same way:

| Mistake | Message |
| --- | --- |
| No `--param limits=...` | `ELCI4001: missing --param limits=<plutus-data-json>` |
| `--param owner=...` | `ELCI4001: validator drop has no parameter 'owner'; declared: admin, limits` |
| `--param admin=887d8fbb` (bare hex, not JSON) | `ELCI4001: parameter admin is not Plutus Data JSON (for example {"int": 5}, {"bytes": "ab"} or {"constructor": 0, "fields": []}): unexpected trailing content at offset 3` |

:::caution[The check is about shape, not meaning]
`apply` checks the kind and layout of each value, not its meaning. It accepts `{"constructor": 0, "fields": [{"int": 1}, {"int": 10}]}` for `limits`, although that means `minimum = 10, maximum = 1` and nothing could ever be minted. It also accepts a `PubKeyHash` of the wrong length, because Elci adds no length rule to ledger hashes. Double-check values against `abi.json`, and test the applied parameters in scenarios.
:::

### Values from files

Long values are easier to keep in files. Write `@path` instead of the JSON. The path is resolved against the **project directory**, not your current directory:

```json title="params/limits.json"
{
  "constructor": 0,
  "fields": [
    { "int": 10 },
    { "int": 1 }
  ]
}
```

```sh
elci apply . --validator drop \
  --param 'admin={"bytes": "887d8fbb82ce756a9dac9210c3d1235e9d3ff2457a667d311d318142"}' \
  --param limits=@params/limits.json
```

### Where the result goes

By default the result is `build/validators/<name>/applied.plutus.json`. It belongs to the build: the next `elci build` of that validator removes it, because it was applied to the previous script. To keep an applied script, write it elsewhere with `--output`, which is resolved against your current directory:

```sh
elci apply token-drop --validator drop \
  --param 'admin={"bytes": "887d8fbb82ce756a9dac9210c3d1235e9d3ff2457a667d311d318142"}' \
  --param limits=@params/limits.json --output drop-preprod.plutus.json
```

```text
validator drop: applied 2 parameters; hash 4ba1e0d80a5891c79032b5eccdf0514392f90e90278ce6567a7d3d76; wrote .../drop-preprod.plutus.json
```

If the validator sets `expected-abi` and the current ABI differs, `apply` refuses to apply parameters. See [Build and deploy](https://elci-lang.dev/contracts/build-and-deploy/).

## Applying parameters from Java

Off-chain Java code can apply the same parameters to the unapplied artifact with Julc's Cardano Client Lib adapter. Pass `PlutusData` values in the declared order. This example gives the same hash as `elci apply` above:

```java title="ApplyParams.java (example)"
import java.math.BigInteger;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.util.HexFormat;
import java.util.List;
import org.julclang.clientlib.JulcScriptAdapter;
import org.julclang.clientlib.ValidatorOutput;
import org.julclang.core.PlutusData;

var output = ValidatorOutput.fromJson(Files.readString(
        Path.of("build/validators/drop/validator.plutus.json")));

var admin = PlutusData.bytes(HexFormat.of().parseHex(
        "887d8fbb82ce756a9dac9210c3d1235e9d3ff2457a667d311d318142"));
// Limits { minimum = 1, maximum = 10 }: fields are sorted by name, so maximum comes first.
var limits = new PlutusData.ConstrData(BigInteger.ZERO, List.of(
        PlutusData.integer(BigInteger.TEN),
        PlutusData.integer(BigInteger.ONE)));

var program = JulcScriptAdapter.toProgram(output.cborHex()).applyParams(admin, limits);
var script = JulcScriptAdapter.fromProgram(program); // a Cardano Client Lib PlutusV3Script
System.out.println(HexFormat.of().formatHex(script.getScriptHash()));
```

```text
4ba1e0d80a5891c79032b5eccdf0514392f90e90278ce6567a7d3d76
```

It needs `org.julclang:julc-cardano-client-lib` (at the Julc version your compiler uses) and Cardano Client Lib on the classpath. Unlike `elci apply`, this path doesn't check the values against their types, so validate them yourself.

---

# Build and deploy

> What elci build writes, how abi.json and expected-abi guard your data layout, where script hashes come from, and how to load an artifact in Java with Cardano Client Lib.

Source: https://elci-lang.dev/contracts/build-and-deploy/

This page walks through the files `elci build` produces, how to protect your on-chain data layout from accidental changes, and how off-chain code loads the compiled script. The examples use the vesting contract from the [vesting tutorial](https://elci-lang.dev/tutorials/vesting/).

## Building

```sh
elci build .
```

```text
validator vesting (spend): checked; 533 FLAT bytes; plutus-v3-pv11-uplc-1.1.0
```

Each validator gets its own directory:

- build/
  - validators/
    - elci-outputs.json the files Elci owns, per validator
    - vesting/
      - validator.flat the script, FLAT-encoded UPLC
      - validator.plutus a Plutus V3 text envelope
      - validator.plutus.json the Julc artifact for off-chain code
      - abi.json the data layout of parameters, datums and redeemers

| File | Contents | Use it for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `validator.flat` | The raw UPLC program in FLAT encoding | Tools that read FLAT directly |
| `validator.plutus` | A text envelope: `type`, `description` and `cborHex`, with the script bytes CBOR-wrapped twice | Tools that read Plutus script envelopes |
| `validator.plutus.json` | Julc's validator artifact: `cborHex`, `hash`, `params`, `purpose`, `sizeBytes` | Loading the script with Cardano Client Lib |
| `abi.json` | Handlers, datum, redeemer and parameter schemas, constructor tags and field order | Building data off-chain; detecting layout changes |

Neither `validator.plutus.json` nor `abi.json` is a CIP-57 blueprint; Elci doesn't generate blueprints yet.

### How a build writes files

- **All or nothing.** Every selected validator is compiled, and checked against its `expected-abi`, before any file is written. If one fails, nothing is published and the previous outputs stay as they were.
- **Selection.** `elci build . --validator vesting` builds only the named validators (repeat the option for more) and leaves the others' outputs alone.
- **Cleanup.** A full build removes the outputs of validators you have deleted from `elci.toml`. It only removes files listed in `elci-outputs.json`, so anything else you put in those directories is kept.
- **Applied scripts.** An `applied.plutus.json` written by `elci apply` is removed by the next build of its validator, because it was applied to the previous script.

## The Julc artifact

`validator.plutus.json` is the file off-chain code loads (`cborHex` shortened):

```json title="build/validators/vesting/validator.plutus.json"
{
  "type": "PlutusScriptV3",
  "purpose": "spending",
  "description": "vesting",
  "cborHex": "590218590215010100323232323232323232322323232323...",
  "hash": "cdf09c382832689b016adac7ef1470488e9ff58b8a474b9086c7a0c3",
  "params": "",
  "sizeBytes": 533
}
```

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `type` | Always `PlutusScriptV3` |
| `purpose` | `spending`, `minting`, `withdraw`, `certifying`, `voting` or `proposing` for one handler; `multi` for several |
| `description` | The validator's name |
| `cborHex` | The script, CBOR-wrapped twice as Cardano Client Lib expects |
| `hash` | The script hash; empty while parameters are still to be applied |
| `params` | The parameters still to be applied, as `name:type`, comma-separated; records show as `Record` |
| `sizeBytes` | The size of the FLAT script |

## The ABI

`abi.json` describes everything off-chain code needs to talk to the script. Its top level:

```sh
jq '{formatVersion, validator, purpose, target, julcVersion, compiler, boundary, ledgerArguments, parameters, definitions}' build/validators/vesting/abi.json
```

```json
{
  "formatVersion": 2,
  "validator": "vesting",
  "purpose": "spend",
  "target": "plutus-v3-pv11-uplc-1.1.0",
  "julcVersion": "0.1.0-pre20-ebaf028-SNAPSHOT",
  "compiler": "elci-0.1.0-dev",
  "boundary": "julc-strict-v1",
  "ledgerArguments": 1,
  "parameters": [],
  "definitions": {}
}
```

`handlers` lists one entry per handler, with its function, its purpose and the ledger's tag for that purpose, plus the datum profile and the datum and redeemer schemas. `parameters` holds the parameter schemas in application order, and `definitions` holds shared definitions such as recursive types. Each schema gives the kind of data, the constructor tags and the field order. The vesting datum:

```sh
jq '.handlers[0] | {datum, redeemer}' build/validators/vesting/abi.json
```

```json
{
  "datum": {
    "profile": "required",
    "schema": {
      "fields": [
        {
          "name": "beneficiary",
          "schema": {
            "encoding": "B",
            "kind": "bytes"
          }
        },
        {
          "name": "deadline",
          "schema": {
            "encoding": "I",
            "kind": "integer"
          }
        }
      ],
      "identity": "elci.Record:beneficiary,deadline [org.julclang.ledger.PubKeyHash, Int]",
      "kind": "record",
      "tag": 0
    },
    "sourceType": "Record:beneficiary,deadline [org.julclang.ledger.PubKeyHash, Int]"
  },
  "redeemer": {
    "schema": {
      "constructors": [
        {
          "fields": [],
          "name": "Vesting.Claim",
          "tag": 0
        }
      ],
      "identity": "elci.Vesting.VestingAction",
      "kind": "union"
    },
    "sourceType": "Vesting.VestingAction"
  }
}
```

Keep the ABI with the application code that builds datums and redeemers. The encoding rules behind it are on [Datums and redeemers](https://elci-lang.dev/contracts/datums-and-redeemers/).

## Guarding the ABI with `expected-abi`

Once outputs exist on-chain, their datums must keep decoding. A harmless-looking refactor, such as reordering constructors, can silently change the layout. To catch that, commit a copy of the ABI outside `build/` and point the validator at it:

```sh
mkdir -p abi
cp build/validators/vesting/abi.json abi/vesting.json
```

```toml title="elci.toml" ins={4}
[validators.vesting]
boundary = "julc-strict-v1"
spend = "Vesting.validate"
expected-abi = "abi/vesting.json"
```

The path is relative to the project directory. From now on, `elci check`, `elci build` and `elci apply` compare the current ABI with the committed one before writing anything. Changes that keep the layout pass. Reordering the fields of the datum's declaration, for example, still builds:

```elm
type alias VestingDatum =
    { deadline : Int
    , beneficiary : PubKeyHash
    }
```

```text
validator vesting (spend): checked; 533 FLAT bytes; plutus-v3-pv11-uplc-1.1.0
```

Renaming `deadline` to `unlockAt` does not:

```text
elci: ELCI4001: .../vesting/elci.toml:6: [validators.vesting]: ABI drift from abi/vesting.json; compare constructor tags, field order, handler roles and parameters
```

The field names are part of the ABI, because off-chain code uses them. Constructor order, field names and types, handler roles and parameters are all compared. Nothing is written when the check fails, so the old artifacts stay in `build/`.

When the change is intended, remove the `expected-abi` line, build, review the difference, then copy the new ABI over the committed one and restore the line:

```sh
diff <(jq . abi/vesting.json) <(jq . build/validators/vesting/abi.json)
```

```text
20c20
<               "name": "deadline",
---
>               "name": "unlockAt",
27c27
<           "identity": "elci.Record:beneficiary,deadline [org.julclang.ledger.PubKeyHash, Int]",
---
>           "identity": "elci.Record:beneficiary,unlockAt [org.julclang.ledger.PubKeyHash, Int]",
31c31
<         "sourceType": "Record:beneficiary,deadline [org.julclang.ledger.PubKeyHash, Int]"
---
>         "sourceType": "Record:beneficiary,unlockAt [org.julclang.ledger.PubKeyHash, Int]"
```

## Script hashes

The script hash identifies a deployed script:

- For a **spending** validator, the script address is built from it.
- For a **minting** policy, it is the policy id.
- For **withdraw** and **certify**, it is the stake credential.

A validator without parameters has its hash in `validator.plutus.json`. A parameterized validator has an empty `hash` until you apply its parameters with `elci apply`, which prints the hash and writes it into `applied.plutus.json` (see [Parameterized validators](https://elci-lang.dev/contracts/parameters/)). Any change to the source, the handlers, the parameters or the compiler version can change the hash, so record which build you deployed.

## Loading the script in Java

Cardano Client Lib can load the artifact directly with Julc's adapter, `org.julclang:julc-cardano-client-lib`. This example reads `validator.plutus.json` (or an `applied.plutus.json`), checks the hash and derives the script's address on the preprod test network:

```java title="LoadScript.java (example)"
import com.bloxbean.cardano.client.address.AddressProvider;
import com.bloxbean.cardano.client.common.model.Networks;
import com.bloxbean.cardano.client.plutus.spec.PlutusV3Script;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.util.HexFormat;
import org.julclang.clientlib.ValidatorOutput;

public class LoadScript {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        var output = ValidatorOutput.fromJson(
                Files.readString(Path.of(args[0])));
        var script = PlutusV3Script.builder().cborHex(output.cborHex()).build();

        String hash = HexFormat.of().formatHex(script.getScriptHash());
        if (!hash.equals(output.hash())) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("Script hash mismatch");
        }
        var address = AddressProvider.getEntAddress(script, Networks.preprod());
        System.out.println("hash    " + hash);
        System.out.println("address " + address.toBech32());
    }
}
```

Run with Cardano Client Lib 0.7.2 and the Julc adapter on the classpath, it prints:

```text
hash    cdf09c382832689b016adac7ef1470488e9ff58b8a474b9086c7a0c3
address addr_test1wrxlp8pc9qex3xcpdtdv0mc5wpyga8l43w9ywjussmr6psceanc6r
```

The `PlutusV3Script` is an ordinary Cardano Client Lib script: attach it to transactions, together with datums and redeemers you build as `PlutusData` following `abi.json`. Parameterized scripts need their parameters first, either with `elci apply` or in Java, as shown on [Parameterized validators](https://elci-lang.dev/contracts/parameters/). To test Elci scripts from JUnit, see [Testing from Java](https://elci-lang.dev/testing/java/).

## Before you deploy

Elci is a development preview, and its output has not been audited. Deploy to a test network first, and treat any mainnet use as experimental. Before deploying a script:

- Run `elci test`, with scenarios for every purpose and every way a transaction should be rejected.
- Check the budgets your scenarios report. The ledger limits every transaction's CPU and memory, and the fee grows with both.
- Commit the ABI and set `expected-abi`, so that later changes can't silently break existing datums.
- Apply parameters with `elci apply`, which checks their shape, and double-check their meaning against `abi.json`.
- Record the script hash you deployed.

---

# Unit tests

> Write Bool and Expect tests for your Elci code, run them with elci test, read the results and choose which tests run.

Source: https://elci-lang.dev/testing/unit-tests/

In this page you write your first tests in Elci, run them with `elci test` and learn to read what it prints. Unit tests are the quickest way to check the pure functions your validators rely on, such as fee calculations or datum helpers.

Every test compiles to its own small program and runs on the same Plutus VM that evaluates your contracts. So a test tells you both whether your code is right and what it costs in CPU and memory.

## A function to test

Start from a project made by `elci init shop`. It already contains a validator, `src/Main.elm`, and two tests for it in `tests/MainTest.elm`. Add a module that computes a 0.3% trading fee:

```elm title="src/Pricing.elm"
module Pricing exposing (Quote, fee, quote)

type alias Quote =
    { amount : Int
    , fee : Int
    , total : Int
    }

{-| A 0.3% fee (30 basis points), rounded down.
-}
fee : Int -> Int
fee amount =
    amount * 30 // 10000

quote : Int -> Quote
quote amount =
    { amount = amount
    , fee = fee amount
    , total = amount + fee amount
    }
```

`//` is integer division that truncates toward zero, so small amounts pay no fee at all. That is exactly the kind of detail worth pinning down with a test.

## Your first tests

Tests live in modules under `tests/`. Create `tests/PricingTest.elm`:

```elm title="tests/PricingTest.elm"
module PricingTest exposing
    ( feeOnTenThousand
    , feesRoundDown
    , feesStayUnderOnePercent
    , quotesAddTheFee
    , smallAmountsAreFree
    )

import Expect exposing (Expectation)
import Pricing

smallAmountsAreFree : Bool
smallAmountsAreFree =
    Pricing.fee 300 == 0

feeOnTenThousand : Expectation
feeOnTenThousand =
    Expect.equal 30 (Pricing.fee 10000)

quotesAddTheFee : Expectation
quotesAddTheFee =
    Expect.equal { amount = 10000, fee = 30, total = 10030 } (Pricing.quote 10000)

feesRoundDown : Expectation
feesRoundDown =
    Expect.every
        [ Expect.equal 0 (Pricing.fee 333)
        , Expect.equal 1 (Pricing.fee 334)
        , Expect.equal 1 (Pricing.fee 666)
        ]

feesStayUnderOnePercent : Expectation
feesStayUnderOnePercent =
    Expect.lessThan 10000 (Pricing.fee 1000000)
        |> Expect.onFail "a fee must stay under 1% of the amount"
```

There are two kinds of unit test here:

- A **`Bool` test** passes when it evaluates to `True`. It is the simplest possible check.
- An **`Expectation` test** uses the `Expect` module. When it fails, it tells you what it expected and what it got, which a `Bool` cannot.

The project now looks like this:

- shop/
  - elci.toml
  - src/
    - Main.elm the validator from elci init
    - Pricing.elm
  - tests/
    - MainTest.elm scenarios from elci init
    - PricingTest.elm

## Run the tests

Run `elci test` from the project directory, or pass the directory as an argument:

```sh
elci test
```

```text
PASS MainTest.ownerSigns (cpu 7675163, mem 29990)
PASS MainTest.othersAreRejected (cpu 8053596, mem 31922)
PASS PricingTest.smallAmountsAreFree (cpu 675727, mem 2604)
PASS PricingTest.feeOnTenThousand (cpu 929121, mem 4068)
PASS PricingTest.quotesAddTheFee (cpu 4498493, mem 12685)
PASS PricingTest.feesRoundDown (cpu 5947066, mem 24719)
PASS PricingTest.feesStayUnderOnePercent (cpu 1794288, mem 8097)
7 passed, 0 failed
```

Each line names the test as `Module.name` and shows the CPU steps and memory units its evaluation consumed. Modules run in alphabetical order, and the tests of a module in source order. The two `MainTest` tests are [transaction scenarios](https://elci-lang.dev/testing/scenarios/): for those, the numbers are the cost of the validator itself.

`elci test` only reads your project. It never writes `build/` and its tests never become part of `elci check`, `elci build` or the published scripts.

## When a test fails

To see failures, break three tests on purpose. Check `Pricing.fee 400 == 0` in the `Bool` test, expect `31` in `feeOnTenThousand`, and expect a `total` of `10031` in `quotesAddTheFee`:

```text
FAIL PricingTest.smallAmountsAreFree (cpu 675727, mem 2604)
    evaluated to False
FAIL PricingTest.feeOnTenThousand (cpu 1991208, mem 7866)
    Expect.equal
        expected: 31
        actual:   30
FAIL PricingTest.quotesAddTheFee (cpu 5657982, mem 17219)
    Expect.equal
        expected: Constr 0 [10000, 30, 10031]
        actual:   Constr 0 [10000, 30, 10030]
PASS PricingTest.feesRoundDown (cpu 5947066, mem 24719)
PASS PricingTest.feesStayUnderOnePercent (cpu 1794288, mem 8097)
2 passed, 3 failed
```

The `Bool` test can only say that it evaluated to `False`. The expectations show both values.

Values in a failure are printed as their **Plutus Data encoding**, because that is the form the test program returns from the VM. The encoding follows the rules of your datums and redeemers:

| Elci value | Printed as |
| --- | --- |
| `30`, `-5` | `30`, `-5` |
| `Bytes.fromString "GOLD"` and the `String` `"GOLD"` | `#474f4c44` (hex of the UTF-8 bytes) |
| `False`, `True` | `Constr 0`, `Constr 1` |
| `Nothing`, `Just 5` | `Constr 0`, `Constr 1 [5]` |
| `[ 1, 2 ]` | `[1, 2]` |
| `( 1, True )` | `Constr 0 [1, Constr 1]` |
| a record | `Constr 0 [...]`, with the fields in alphabetical order of their names |
| a custom type | `Constr tag [...]`, where the tag is the constructor's position, from 0 |

So `Constr 0 [10000, 30, 10031]` is the `Quote` record with fields `amount`, `fee` and `total`.

A test can also fail at runtime, for example by dividing by zero. It is then reported with the VM's error, such as `evaluation failed: QuotientInteger: division by zero`. [Debugging and budgets](https://elci-lang.dev/testing/debugging/) covers these messages and how to add traces.

## The Expect module

`Expect` has a small set of functions in the style of elm-test. Import it with `import Expect exposing (Expectation)`.

| Function | Passes when |
| --- | --- |
| `Expect.equal expected actual` | the two values are structurally equal |
| `Expect.notEqual unexpected actual` | the two values differ |
| `Expect.atMost bound actual` | `actual <= bound` |
| `Expect.atLeast bound actual` | `actual >= bound` |
| `Expect.lessThan bound actual` | `actual < bound` |
| `Expect.greaterThan bound actual` | `actual > bound` |
| `Expect.pass` | always |
| `Expect.fail message` | never; the failure shows `message` |
| `Expect.every [ e1, e2 ]` | every expectation passes; the first failure is reported |
| `Expect.onFail message expectation` | `expectation` passes; otherwise its message is replaced |

The comparisons work on any comparable values, such as integers, strings and bytes. They take the bound first and the actual value last, so they read well in a pipeline. When one fails, the report lists the bound and then the actual value:

```elm
feesAreCapped : Expectation
feesAreCapped =
    Expect.atMost 100 (Pricing.fee 50000)
```

```text
FAIL PricingTest.feesAreCapped (cpu 2126712, mem 8766)
    Expect.atMost
        values: 100, 150
```

`Expect.onFail` puts your own explanation in place of the function name:

```elm
feesAreCappedExplained : Expectation
feesAreCappedExplained =
    Expect.atMost 100 (Pricing.fee 50000)
        |> Expect.onFail "fees are capped at 100 lovelace"
```

```text
FAIL PricingTest.feesAreCappedExplained (cpu 5046289, mem 18138)
    fees are capped at 100 lovelace
        values: 100, 150
```

`Expect.every` combines several checks into one test and reports the first that fails. Its argument is a list of evaluated expectations: Elci lists hold data, not functions, so there is no elm-test style `Expect.all` that takes checks as functions.

:::note
`Expect.equal` and `Expect.notEqual` need the same structural equality as `==`. They accept numbers, bytes, strings, `Data`, lists, tuples, records and custom types, and reject `Map`, functions and imported types without approved equality at compile time.
:::

## How tests are discovered

`elci test` treats a declaration in a test module as a test when it is:

1. **exposed** by its module,
2. a **top-level** declaration with **no arguments**, and
3. of type `Bool`, `Expect.Expectation`, `Scenario.Scenario` or `Property.Property`.

An exposed **function** whose result is a `Property` is also a test: a [property-based test](https://elci-lang.dev/testing/properties/) that runs many times with generated arguments.

Everything else is a helper. That includes functions that return an `Expectation`, a `Scenario` or a `Bool`, such as a function that builds a transaction for a given signer. With an explicit `exposing` list you choose exactly which declarations are tests. With `exposing (..)`, every zero-argument declaration of a test type runs, and declarations of other types, such as a test key of type `PubKeyHash`, are skipped.

## Choose which tests run

`--match` runs only the tests whose full name contains a substring. The match ignores case and includes the module name:

```sh
elci test --match fee
```

```text
PASS PricingTest.feeOnTenThousand (cpu 929121, mem 4068)
PASS PricingTest.quotesAddTheFee (cpu 4498493, mem 12685)
PASS PricingTest.feesRoundDown (cpu 5947066, mem 24719)
PASS PricingTest.feesStayUnderOnePercent (cpu 1794288, mem 8097)
4 passed, 0 failed
```

`quotesAddTheFee` matches because its name contains `Fee`. Use `--match PricingTest` to run one module.

## Where tests live

By default, test modules are the `.elm` files under `tests/`. To use other directories, list them in `elci.toml`:

```toml title="elci.toml"
[tests]
source-directories = ["tests", "spec"]
```

A few rules apply to test modules:

- **Imports.** A test module can import your project's modules, the Java modules configured in `[java-modules]`, the test library (`Expect`, `Scenario` and `Property`) and other test modules. A shared module such as `tests/Fixtures.elm` is a good home for test keys and sample datums. Source modules cannot import the test library: `elci test` rejects such an import with `ELCI2101`.
- **Names.** A test module cannot have the same name as a source module, or as `Expect`, `Scenario` or `Property`. `elci test` stops with `ELCI4001: module Pricing is both a source and a test module` if you try.
- **Isolation.** Test modules are compiled only by `elci test`. They cannot change what `elci build` produces.

## Use elci test in CI

`elci test` exits with status `1` when any test fails, and also when no test is found or none matches `--match`:

```text
No tests match 'nothing-here'
```

Otherwise it exits with `0`. You can run it as a step in any CI pipeline without extra configuration.

## Next steps

- Test whole transactions against your validators with [transaction scenarios](https://elci-lang.dev/testing/scenarios/).
- Check a rule for many generated inputs with [property-based tests](https://elci-lang.dev/testing/properties/).
- Look up every function in the [test library reference](https://elci-lang.dev/reference/test-library/).

---

# Transaction scenarios

> Test validators with whole transactions. Describe a spend, mint or withdrawal in Elci and elci test runs the deployed script in a complete ledger context.

Source: https://elci-lang.dev/testing/scenarios/

A scenario describes one transaction against one of your validators, and `elci test` checks that the validator accepts or rejects it. In this page you test a small marketplace: spending with a payment, a validity range and a continuing output, minting, and withdrawing staking rewards.

Unit tests check functions. Scenarios check what actually goes on-chain: the compiled script, its purpose dispatch, the strict decoding of the datum and redeemer, and your logic, all against a realistic `ScriptContext`.

## How a scenario runs

A `Scenario` is plain data: a record that names a validator and lists the transaction's details. You build it with a pipeline of functions from the `Scenario` module, starting with the purpose. These two come from the test module that `elci init` generates:

```elm
transaction : Scenario
transaction =
    Scenario.spend "main" (Scenario.outRef "main" 0) Scenario.unit
        |> Scenario.parameters [ Data.encode owner ]

ownerSigns : Scenario
ownerSigns =
    transaction
        |> Scenario.signedBy owner
```

`transaction` spends an output of the validator `main`, and `ownerSigns` is the same transaction signed by the owner. Only `ownerSigns` is a test: `transaction` is not exposed.

When `elci test` finds an exposed `Scenario` value, it:

1. compiles the named validator exactly as `elci build` does, and applies the scenario's `parameters` in the order the validator declares them;
2. computes the applied script's hash, which gives the validator its own address, minting policy and staking credential;
3. builds the complete ledger context with julc-testkit's `ScriptContextTestBuilder`: purpose, redeemer, signers, inputs, outputs, minted tokens, fee and validity range;
4. runs the **deployed script** against that context, so purpose dispatch and strict datum and redeemer decoding happen exactly as on-chain;
5. compares the outcome with the expectation: success by default, or rejection after `Scenario.expectFailure`, plus an optional budget.

Because the script is the one `elci build` publishes, a passing scenario is evidence about your real artifact, not about a simulation of it.

## The example project

The marketplace has two validators. `market` holds listings and earns staking rewards: its `spend` handler lets anyone buy a listing before it expires by paying the seller, and lets the seller change the price or delist. Its `withdraw` handler lets only the operator withdraw rewards. `ticket` is a minting policy for event tickets.

```toml title="elci.toml"
[project]
source-directories = ["src"]
target = "plutus-v3-pv11-uplc-1.1.0"
julc-version = "0.1.0-pre20-ebaf028-SNAPSHOT"

# The market script: holds listings and earns staking rewards.
[validators.market]
boundary = "julc-strict-v1"
parameters = ["operator"]
spend = "Market.spend"
withdraw = "Market.withdraw"

# The ticket minting policy.
[validators.ticket]
boundary = "julc-strict-v1"
parameters = ["organizer"]
mint = "Ticket.mint"
```

```elm title="src/Market.elm"
module Market exposing (Action(..), Listing, spend, withdraw)

import Interval
import Julc.Data as Data
import Julc.Ledger exposing (Credential(..), PubKeyHash, ScriptContext, TxOut)
import Tx
import Value

type alias Listing =
    { seller : PubKeyHash
    , price : Int
    , expires : Int
    }

type Action
    = Buy
    | Reprice Int
    | Delist

{-| Anyone may buy before the listing expires by paying the seller the price.
The seller may change the price or delist at any time.
-}
spend : PubKeyHash -> Listing -> Action -> ScriptContext -> Bool
spend _ listing action ctx =
    case action of
        Buy ->
            sellerPaid listing ctx
                && Interval.isEntirelyBefore listing.expires ctx.txInfo.validRange

        Reprice newPrice ->
            Tx.signedBy listing.seller ctx
                && List.any (holds { listing | price = newPrice }) (Tx.continuingOutputs ctx)

        Delist ->
            Tx.signedBy listing.seller ctx

{-| Only the operator withdraws the market's staking rewards.
-}
withdraw : PubKeyHash -> () -> ScriptContext -> Bool
withdraw operator _ ctx =
    Tx.signedBy operator ctx

{-| An output pays the seller the price and carries this listing's output reference, so
that it can't also pay for another listing in the same transaction.
-}
sellerPaid : Listing -> ScriptContext -> Bool
sellerPaid listing ctx =
    case Tx.ownRef ctx of
        Just ref ->
            List.any
                (\output ->
                    (Value.lovelaceOf output.value >= listing.price)
                        && (Tx.inlineDatum output == Just (Data.encode ref))
                )
                (Tx.outputsTo (PubKeyCredential listing.seller) ctx)

        Nothing ->
            False

holds : Listing -> TxOut -> Bool
holds expected output =
    Tx.inlineDatum output == Just (Data.encode expected)
```

```elm title="src/Ticket.elm"
module Ticket exposing (mint)

import Bytes
import Julc.Ledger exposing (PubKeyHash, ScriptContext, TokenName(..))
import Tx
import Value

{-| The organizer mints exactly one TICKET per transaction.
-}
mint : PubKeyHash -> () -> ScriptContext -> Bool
mint organizer _ ctx =
    case Tx.ownPolicy ctx of
        Just policy ->
            (Value.quantityOf policy (TokenName (Bytes.fromString "TICKET")) ctx.txInfo.mint == 1)
                && Tx.signedBy organizer ctx

        Nothing ->
            False
```

The validators read the transaction with the core [`Tx` and `Interval`](https://elci-lang.dev/reference/core-modules/#tx)
modules. A buyer's payment must carry the listing's output reference as its inline datum, so one payment
can't pay for two listings bought in the same transaction; [reading the
transaction](https://elci-lang.dev/contracts/reading-the-transaction/#one-payment-per-input) explains why.

## Test keys and a helper

Start the test module with the people involved and helpers that build the common parts of every spend.
`Scenario.key` derives a deterministic 28-byte key hash from a name, so `Scenario.key "seller"` is the same
in every test and every run:

```elm title="tests/MarketTest.elm"
module MarketTest exposing
    ( buyerPaysTheSeller
    , buyingAfterExpiryFails
    , buyingWithoutADeadlineFails
    , operatorWithdrawsRewards
    , othersCannotWithdraw
    , paymentForAnotherListingFails
    , sellerDelists
    , sellerReprices
    , strangerCannotDelist
    , underpayingFails
    )

import Julc.Data as Data
import Julc.Ledger exposing (PubKeyHash)
import Market exposing (Action(..), Listing)
import Scenario exposing (Output, Scenario)

operator : PubKeyHash
operator =
    Scenario.key "operator"

seller : PubKeyHash
seller =
    Scenario.key "seller"

listing : Listing
listing =
    { seller = seller, price = 50000000, expires = 2000 }

{-| Spend the listed output with an action.
-}
settle : Action -> Scenario
settle action =
    Scenario.spend "market" (Scenario.outRef "listing" 0) (Data.encode listing)
        |> Scenario.parameters [ Data.encode operator ]
        |> Scenario.redeemer (Data.encode action)

{-| A payment to the seller, tagged with the listing's output reference.
-}
payment : Int -> Output
payment lovelace =
    Scenario.toKey seller lovelace
        |> Scenario.withDatum (Data.encode (Scenario.outRef "listing" 0))
```

`settle` returns a `Scenario` but takes an argument, so it is a helper, not a test. The same goes for `operator`, `seller`, `listing` and `payment`, whose types are not test types. `payment` builds an output with `Scenario.toKey`, which pays a key's address without a staking part, and tags it with the listing's reference.

Everything that crosses into the script is `Data`, so datums, redeemers and parameters are encoded with `Data.encode`. `Scenario.parameters` must give every parameter the validator declares, in order; `market` declares one, `operator`. `Scenario.outRef "listing" 0` makes a deterministic output reference from a name and an index; `settle` spends that output, and `payment` tags with the same reference.

## Spending

`Scenario.spend validator ref datum` spends `ref`. The runner adds the spent output to the transaction's inputs, at the validator's own address, holding 2 ADA and the datum inline. Then you add what the transaction does. A buyer pays the seller and the transaction must end before the listing expires:

```elm
buyerPaysTheSeller : Scenario
buyerPaysTheSeller =
    settle Buy
        |> Scenario.output (payment 50000000)
        |> Scenario.validBefore 1500

underpayingFails : Scenario
underpayingFails =
    settle Buy
        |> Scenario.output (payment 49999999)
        |> Scenario.validBefore 1500
        |> Scenario.expectFailure
```

`Scenario.expectFailure` turns a scenario into a negative test: it passes only when the validator rejects the transaction. Write one next to each rule: a validator that accepts everything passes every positive test.

Test the attacks too. A payment tagged with another listing's reference must not pay for this one:

```elm
{-| A payment tagged for another listing can't also pay for this one.
-}
paymentForAnotherListingFails : Scenario
paymentForAnotherListingFails =
    settle Buy
        |> Scenario.output
            (Scenario.toKey seller 50000000
                |> Scenario.withDatum (Data.encode (Scenario.outRef "listing" 1))
            )
        |> Scenario.validBefore 1500
        |> Scenario.expectFailure
```

Signatures work the same way. `Scenario.signedBy` adds a required signer, and you can call it more than once:

```elm
sellerDelists : Scenario
sellerDelists =
    settle Delist
        |> Scenario.signedBy seller

strangerCannotDelist : Scenario
strangerCannotDelist =
    settle Delist
        |> Scenario.signedBy (Scenario.key "stranger")
        |> Scenario.expectFailure
```

For a spend without a datum, as with `spend-datum = "optional"` or `"absent"`, use `Scenario.spendWithoutDatum validator ref`.

## Validity ranges

A transaction without `validFrom` or `validBefore` is valid at any time: both bounds are infinite. The two functions set the bounds in POSIX time:

- `Scenario.validFrom time` sets an **inclusive** lower bound: the transaction is valid from `time`.
- `Scenario.validBefore time` sets an **exclusive** upper bound: the transaction is valid before `time`.

```elm
buyingAfterExpiryFails : Scenario
buyingAfterExpiryFails =
    settle Buy
        |> Scenario.output (payment 50000000)
        |> Scenario.validFrom 1800
        |> Scenario.validBefore 2500
        |> Scenario.expectFailure

buyingWithoutADeadlineFails : Scenario
buyingWithoutADeadlineFails =
    settle Buy
        |> Scenario.output (payment 50000000)
        |> Scenario.expectFailure
```

The second test matters: a transaction without an upper bound could run long after the listing expired. `Interval.isEntirelyBefore` needs a finite end, so the validator rejects it.

## Outputs, datums and tokens

An output is built with one of four functions and then extended:

- `Scenario.toKey key lovelace` pays a key's address, without a staking part.
- `Scenario.toAddress address lovelace` pays any address, such as one with a staking part.
- `Scenario.toScript lovelace` pays the validator's own script address, which has no staking part.
- `Scenario.toStakedScript stake lovelace` pays the validator's own payment credential with a staking part. That is another address: `Tx.continuingOutputs` of an output spent from `toScript`'s address doesn't include it.
- `Scenario.withDatum data` attaches an inline datum.
- `Scenario.withDatumHash data` holds the datum by hash instead: the output carries the datum's hash, and the transaction carries the datum among its witnesses. `Tx.datumOf` finds it there; `Tx.inlineDatum` returns `Nothing` for such an output.
- `Scenario.withToken policy name quantity` adds tokens. The policy is `Scenario.Own`, the validator's own policy, or `Scenario.Policy bytes` for any other.

The runner builds every value the ledger's way, as the script expects a [`Value`](https://elci-lang.dev/reference/core-modules/#value) to be: policies and token names in ascending order, quantities of a repeated token added up, and zero quantities left out. So the order of your `withToken` and `Scenario.minting` calls never matters, and `Scenario.minting name 0` mints nothing. The ledger limits policy ids and token names to 32 bytes, and so does the runner: a longer one fails the scenario before the validator runs, even with `expectFailure`, with `cannot build the transaction: A scenario value has a policy id or token name longer than 32 bytes, which the ledger does not allow`.

Repricing requires a continuing output, one of `Tx.continuingOutputs`: an output back at the market's address that carries the updated listing:

```elm
sellerReprices : Scenario
sellerReprices =
    settle (Reprice 40000000)
        |> Scenario.signedBy seller
        |> Scenario.output
            (Scenario.toScript 2000000
                |> Scenario.withDatum (Data.encode { listing | price = 40000000 })
            )
```

To give the spent output tokens or a different value, list it yourself with `Scenario.input` and the same reference. The runner then uses your input instead of the default one. As on the ledger, it must hold the datum that `Scenario.spend` gives, inline or by hash; otherwise the scenario fails before the validator runs with `cannot build the transaction: the spent output ... is listed with a different datum from the one Scenario.spend gives`. This test also needs `import Bytes`:

```elm
listingHoldsAnNft : Scenario
listingHoldsAnNft =
    settle Delist
        |> Scenario.signedBy seller
        |> Scenario.input (Scenario.outRef "listing" 0)
            (Scenario.toScript 2000000
                |> Scenario.withDatum (Data.encode listing)
                |> Scenario.withToken (Scenario.Policy (Bytes.replicate 28 7)) (Bytes.fromString "ART") 1
            )
```

`Scenario.referenceInput ref output` adds a reference input, such as an oracle output your validator reads, and `Scenario.worth lovelace` changes the lovelace of the default spent output.

## Minting

`Scenario.mint validator` runs the validator as a minting policy. Its policy id is the applied script's hash, so the tokens you add with `Scenario.minting name quantity` are minted under that policy. Token names are bytes, usually written with `Bytes.fromString`:

```elm title="tests/TicketTest.elm"
module TicketTest exposing
    ( burningIsRejected
    , organizerMintsOneTicket
    , twoTicketsAreRejected
    , unsignedMintIsRejected
    )

import Bytes
import Julc.Data as Data
import Julc.Ledger exposing (PubKeyHash)
import Scenario exposing (Scenario)

organizer : PubKeyHash
organizer =
    Scenario.key "organizer"

tickets : Int -> Scenario
tickets quantity =
    Scenario.mint "ticket"
        |> Scenario.parameters [ Data.encode organizer ]
        |> Scenario.minting (Bytes.fromString "TICKET") quantity

organizerMintsOneTicket : Scenario
organizerMintsOneTicket =
    tickets 1
        |> Scenario.signedBy organizer

twoTicketsAreRejected : Scenario
twoTicketsAreRejected =
    tickets 2
        |> Scenario.signedBy organizer
        |> Scenario.expectFailure

burningIsRejected : Scenario
burningIsRejected =
    tickets -1
        |> Scenario.signedBy organizer
        |> Scenario.expectFailure

unsignedMintIsRejected : Scenario
unsignedMintIsRejected =
    tickets 1
        |> Scenario.expectFailure
```

A negative quantity burns, so `tickets -1` burns one ticket, which this policy rejects. As in Elm, `tickets -1` passes the argument `-1`, while `quantity - 1` subtracts.

```sh
elci test --match TicketTest
```

```text
PASS TicketTest.organizerMintsOneTicket (cpu 11788207, mem 41590)
PASS TicketTest.twoTicketsAreRejected (cpu 9157880, mem 32745)
PASS TicketTest.burningIsRejected (cpu 9157880, mem 32745)
PASS TicketTest.unsignedMintIsRejected (cpu 11483010, mem 39957)
4 passed, 0 failed
```

## Withdrawing rewards

`Scenario.withdraw validator` runs the validator for a withdrawal from its own staking credential:

```elm
operatorWithdrawsRewards : Scenario
operatorWithdrawsRewards =
    Scenario.withdraw "market"
        |> Scenario.parameters [ Data.encode operator ]
        |> Scenario.signedBy operator

othersCannotWithdraw : Scenario
othersCannotWithdraw =
    Scenario.withdraw "market"
        |> Scenario.parameters [ Data.encode operator ]
        |> Scenario.signedBy seller
        |> Scenario.expectFailure
```

`market` is one script with two handlers, so these scenarios and the spending ones above run the same compiled script. The purpose in the context selects the handler.

## Certificates, votes and proposals

The remaining purposes take what the ledger supplies for them, built with `Julc.Ledger` constructors. These are the transactions that `elci init --purpose certify`, `vote` and `propose` generate, with `import Julc.Data as Data`, `import Julc.Ledger as Ledger` and a test key `owner`:

```elm
Scenario.certify "main" 0 (Ledger.RegStaking (Ledger.PubKeyCredential owner) (Data.toOptional Nothing))

Scenario.vote "main" (Ledger.DRepVoter (Ledger.PubKeyCredential owner))

Scenario.propose "main" 0 (Ledger.ProposalProcedure 0 (Ledger.PubKeyCredential owner) Ledger.InfoAction)
```

The integer after the validator name is the index of the certificate or proposal in the transaction.

## Run the scenarios

```sh
elci test --match MarketTest
```

```text
PASS MarketTest.buyerPaysTheSeller (cpu 33518015, mem 117583)
PASS MarketTest.underpayingFails (cpu 24050900, mem 93018)
PASS MarketTest.paymentForAnotherListingFails (cpu 27935021, mem 101832)
PASS MarketTest.sellerDelists (cpu 15573596, mem 65977)
PASS MarketTest.strangerCannotDelist (cpu 15952029, mem 67909)
PASS MarketTest.buyingAfterExpiryFails (cpu 33502015, mem 117483)
PASS MarketTest.buyingWithoutADeadlineFails (cpu 31346102, mem 111033)
PASS MarketTest.sellerReprices (cpu 36080596, mem 124349)
PASS MarketTest.operatorWithdrawsRewards (cpu 7879274, mem 35433)
PASS MarketTest.othersCannotWithdraw (cpu 8257707, mem 37365)
10 passed, 0 failed
```

For a scenario, the CPU and memory are what the **validator** consumed for that transaction, including a rejected one. These execution units are what the script adds to your transaction's fee.

When a scenario does not get the outcome it expects, the report says why. Here, `strangerDelists` is `strangerCannotDelist` without `expectFailure`, `sellerCannotDelist` is `sellerDelists` with it, `typo` names a validator that does not exist, and `unparameterized` is `operatorWithdrawsRewards` without `Scenario.parameters`:

```text
FAIL MarketTest.strangerDelists (cpu 15952029, mem 67909)
    validator market rejected the transaction: Error term encountered
FAIL MarketTest.sellerCannotDelist (cpu 15573596, mem 65977)
    validator market accepted a transaction expected to fail
FAIL MarketTest.typo
    cannot prepare validator 'markt': no [validators.markt] in elci.toml
FAIL MarketTest.unparameterized
    cannot prepare validator 'market': it takes 1 parameter [operator], but the scenario gives 0; set them with Scenario.parameters
```
