The last two fail before the validator runs, so they fail even with `Scenario.expectFailure`: a scenario cannot pass just because it was set up wrongly.

A validator that returns `False` fails with `Error term encountered`. [Debugging and budgets](https://elci-lang.dev/testing/debugging/) shows how to find out which check failed.

:::caution[Set the redeemer]
The default redeemer is `Scenario.unit`, which encodes as `Constr 0 []`. That is also the encoding of the first constructor of a union without fields, such as `Buy`. A scenario that forgets `Scenario.redeemer` can therefore run a different action than you meant. Set the redeemer explicitly.
:::

## All builder functions

The complete signatures are in the [test library reference](https://elci-lang.dev/reference/test-library/).

**Start a scenario** with the purpose. `validator` is the name of a `[validators.<name>]` table.

| Function | Transaction |
| --- | --- |
| `spend validator ref datum` | spends `ref`, held at the script address with an inline `datum` |
| `spendWithoutDatum validator ref` | spends `ref`, held at the script address without a datum |
| `mint validator` | mints or burns under the validator's own policy |
| `withdraw validator` | withdraws from the validator's own staking credential |
| `certify validator index certificate` | publishes a `TxCert` at an index |
| `vote validator voter` | votes as `voter` |
| `propose validator index procedure` | submits a `ProposalProcedure` at an index |

**Describe the transaction.**

| Function | Effect | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `redeemer data` | the redeemer | `Scenario.unit` |
| `parameters [ data, ... ]` | deployment parameters, in declared order; required when the validator has parameters | none |
| `signedBy key` | adds a required signer | no signers |
| `fee lovelace` | the transaction fee | 200000 |
| `validFrom time` | inclusive lower bound of the validity range | unbounded |
| `validBefore time` | exclusive upper bound of the validity range | unbounded |

**Add inputs, outputs and tokens.**

| Function | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `input ref output` | adds an input; with the spent `ref`, replaces the default spent output, and must hold the spend's datum |
| `referenceInput ref output` | adds a reference input |
| `output out` | adds an output |
| `minting name quantity` | mints (positive) or burns (negative) under the own policy |
| `worth lovelace` | lovelace held by the default spent output (default 2000000) |
| `toKey key lovelace` | an output to the key's address, without a staking part |
| `toScript lovelace` | an output to the validator's own address |
| `toStakedScript stake lovelace` | an output to the validator's own payment credential with the staking credential `stake` |
| `toAddress address lovelace` | an output to `address` |
| `withDatum data` | gives an output an inline datum |
| `withDatumHash data` | gives an output the datum's hash, and the transaction the datum as a witness |
| `withToken policy name quantity` | adds tokens to an output; `policy` is `Own` or `Policy bytes` |

**Set the expectation.**

| Function | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `expectFailure` | the validator must reject the transaction |
| `withinBudget cpu memory` | the execution must cost at most this CPU and memory |

**Make test data.**

| Function | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `key name` | a deterministic 28-byte `PubKeyHash` derived from `name` |
| `outRef name index` | a deterministic `TxOutRef` derived from `name` and `index` |
| `unit` | the `Data` of `()` |

## Limits

Scenarios cover single and multiple signatures, validity ranges, lovelace, tokens of the own policy and of other policies, inline datums, datums by hash, reference inputs and every purpose. The validator's own address has no staking part. The following need a [Java test suite](https://elci-lang.dev/testing/java/), where you build the context yourself:

- reference scripts;
- other staking credentials and additional withdrawals;
- more than one script in a transaction.

## Next steps

- Run a scenario for many generated inputs with [property-based tests](https://elci-lang.dev/testing/properties/).
- Find out why a validator rejects a transaction in [Debugging and budgets](https://elci-lang.dev/testing/debugging/).

---

# Property-based tests

> State a rule that must hold for every input, let elci test generate hundreds of inputs, and get the smallest counterexample when the rule breaks.

Source: https://elci-lang.dev/testing/properties/

A property is a rule that should hold for **every** input, such as "a buyer who pays less than the price is rejected". In this page you write properties for pure functions and for whole transactions, read a shrunk counterexample, and learn to shape generated inputs so they find real bugs.

## Why properties

A unit test or a scenario checks one input you thought of. The bugs that hurt in smart contracts usually sit at inputs nobody thought of: a negative amount, an empty byte string, a validity range that ends exactly at the deadline, a 64-bit number. A property describes the rule once. `elci test` then:

1. generates arguments from the property's parameter types;
2. runs the property 100 times, starting with small values;
3. when a run fails, shrinks the arguments to a small counterexample and reports it.

## Your first property

Take the `Pricing` module from [Unit tests](https://elci-lang.dev/testing/unit-tests/). Adding the fee to an amount should never give a total below the amount. Write that as a property in `tests/PricingProperties.elm`:

```elm title="tests/PricingProperties.elm"
module PricingProperties exposing (quotesNeverLoseValue)

import Pricing
import Property exposing (Property)

quotesNeverLoseValue : Int -> Property
quotesNeverLoseValue amount =
    Property.holds ((Pricing.quote amount).total >= amount)
```

A property is an exposed function whose result type is `Property`. Its parameters are the inputs to generate: here one `Int`. Run it:

```sh
elci test --seed 42 --match PricingProperties
```

```text
FAIL PricingProperties.quotesNeverLoseValue (15 runs, cpu 5409589, mem 21823)
    counterexample after 15 runs, shrunk 4 times:
        quotesNeverLoseValue (-334)
    the property does not hold
0 passed, 1 failed (seed 42)
```

The 15th run failed on a negative number, and the runner shrank it four times to `-334`. That is the negative amount closest to zero that breaks the rule: `-334 * 30 // 10000` is `-1`, because `//` truncates toward zero, so the total is `-335`. No amount between `-333` and `0` fails, which is why shrinking stopped there.

The counterexample is printed as an Elci call, so you can reproduce it directly in a unit test.

### State the real rule

The property found a real question: what should a quote for a negative amount be? A lovelace amount can never be negative, so the honest fix is to state that in the property. Use `modBy` to turn any generated integer into a valid amount:

```elm title="tests/PricingProperties.elm"
module PricingProperties exposing (quotesNeverLoseValue)

import Pricing
import Property exposing (Property)

{-| Any amount of lovelace up to the 45 billion ADA supply.
-}
quotesNeverLoseValue : Int -> Property
quotesNeverLoseValue raw =
    let
        amount =
            modBy 45000000000000000 raw
    in
    Property.holds ((Pricing.quote amount).total >= amount)
```

```text
PASS PricingProperties.quotesNeverLoseValue (100 runs, max cpu 4641008, mem 18984)
1 passed, 0 failed (seed 42)
```

For a passing property, the budget is the costliest of its runs. For a failing one, it is the counterexample's run.

## The Property module

`Property` has one type and three ways to build it:

| Function | The property holds when |
| --- | --- |
| `Property.holds condition` | the `Bool` is `True` |
| `Property.expect expectation` | the `Expectation` passes, so failures show `expected` and `actual` |
| `Property.scenario transaction` | the `Scenario` has its expected outcome, so a property can run your deployed validator |

The result type is what makes a function a property. An exposed function that returns a `Bool`, an `Expectation` or a `Scenario` is a helper, never a test, however many arguments it takes. So you can write helpers freely. The only helpers to keep unexposed are those that themselves return a `Property`, because an exposed function returning `Property` is run as a property.

A zero-argument value of type `Property` is allowed too. It runs once, like a unit test.

## Properties over transactions

`Property.scenario` runs a transaction against the deployed validator on every run. Here are four properties for the marketplace from [Transaction scenarios](https://elci-lang.dev/testing/scenarios/). The module repeats the scenario helpers; in a larger project, put them in a shared test module.

```elm title="tests/MarketProperties.elm"
module MarketProperties exposing
    ( buyersMustPayThePrice
    , buyingClosesAtExpiry
    , listingsRoundTrip
    , onlyTheSellerDelists
    )

import Expect
import Julc.Data as Data
import Julc.Ledger exposing (PubKeyHash)
import Market exposing (Action(..), Listing)
import Property exposing (Property)
import Scenario exposing (Output, Scenario)

seller : PubKeyHash
seller =
    Scenario.key "seller"

listing : Listing
listing =
    { seller = seller, price = 50000000, expires = 2000 }

settle : Action -> Scenario
settle action =
    Scenario.spend "market" (Scenario.outRef "listing" 0) (Data.encode listing)
        |> Scenario.parameters [ Data.encode (Scenario.key "operator") ]
        |> Scenario.redeemer (Data.encode action)

payment : Int -> Output
payment lovelace =
    Scenario.toKey seller lovelace
        |> Scenario.withDatum (Data.encode (Scenario.outRef "listing" 0))

{-| Succeeds when `ok`, and must be rejected otherwise.
-}
expecting : Bool -> Scenario -> Property
expecting ok transaction =
    if ok then
        Property.scenario transaction

    else
        Property.scenario (Scenario.expectFailure transaction)

listingsRoundTrip : Listing -> Property
listingsRoundTrip generated =
    Property.expect (Expect.equal generated (Data.decode (Data.encode generated)))

{-| Whatever a listing holds, only its seller can delist it.
-}
onlyTheSellerDelists : Listing -> Bool -> Property
onlyTheSellerDelists generated bySeller =
    let
        signer =
            if bySeller then
                generated.seller

            else
                Scenario.key "stranger"
    in
    Scenario.spend "market" (Scenario.outRef "listing" 0) (Data.encode generated)
        |> Scenario.parameters [ Data.encode (Scenario.key "operator") ]
        |> Scenario.redeemer (Data.encode Delist)
        |> Scenario.signedBy signer
        |> expecting bySeller

buyersMustPayThePrice : Int -> Property
buyersMustPayThePrice shortBy =
    settle Buy
        |> Scenario.output (payment (listing.price - shortBy))
        |> Scenario.validBefore 1500
        |> expecting (shortBy <= 0)

buyingClosesAtExpiry : Int -> Property
buyingClosesAtExpiry offset =
    let
        end =
            listing.expires + offset
    in
    settle Buy
        |> Scenario.output (payment listing.price)
        |> Scenario.validBefore end
        |> expecting (end <= listing.expires)
```

- `listingsRoundTrip` checks that any `Listing` survives encoding and strict decoding, the path every datum takes into your script.
- `onlyTheSellerDelists` generates whole listings and signs either with the listing's own seller or with a stranger. The validator must accept exactly the first case.
- `buyersMustPayThePrice` pays the seller `shortBy` lovelace less than the price. Any shortfall above zero must be rejected, and paying the price or more must succeed.
- `buyingClosesAtExpiry` ends the validity range `offset` milliseconds from the listing's expiry.

`expecting` is the helper that turns "should this succeed?" into the right scenario. It returns a `Property`, so it stays unexposed.

```sh
elci test --seed 7 --match MarketProperties
```

```text
PASS MarketProperties.listingsRoundTrip (100 runs, max cpu 11509152, mem 46989)
PASS MarketProperties.onlyTheSellerDelists (100 runs, max cpu 15953522, mem 67909)
PASS MarketProperties.buyersMustPayThePrice (100 runs, max cpu 33518015, mem 117583)
PASS MarketProperties.buyingClosesAtExpiry (100 runs, max cpu 33518015, mem 117583)
4 passed, 0 failed (seed 7)
```

### A property catches a bug

Suppose someone changes `sellerPaid` in `src/Market.elm` to accept payments 100 lovelace short of the price, `(listing.price - 100)`. The property finds the boundary on its own:

```text
FAIL MarketProperties.buyersMustPayThePrice (1 run, cpu 33683223, mem 117985)
    counterexample after 1 run, shrunk 5 times:
        buyersMustPayThePrice 1
    validator market accepted a transaction expected to fail
0 passed, 1 failed (seed 7)
```

Paying 1 lovelace short is accepted. The `underpayingFails` scenario catches this particular bug as well, but only because it underpays by exactly 1 lovelace. The property does not depend on you picking the right example.

### A property finds an edge case

The first version of `buyingClosesAtExpiry` stated the rule as "succeed when the range ends before the expiry", a negative offset:

```elm
buyingClosesAtExpiry : Int -> Property
buyingClosesAtExpiry offset =
    settle Buy
        |> Scenario.output (payment listing.price)
        |> Scenario.validBefore (listing.expires + offset)
        |> expecting (offset < 0)
```

```text
FAIL MarketProperties.buyingClosesAtExpiry (1 run, cpu 33518015, mem 117583)
    counterexample after 1 run:
        buyingClosesAtExpiry 0
    validator market accepted a transaction expected to fail
0 passed, 1 failed (seed 7)
```

An offset of `0` ends the range at the expiry, and the validator accepts it. The validator is right: `validBefore` is exclusive, so a transaction valid before `2000` can't run at `2000`, and every time it can run at is before the expiry. The final version states the complete rule: `end <= listing.expires`.

## Seeds and runs

The summary line of a run with properties shows its seed. Without `--seed`, the seed is random, so each run explores new inputs:

```text
8 passed, 0 failed (seed -2828489748881525870)
```

Two options control properties:

- `--seed <n>` reproduces a run exactly. Each property derives its own seed from `n` and its name, so a property sees the same inputs whatever `--match` selects. Pass the seed from a failing run to reproduce the failure.
- `--fuzz <runs>` changes the number of runs per property. The default is 100.

```sh
elci test --seed 42 --fuzz 1000 --match PricingProperties
```

```text
PASS PricingProperties.quotesNeverLoseValue (1000 runs, max cpu 4641008, mem 18984)
1 passed, 0 failed (seed 42)
```

## Generated values

Every generated argument is a valid value of its type. It is produced as Plutus Data and decoded by the same strict decoder a validator uses for its datum and redeemer, so a property sees exactly what the ledger could send.

| Type | Generated values | Shrinks toward |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Int` | mostly small values around 0, the edge cases 0, 1 and -1, and some values up to 64 bits | `0` |
| `Bytes`, `String` | up to 64 bytes, sometimes exactly 28 or 32 (hash sizes) | `#(empty)`, `""` |
| `PubKeyHash`, `ScriptHash`, `ValidatorHash`, `PolicyId` parameter | exactly 28 bytes | 28 zero bytes |
| `TxId`, `DatumHash` parameter | exactly 32 bytes | 32 zero bytes |
| `TokenName` parameter | 0 to 32 bytes | `#(empty)` |
| `List a`, `Map k v` | grow with the run; map keys are distinct | shorter lists and maps |
| `Dict k v` | grow with the run; keys are sorted and distinct, as decoding requires | smaller dictionaries, still sorted |
| `Value` | canonical values: often some lovelace, and a few tokens under 28-byte policies; quantities may be negative, never zero | fewer policies, down to the empty value |
| records, tuples | built from their fields | each field shrinks |
| unions, `Maybe` | every constructor is used | earlier constructors, such as `Nothing` |
| recursive unions | always finite; the first runs use the shallowest constructors | their own subterms |

The exact lengths apply to a **parameter** of a hash type. A hash inside a record, such as a listing's `seller`, follows its Data representation and can have any length, including zero.

Counterexamples are printed in Elci syntax. Byte strings are hex, record fields appear in alphabetical order, and constructors appear without their module name. Some shrunk counterexamples from failing properties:

| Property parameters | Counterexample |
| --- | --- |
| `Listing -> Bool` | `onlyTheSellerDelists { expires = 0, price = 0, seller = #(empty) } False` |
| `Action -> Maybe Int -> ( Int, Bool )` | `unions Buy Nothing ( 0, False )` |
| `Map Int Bytes`, failing for two or more entries | `maps (Map.fromList [( 0, #(empty) ), ( 1, #(empty) )])` |
| `Shape`, a recursive union with constructors `Dot`, `Line Int` and `Pair Shape Shape` | `smallShapes (Pair (Pair Dot Dot) Dot)` |

## Shape the inputs

Generated integers cluster around 0, and shrinking moves toward 0. Design your parameters so that 0 sits where the interesting behavior is.

**Generate an offset from the boundary.** `buyersMustPayThePrice` takes a shortfall and `buyingClosesAtExpiry` an offset from the expiry, rather than a price or a time. The boundary between success and failure is then at 0, where most generated values fall, and a counterexample shrinks to the smallest step across it, such as `buyersMustPayThePrice 1`.

**Bound values with `modBy`.** When the rule only makes sense in a range, such as non-negative amounts, transform the raw argument with `modBy` as in `quotesNeverLoseValue`. `modBy n` always gives a result from 0 to `n - 1`.

Prefer offsets when a boundary matters. With `end = modBy 4000 raw` instead of an offset, a validator bug that accepted purchases up to 50 ms after the expiry passed in 9 of 10 seeds: the generated values rarely land in a 50-wide window. The offset version reported `buyingClosesAtExpiry 1` on its first failing run.

:::note[Counterexamples show the raw argument]
Arguments are shrunk before your transformation runs, and the report shows the generated argument, not the transformed value. For a property that computes `amount = 1000 + modBy 1000000 raw`, a failure is reported as `bigOrdersPayAtLeastFour 0` although the property checked `amount = 1000`. Apply the same transformation to read it.
:::

## Limits

A property's parameters must be concrete, Data-encodable types. `elci test` rejects others before running anything. For `applies : (Int -> Int) -> Property` it reports:

```text
tests/Lim.elm:6:1: ELCI2009: Property applies needs Data-encodable parameters to generate; functions, arrays and ScriptContext cannot be generated (take a List and use Array.fromList)

6| applies : (Int -> Int) -> Property
   ^^^^^^^
```

- **Functions** cannot be generated.
- **Arrays** have no Data encoding. Take a `List` and convert it with `Array.fromList` inside the property.
- **`ScriptContext`** cannot be generated. Use `Property.scenario` to run the validator in a complete context instead.
- **Type variables** must be concrete: `anything : a -> Property` is rejected with `ELCI2009: Property anything needs concrete parameter types; add a type annotation`.

Generation and shrinking come from julc-testkit's `DataGenerators` and `PropertyCheck`. They are seeded and need no reflection, so the native `elci` binary runs properties too. For property tests driven from Java with jqwik, see [Testing from Java](https://elci-lang.dev/testing/java/).

---

# Testing from Java

> Load the scripts elci build publishes into JUnit, build ledger contexts with julc-testkit and run jqwik property tests with datums generated from the validator's ABI.

Source: https://elci-lang.dev/testing/java/

`elci test` covers most contracts. When you need full control over the ledger context, or want your contract tests next to the Java code of your off-chain application, you can test the same scripts from JUnit. In this page you set up a Gradle test suite, evaluate a validator with julc-testkit, and write jqwik properties with generated datums and redeemers.

Reach for Java when a test needs something [scenarios](https://elci-lang.dev/testing/scenarios/) cannot describe: reference scripts, other staking credentials or several withdrawals, or more than one script in a transaction.

## Set up a test suite

Elci is a development preview and is not published to a Maven repository. Put the JARs of your Elci build on the test classpath instead: `./gradlew installDist` in the Elci repository writes them to `build/install/elci/lib`, together with the pinned Julc libraries they need. The jqwik integration, `julc-testkit-jqwik`, comes from the BloxBean Maven repository, which publishes the pinned Julc snapshot.

```groovy title="build.gradle"
plugins {
    id 'java'
}

repositories {
    mavenCentral()
    maven {
        url = uri('https://repo.bloxbean.org/maven/snapshots')
        mavenContent { snapshotsOnly() }
    }
}

java {
    toolchain { languageVersion = JavaLanguageVersion.of(25) }
}

// The Elci installation: the elci-lang JAR and its pinned Julc libraries.
def elciLib = '/path/to/elci-lang/build/install/elci/lib'

dependencies {
    testImplementation fileTree(elciLib) { include '*.jar' }
    testImplementation 'org.julclang:julc-testkit-jqwik:0.1.0-pre20-ebaf028-SNAPSHOT'
    testImplementation 'net.jqwik:jqwik:1.9.2'
    testImplementation platform('org.junit:junit-bom:5.11.4')
    testImplementation 'org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter'
    testRuntimeOnly 'org.junit.platform:junit-platform-launcher'
}

test {
    useJUnitPlatform()
    testLogging { events 'passed', 'failed', 'skipped' }
}
```

Keep the Elci project in its own directory next to the Java sources. Tests run from the Gradle project directory, so `Path.of("market")` finds it:

- my-dapp/
  - build.gradle
  - settings.gradle
  - market/ the Elci project from Transaction scenarios
    - elci.toml
    - src/
    - tests/
  - src/
    - test/
      - java/
        - market/
          - MarketValidatorTest.java
          - MarketProperties.java

## ElciTestkit

`org.elci.testkit.ElciTestkit` compiles Elci code exactly as the CLI does, so your JUnit tests evaluate the scripts you deploy.

| Method | Returns |
| --- | --- |
| `validator(project, name, parameters...)` | the `[validators.<name>]` script as a `Program`, with its deployment parameters applied in declared order |
| `abi(project, name)` | the validator's `ValidatorAbi`: its parameter, datum and redeemer types |
| `entrypoint(project)` | the `[entrypoint]` function as a `Program`, as `elci eval` runs it |
| `value(project, module, name)` | any exposed zero-argument declaration of a source or test module, as a `Program` |

`project` is the directory that contains `elci.toml`. All four methods declare `IOException` for a project that cannot be read. `validator` and `abi` throw `IllegalArgumentException` for an unknown validator, and `validator` also when the number of parameters is wrong:

```java
@Test
void theValidatorNeedsItsParameter() {
    assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class, () -> ElciTestkit.validator(MARKET, "market"));
}
```

## Encode datums and redeemers

In Java you pass `PlutusData`, so you encode values by hand with the same rules Elci uses:

- A **record** is constructor 0 with its fields in **alphabetical order of their names**. `Listing { seller, price, expires }` is `Constr 0 [expires, price, seller]`.
- A **custom type** constructor is numbered by its position in the declaration, from 0: `Buy` is 0, `Reprice` 1 and `Delist` 2.
- Ledger types such as `PubKeyHash` and `TxOutRef` have `toPlutusData()`. `PlutusData.UNIT` is the Data of `()`.

```java
/** A Listing record encodes its fields in name order: expires, price, seller. */
static PlutusData listing(long price, long expires) {
    return PlutusData.constr(0, PlutusData.integer(expires), PlutusData.integer(price), SELLER.toPlutusData());
}

/** Action constructors are numbered in declaration order: Buy 0, Reprice 1, Delist 2. */
static final PlutusData DELIST = PlutusData.constr(2);
```

## A JUnit test

julc-testkit provides the rest:

- `ScriptContextTestBuilder` builds the ledger context. Start with the purpose, `spending(ref, datum)`, `spending(ref)`, `minting(policyId)`, `rewarding(credential)`, `certifying(index, cert)`, `voting(voter)` or `proposing(index, procedure)`, then add `redeemer`, `signer`, `input`, `referenceInput`, `output`, `mint`, `fee`, `validRange`, `withdrawal`, `datum` (a datum hash and its datum) and more. Finish with `buildPlutusData()`.
- `ValidatorTest.evaluate(program, context)` runs a script and returns an `EvalResult`. `assertValidates` and `assertRejects` evaluate and assert in one step.
- `BudgetAssertions` checks an `EvalResult`: `assertSuccess`, `assertFailure`, `assertBudgetUnder(result, cpu, memory)`, `assertTrace(result, messages...)`, `assertTraceExact` and `assertNoTraces`.

Unlike a scenario, the builder fills in nothing about your script. You choose the spent reference, credentials and policy ids yourself, and `spending(ref, datum)` sets the purpose without adding the spent output to the inputs: add it with `input` when your validator looks for its own input, for example through `Tx.ownInput` or `Tx.continuingOutputs`. The fee defaults to 0 and the validity range to always.

Here is a complete test class for the marketplace's `market` validator:

```java title="src/test/java/market/MarketValidatorTest.java"
package market;

import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.*;

import java.io.IOException;
import java.math.BigInteger;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.util.Arrays;
import org.elci.testkit.ElciTestkit;
import org.julclang.core.PlutusData;
import org.julclang.core.Program;
import org.julclang.ledger.*;
import org.julclang.testkit.BudgetAssertions;
import org.julclang.testkit.ScriptContextTestBuilder;
import org.julclang.testkit.ValidatorTest;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

class MarketValidatorTest {
    static final Path MARKET = Path.of("market");
    static final PubKeyHash OPERATOR = new PubKeyHash(new byte[28]);
    static final PubKeyHash SELLER = new PubKeyHash(filled(28, 1));
    static final TxOutRef LISTED = new TxOutRef(new TxId(new byte[32]), BigInteger.ZERO);

    static byte[] filled(int length, int value) {
        var bytes = new byte[length];
        Arrays.fill(bytes, (byte) value);
        return bytes;
    }

    /** A Listing record encodes its fields in name order: expires, price, seller. */
    static PlutusData listing(long price, long expires) {
        return PlutusData.constr(0, PlutusData.integer(expires), PlutusData.integer(price), SELLER.toPlutusData());
    }

    /** Action constructors are numbered in declaration order: Buy 0, Reprice 1, Delist 2. */
    static final PlutusData DELIST = PlutusData.constr(2);

    @Test
    void theSellerDelists() throws IOException {
        Program market = ElciTestkit.validator(MARKET, "market", OPERATOR.toPlutusData());
        var ctx = ScriptContextTestBuilder.spending(LISTED, listing(50_000_000, 2000))
                .redeemer(DELIST)
                .signer(SELLER)
                .buildPlutusData();
        ValidatorTest.assertValidates(market, ctx);
    }

    @Test
    void onlyTheOperatorWithdrawsRewards() throws IOException {
        Program market = ElciTestkit.validator(MARKET, "market", OPERATOR.toPlutusData());
        var credential = new Credential.ScriptCredential(new ScriptHash(new byte[28]));
        var signed = ScriptContextTestBuilder.rewarding(credential)
                .signer(OPERATOR)
                .redeemer(PlutusData.UNIT)
                .buildPlutusData();
        var result = ValidatorTest.evaluate(market, signed);
        BudgetAssertions.assertSuccess(result);
        BudgetAssertions.assertBudgetUnder(result, 10_000_000, 50_000);

        var unsigned = ScriptContextTestBuilder.rewarding(credential)
                .redeemer(PlutusData.UNIT)
                .buildPlutusData();
        ValidatorTest.assertRejects(market, unsigned);
    }

    @Test
    void theValidatorNeedsItsParameter() {
        assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class, () -> ElciTestkit.validator(MARKET, "market"));
    }
}
```

Run it with `./gradlew test`.

:::tip
`BudgetAssertions.assertTrace` pairs well with `Debug.trace` in your validator: it checks that a rejected transaction was rejected for the reason you expect. See [Debugging and budgets](https://elci-lang.dev/testing/debugging/).
:::

## Properties with jqwik

`SchemaArbitraries` from `julc-testkit-jqwik` reads a validator's ABI and generates valid datums, redeemers and parameters for jqwik. jqwik then runs each property many times and shrinks failures with its own strategies.

| Method | Generates |
| --- | --- |
| `SchemaArbitraries.datum(abi)` | datums of the validator's spend handler |
| `SchemaArbitraries.redeemer(abi, purpose)` | redeemers of the handler for a `ContractSchema.Purpose`, such as `SPEND` |
| `SchemaArbitraries.parameters(abi)` | lists of deployment parameters |
| `SchemaArbitraries.forType(type)` | values of any `PirType` |

```java title="src/test/java/market/MarketProperties.java"
package market;

import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.*;

import java.io.IOException;
import java.io.UncheckedIOException;
import java.math.BigInteger;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import net.jqwik.api.*;
import org.elci.testkit.ElciTestkit;
import org.julclang.compiler.backend.ValidatorAbi;
import org.julclang.compiler.schema.ContractSchema;
import org.julclang.core.PlutusData;
import org.julclang.core.Program;
import org.julclang.ledger.PubKeyHash;
import org.julclang.ledger.TxId;
import org.julclang.ledger.TxOutRef;
import org.julclang.testkit.ScriptContextTestBuilder;
import org.julclang.testkit.ValidatorTest;
import org.julclang.testkit.jqwik.SchemaArbitraries;

class MarketProperties {
    static final Path MARKET = Path.of("market");
    static final PubKeyHash OPERATOR = new PubKeyHash(new byte[28]);
    static final TxOutRef LISTED = new TxOutRef(new TxId(new byte[32]), BigInteger.ZERO);
    static final ValidatorAbi ABI;
    static final Program SCRIPT;

    static {
        try {
            ABI = ElciTestkit.abi(MARKET, "market");
            SCRIPT = ElciTestkit.validator(MARKET, "market", OPERATOR.toPlutusData());
        } catch (IOException e) {
            throw new UncheckedIOException(e);
        }
    }

    @Provide
    Arbitrary<PlutusData> listings() {
        return SchemaArbitraries.datum(ABI);
    }

    @Provide
    Arbitrary<PlutusData> actions() {
        return SchemaArbitraries.redeemer(ABI, ContractSchema.Purpose.SPEND);
    }

    /** With no outputs and no signature, no action can succeed. */
    @Property(tries = 100)
    void emptyTransactionsAreRejected(@ForAll("listings") PlutusData listing,
                                      @ForAll("actions") PlutusData action) {
        var ctx = ScriptContextTestBuilder.spending(LISTED, listing).redeemer(action).buildPlutusData();
        assertFalse(ValidatorTest.evaluate(SCRIPT, ctx).isSuccess(), () -> listing + " " + action);
    }

    /** A listing encodes its fields in name order: expires, price, seller. */
    @Property(tries = 100)
    void theSellerCanAlwaysDelist(@ForAll("listings") PlutusData listing) {
        var fields = ((PlutusData.ConstrData) listing).fields();
        var seller = new PubKeyHash(((PlutusData.BytesData) fields.get(2)).value());
        var ctx = ScriptContextTestBuilder.spending(LISTED, listing)
                .redeemer(PlutusData.constr(2))
                .signer(seller)
                .buildPlutusData();
        assertTrue(ValidatorTest.evaluate(SCRIPT, ctx).isSuccess(), listing::toString);
    }
}
```

The script and ABI are compiled once, in the static initializer, and shared by every try.

`elci test` properties and jqwik properties complement each other. `elci test` needs no Java and generates Elci-typed arguments, including records and unions you define in tests. With jqwik you build and vary the whole ledger context in Java, and its generators compose with the rest of your Java test code.

## Evaluate other declarations

`ElciTestkit.value` compiles any exposed zero-argument declaration, including tests and helpers in test modules, and `ElciTestkit.entrypoint` compiles a function project's `[entrypoint]`. Evaluate them with `ValidatorTest.evaluate` and read the result term:

```java
static Constant resultOf(EvalResult result) {
    var success = assertInstanceOf(EvalResult.Success.class, result);
    return ((Term.Const) success.resultTerm()).value();
}

@Test
void unitTestsAndEntrypointsEvaluate() throws IOException {
    var free = ElciTestkit.value(Path.of("shop"), "PricingTest", "smallAmountsAreFree");
    assertEquals(new Constant.BoolConst(true), resultOf(ValidatorTest.evaluate(free)));

    var main = ElciTestkit.entrypoint(Path.of("fn"));
    assertEquals(new Constant.IntegerConst(BigInteger.valueOf(42)), resultOf(ValidatorTest.evaluate(main)));
}
```

Here `shop` is the project from [Unit tests](https://elci-lang.dev/testing/unit-tests/), and `fn` is a project made by `elci init fn --purpose function`, whose `main` is `42`. `Constant` and `Term` are in `org.julclang.core`, and `EvalResult` is in `org.julclang.vm`.

---

# Debugging and budgets

> Read elci test failures, find out why a validator rejects a transaction with Debug.trace, and keep execution budgets in check with Scenario.withinBudget.

Source: https://elci-lang.dev/testing/debugging/

When a test fails, `elci test` tells you what it expected and what happened. In this page you learn to read those reports, to add traces that explain a rejection, and to use the CPU and memory numbers to keep your contracts cheap.

## Read a failure

Every failing test prints a `FAIL` line, then indented details, then any traces. The details depend on the kind of test:

| Kind of test | Typical detail |
| --- | --- |
| `Bool` | `evaluated to False` |
| `Expect.equal` | `expected:` and `actual:`, as Data |
| other `Expect` functions | the function name or your `onFail` message, then `values:` |
| runtime error in a test | `evaluation failed:` and the VM's error |
| scenario | `validator <name> rejected the transaction: ...` or `validator <name> accepted a transaction expected to fail` |
| scenario with `withinBudget` | `Budget exceeded: ...` |
| property | `counterexample after N runs, shrunk M times:`, the shrunk call, and the failure of that run |

[Unit tests](https://elci-lang.dev/testing/unit-tests/) explains how values are printed as Data, and [Property-based tests](https://elci-lang.dev/testing/properties/) how to read a counterexample.

Errors inside a test are reported with the VM's own message. Two examples from a test module `TraceTest` that imports `Julc.Data as Data`:

```elm
splitsEvenly : Bool
splitsEvenly =
    1000 // 0 == 0

decodesAnAmount : Expectation
decodesAnAmount =
    let
        amount : Int
        amount =
            Data.decode (Data.encode "ten")
    in
    Expect.equal 10 amount
```

```text
FAIL TraceTest.splitsEvenly (cpu 276441, mem 1001)
    evaluation failed: QuotientInteger: division by zero
FAIL TraceTest.decodesAnAmount (cpu 933360, mem 5469)
    evaluation failed: UnIData: not IntData
```

A failed `Data.decode` never becomes a `Maybe`: like a malformed datum on-chain, it stops evaluation.

## Why a validator rejected a transaction

These are the messages you meet most often in a failing scenario, and what they usually mean:

| Message | Usual cause |
| --- | --- |
| `rejected the transaction: Error term encountered` | a handler returned `False`, or the validator has no handler for the scenario's purpose |
| `rejected the transaction: UnConstrData: not ConstrData` | a datum or redeemer that does not match the handler's type, such as `Data.encode 5` for a union |
| `rejected the transaction: UnBData: not BytesData` | a value that should be bytes is something else, such as `Data.encode 5` given as a `PubKeyHash` parameter |
| `accepted a transaction expected to fail` | a check is missing or too loose |
| `cannot prepare validator 'markt': no [validators.markt] in elci.toml` | a misspelled validator name |
| `cannot prepare validator 'market': it takes 1 parameter [operator], but the scenario gives 0; set them with Scenario.parameters` | `Scenario.parameters` is missing or incomplete |

The first message is the common one, and the least helpful: a validator that returns `False` fails with an error, whichever check was false. Traces tell you which one.

## Debug.trace

`Debug.trace : String -> a -> a` returns its second argument unchanged and emits the message as a Plutus trace. As in Elm, every module imports `Debug`, so it needs no import.

Put a trace in the branch that rejects, so it only fires when that check fails. For the marketplace from [Transaction scenarios](https://elci-lang.dev/testing/scenarios/), move the deadline check of `Buy` in `src/Market.elm` into a function that traces when it fails:

```elm
        Buy ->
            sellerPaid listing ctx && endsBy listing.expires ctx
```

```elm
endsBy : Int -> ScriptContext -> Bool
endsBy time ctx =
    if Interval.isEntirelyBefore time ctx.txInfo.validRange then
        True

    else
        Debug.trace "the validity range does not end by the listing's expiry" False
```

Now remove `Scenario.expectFailure` from `buyingAfterExpiryFails` to see what the validator says about that late purchase:

```sh
elci test --match buyingAfter
```

```text
FAIL MarketTest.buyingAfterExpiryFails (cpu 33817513, mem 119115)
    validator market rejected the transaction: Error term encountered
    trace: the validity range does not end by the listing's expiry
0 passed, 1 failed
```

Traces are printed for failing tests only. Passing tests, including scenarios that are rejected as expected, stay quiet.

`Debug.trace` works in test modules too. There, it helps you see how far a computation got. The expected value below is wrong on purpose, so the test fails and prints its trace:

```elm
feeOfTwoThousand : Expectation
feeOfTwoThousand =
    let
        fee =
            Debug.trace "computing the fee of 2000" (Pricing.fee 2000)
    in
    Expect.equal 7 fee
```

```text
FAIL TraceTest.feeOfTwoThousand (cpu 2178706, mem 8698)
    Expect.equal
        expected: 7
        actual:   6
    trace: computing the fee of 2000
```

:::caution[Remove traces before you deploy]
Traces are part of the compiled script. They make it larger and cost budget whenever they run, and `elci build` does not strip them. The trace in `endsBy` adds 61 bytes to the `market` script: `elci check` reports 1672 FLAT bytes, against 1611 with `False` in its place. Remove your traces before you build for deployment, and rerun your tests.
:::

## Execution budgets

Every `PASS` and `FAIL` line shows the CPU steps and memory units of a run. What the numbers measure depends on the test:

- **`Bool` and `Expectation` tests:** the whole test program, including computing the expected value.
- **Scenarios:** the validator alone, running against the scenario's transaction. This is the cost you pay for on-chain.
- **Properties:** the costliest passing run, shown as `max cpu`; for a failure, the counterexample's run.

Protocol parameters cap the execution units of a transaction (on mainnet, currently 10 billion CPU steps and 14 million memory units), and the units you use add to the transaction fee. So scenario budgets are worth watching as your contract grows. [Costs and performance](https://elci-lang.dev/advanced/costs/) explains where the cost comes from and how to reduce it.

### Guard a budget with withinBudget

`Scenario.withinBudget cpu memory` makes a scenario fail when the validator needs more than the given CPU steps or memory units, whether it accepts or rejects the transaction:

```elm
delistingStaysCheap : Scenario
delistingStaysCheap =
    settle Delist
        |> Scenario.signedBy seller
        |> Scenario.withinBudget 17000000 70000
```

```text
PASS MarketTest.delistingStaysCheap (cpu 15573596, mem 65977)
```

Set the limits a little above today's numbers. A change that makes the path noticeably more expensive then fails the test instead of slipping through. With limits of `10000000` and `50000`, the same scenario fails:

```text
FAIL MarketTest.delistingStaysCheap (cpu 15573596, mem 65977)
    Budget exceeded: CPU steps 15573596 exceeds maximum 10000000; Memory units 65977 exceeds maximum 50000 (consumed: ExBudget{cpu=15573596, mem=65977})
```

The check is julc-testkit's `BudgetAssertions.assertBudgetUnder`, the same assertion you can use in [Java tests](https://elci-lang.dev/testing/java/).

## A debugging routine

When a scenario fails and the reason is not obvious:

1. Run only that test with `--match`, so the output is short.
2. Read the reason. An `accepted` failure means a check is missing; a decoding error means the data you built does not match the handler's types; `Error term encountered` means a check returned `False`.
3. Add a `Debug.trace` to each branch that can reject, and run the test again. The trace lines show which check failed.
4. If a helper computes the wrong value, move it into a module you can unit-test, and test it directly with `Expect.equal`.
5. Remove the traces and rerun the whole suite before you build for deployment.

---

# Build a vesting contract

> Build a vesting validator from an empty directory, with a typed datum and redeemer, a deadline checked against the validity range, a signature check, scenarios and a property test.

Source: https://elci-lang.dev/tutorials/vesting/

In this tutorial you build a vesting contract from scratch: funds are locked for a beneficiary and can only be claimed after a deadline. You write a typed datum and redeemer, check signatures and the transaction's validity range, cover the rules with transaction scenarios and a property test, and build the script.

You need `elci` on your `PATH` (see [Installation](https://elci-lang.dev/start/installation/)). If you haven't yet, work through [Your first validator](https://elci-lang.dev/start/first-validator/) first. The repository's [vesting example](https://github.com/bloxbean/elci-lang/tree/main/examples/vesting) is the finished contract.

## What you'll build

Someone locks funds at the vesting script's address with a datum that names a **beneficiary** and a **deadline**. Later, the beneficiary spends the output with the redeemer `Claim`. The validator accepts the claim only when both hold:

1. the transaction is signed by the beneficiary, and
2. the transaction can only run after the deadline.

## Create the project

```sh
elci init vesting --validator vesting
cd vesting
```

```text
Created Elci project at .../vesting with initial spend handler in validator vesting.
Run: elci check .../vesting
```

`--validator vesting` names the validator, and so its output directory, `vesting` instead of `main`. The starter project already passes its tests:

```sh
elci test .
```

```text
PASS MainTest.ownerSigns (cpu 7675163, mem 29990)
PASS MainTest.othersAreRejected (cpu 8053596, mem 31922)
2 passed, 0 failed
```

You'll replace the starter validator and its tests with your own, so delete them:

```sh
rm src/Main.elm tests/MainTest.elm
```

## Configure the validator

Open `elci.toml` and replace the validator table. The vesting contract has no deployment parameters, and its spend handler will be `validate` in a module called `Vesting`:

```toml title="elci.toml"
[project]
source-directories = ["src"]
target = "plutus-v3-pv11-uplc-1.1.0"
julc-version = "0.1.0-pre20-ebaf028-SNAPSHOT"

[validators.vesting]
boundary = "julc-strict-v1"
spend = "Vesting.validate"
```

## Write the datum, the redeemer and a first handler

Start with the types and the signature rule. Create `src/Vesting.elm`:

```elm title="src/Vesting.elm"
module Vesting exposing (VestingAction(..), VestingDatum, validate)

import Julc.Ledger exposing (PubKeyHash, ScriptContext)
import Tx

type alias VestingDatum =
    { beneficiary : PubKeyHash
    , deadline : Int
    }

type VestingAction
    = Claim

validate : VestingDatum -> VestingAction -> ScriptContext -> Bool
validate datum action ctx =
    case action of
        Claim ->
            Tx.signedBy datum.beneficiary ctx
```

- `VestingDatum` is the datum: a record with the beneficiary's key hash and the deadline. The module exposes the type so tests can build datums.
- `VestingAction` is the redeemer. It has a single constructor today, but a custom type leaves room for more actions later. `VestingAction(..)` exposes the constructor too.
- `validate` has the spend handler shape: datum, redeemer, script context, `Bool`. There are no parameters, so the datum comes first.
- `case action of` handles each redeemer. The compiler insists that every constructor is covered.
- `Tx.signedBy` asks whether the key is among the transaction's signatories. `Tx` is a core module that answers common questions about the transaction; it needs the import, but no configuration.

```sh
elci check .
```

```text
validator vesting (spend): checked; 393 FLAT bytes; plutus-v3-pv11-uplc-1.1.0
```

## Test the signature rule

Create `tests/VestingTest.elm` with two scenarios: the beneficiary claims, and a stranger tries to:

```elm title="tests/VestingTest.elm"
module VestingTest exposing (beneficiaryClaims, strangersCannotClaim)

import Julc.Data as Data
import Julc.Ledger exposing (PubKeyHash)
import Scenario exposing (Scenario)
import Vesting exposing (VestingAction(..), VestingDatum)

beneficiary : PubKeyHash
beneficiary =
    Scenario.key "beneficiary"

datum : VestingDatum
datum =
    { beneficiary = beneficiary, deadline = 1000 }

claim : Scenario
claim =
    Scenario.spend "vesting" (Scenario.outRef "vesting" 0) (Data.encode datum)
        |> Scenario.redeemer (Data.encode Claim)

beneficiaryClaims : Scenario
beneficiaryClaims =
    claim
        |> Scenario.signedBy beneficiary

strangersCannotClaim : Scenario
strangersCannotClaim =
    claim
        |> Scenario.signedBy (Scenario.key "stranger")
        |> Scenario.expectFailure
```

`Scenario.spend` locks an output at the `vesting` script's address with the encoded datum, then spends it. `Data.encode` turns your Elci values into the on-chain Data the ledger passes to the script.

```sh
elci test .
```

```text
PASS VestingTest.beneficiaryClaims (cpu 10873274, mem 42950)
PASS VestingTest.strangersCannotClaim (cpu 11251707, mem 44882)
2 passed, 0 failed
```

## Add the deadline

A script can't read the clock. Instead, every transaction declares a **validity range**, the time interval in which it may be included in a block, and the ledger enforces it. If every time in the range is after the deadline, the transaction can't possibly run at or before the deadline. So the rule is: the range must lie entirely after the deadline.

Times are POSIX times in milliseconds. The tests use small numbers such as `1000` for readability; a real deadline looks like `1767225600000` (1 January 2026, UTC).

1. **Check the range.** The core `Interval` module reads validity ranges. Update the handler:

   ```elm title="src/Vesting.elm" ins={3,22-23}
   module Vesting exposing (VestingAction(..), VestingDatum, validate)

   import Interval
   import Julc.Ledger exposing (PubKeyHash, ScriptContext)
   import Tx

   type alias VestingDatum =
       { beneficiary : PubKeyHash
       , deadline : Int
       }

   type VestingAction
       = Claim

   validate : VestingDatum -> VestingAction -> ScriptContext -> Bool
   validate datum action ctx =
       case action of
           Claim ->
               Interval.isEntirelyAfter datum.deadline ctx.txInfo.validRange
                   && Tx.signedBy datum.beneficiary ctx
   ```

   `Interval.isEntirelyAfter datum.deadline range` holds when the range has a start and every time in it is after the deadline. A range without a start could run at any time, so it never passes. `&&` only evaluates its right side when the left side is `True`, so a claim before the deadline doesn't pay for the signature search.

2. **Run the old tests.**

   ```sh
   elci test .
   ```

   ```text
   FAIL VestingTest.beneficiaryClaims (cpu 11922589, mem 46110)
       validator vesting rejected the transaction: Error term encountered
   PASS VestingTest.strangersCannotClaim (cpu 11922589, mem 46110)
   1 passed, 1 failed
   ```

   `beneficiaryClaims` fails, as it should: its transaction has no validity range, so it could run before the deadline. Notice that `strangersCannotClaim` now passes for a different reason: it fails the deadline check before the signature is ever looked at. Both scenarios cost exactly the same. A test that expects failure needs a nearly identical test that succeeds, or it proves little.

## Test the deadline

Rewrite the tests around a helper that claims from a given time. `Scenario.validFrom` sets the start of the validity range (inclusive) and `Scenario.validBefore` its end (exclusive):

```elm title="tests/VestingTest.elm"
module VestingTest exposing (..)

import Julc.Data as Data
import Julc.Ledger exposing (PubKeyHash)
import Scenario exposing (Scenario)
import Vesting exposing (VestingAction(..), VestingDatum)

beneficiary : PubKeyHash
beneficiary =
    Scenario.key "beneficiary"

datum : VestingDatum
datum =
    { beneficiary = beneficiary, deadline = 1000 }

claimFrom : Int -> Scenario
claimFrom time =
    Scenario.spend "vesting" (Scenario.outRef "vesting" 0) (Data.encode datum)
        |> Scenario.redeemer (Data.encode Claim)
        |> Scenario.validFrom time

claimsJustAfterTheDeadline : Scenario
claimsJustAfterTheDeadline =
    claimFrom 1001
        |> Scenario.signedBy beneficiary

claimsLongAfterTheDeadline : Scenario
claimsLongAfterTheDeadline =
    claimFrom 5000
        |> Scenario.validBefore 6000
        |> Scenario.signedBy beneficiary

claimsAtTheDeadlineFail : Scenario
claimsAtTheDeadlineFail =
    claimFrom 1000
        |> Scenario.signedBy beneficiary
        |> Scenario.expectFailure

strangersCannotClaim : Scenario
strangersCannotClaim =
    claimFrom 2000
        |> Scenario.signedBy (Scenario.key "stranger")
        |> Scenario.expectFailure

claimsWithoutAStartFail : Scenario
claimsWithoutAStartFail =
    Scenario.spend "vesting" (Scenario.outRef "vesting" 0) (Data.encode datum)
        |> Scenario.redeemer (Data.encode Claim)
        |> Scenario.signedBy beneficiary
        |> Scenario.expectFailure
```

The module now uses `exposing (..)`. Test discovery only runs exposed, zero-argument values of the test types (`Scenario` here), so `beneficiary`, `datum` and the function `claimFrom` stay helpers. A zero-argument `Scenario` helper would run as a test, which is why `claimsWithoutAStartFail` builds its own transaction rather than sharing an exposed base scenario.

The tests pin down the edges: one millisecond after the deadline, exactly at it, a stranger after it, and no start at all. A transaction valid from `1000` could run at `1000`, which is not after the deadline, so it is rejected.

```sh
elci test .
```

```text
PASS VestingTest.claimsJustAfterTheDeadline (cpu 16763911, mem 61637)
PASS VestingTest.claimsLongAfterTheDeadline (cpu 16763911, mem 61637)
PASS VestingTest.claimsAtTheDeadlineFail (cpu 13950292, mem 52228)
PASS VestingTest.strangersCannotClaim (cpu 17142344, mem 63569)
PASS VestingTest.claimsWithoutAStartFail (cpu 11922589, mem 46110)
5 passed, 0 failed
```

## Add a property test

Scenarios check the times you thought of. A **property** states a rule for every time, and `elci test` tries it with many generated values. Add the import and the property to `tests/VestingTest.elm`:

```elm title="tests/VestingTest.elm" ins={5}
module VestingTest exposing (..)

import Julc.Data as Data
import Julc.Ledger exposing (PubKeyHash)
import Property exposing (Property)
import Scenario exposing (Scenario)
import Vesting exposing (VestingAction(..), VestingDatum)
```

```elm title="tests/VestingTest.elm (at the end)"
{-| Whenever a signed claim's validity range starts, it succeeds exactly when that is after
the deadline. The start is narrowed to the 20 milliseconds around the deadline.
-}
claimsSucceedOnlyAfterTheDeadline : Int -> Property
claimsSucceedOnlyAfterTheDeadline raw =
    let
        time =
            datum.deadline - 10 + modBy 20 raw

        signed =
            claimFrom time
                |> Scenario.signedBy beneficiary
    in
    if time > datum.deadline then
        Property.scenario signed

    else
        Property.scenario (Scenario.expectFailure signed)
```

- An exposed function whose result is a `Property` is a [property test](https://elci-lang.dev/testing/properties/). `elci test` generates its `Int` argument, 100 times by default.
- Generated integers are mostly small, so the property narrows them with `modBy` to times between 990 and 1009, where the interesting boundary is.
- `Property.scenario` runs the transaction against the real script. The `if` states the expected outcome for each time.

```sh
elci test . --seed 42
```

```text
PASS VestingTest.claimsJustAfterTheDeadline (cpu 16763911, mem 61637)
PASS VestingTest.claimsLongAfterTheDeadline (cpu 16763911, mem 61637)
PASS VestingTest.claimsAtTheDeadlineFail (cpu 13950292, mem 52228)
PASS VestingTest.strangersCannotClaim (cpu 17142344, mem 63569)
PASS VestingTest.claimsWithoutAStartFail (cpu 11922589, mem 46110)
PASS VestingTest.claimsSucceedOnlyAfterTheDeadline (100 runs, max cpu 16763911, mem 61637)
6 passed, 0 failed (seed 42)
```

The summary reports the seed of the run. Without `--seed`, every run picks a random one; passing a reported seed reproduces that run exactly.

### See it catch a bug

To see what the property is for, break the contract on purpose. Change `Interval.isEntirelyAfter datum.deadline` to `Interval.isEntirelyAfter (datum.deadline - 1)` in `src/Vesting.elm`, so a claim valid from the deadline itself is accepted, and run only the property:

```sh
elci test . --match OnlyAfter --seed 4
```

```text
FAIL VestingTest.claimsSucceedOnlyAfterTheDeadline (38 runs, cpu 16929119, mem 62039)
    counterexample after 38 runs, shrunk 1 time:
        claimsSucceedOnlyAfterTheDeadline 10
    validator vesting accepted a transaction expected to fail
0 passed, 1 failed (seed 4)
```

The counterexample is the generated argument, `raw = 10`, which gives `time = 990 + modBy 20 10 = 1000`: exactly the deadline. The property found the off-by-one without you writing that case. Change the check back before you continue. (`claimsAtTheDeadlineFail` catches this bug too; the property would also catch the ones you didn't think to write a scenario for.)

## Build the script

```sh
elci build .
```

```text
validator vesting (spend): checked; 533 FLAT bytes; plutus-v3-pv11-uplc-1.1.0
```

Your project now looks like this:

- vesting/
  - elci.toml
  - README.md
  - .gitignore
  - src/
    - Vesting.elm
  - tests/
    - VestingTest.elm
  - build/
    - validators/
      - elci-outputs.json
      - vesting/
        - abi.json
        - validator.flat
        - validator.plutus
        - validator.plutus.json

The validator has no parameters, so its artifact already carries the script hash, from which the script address is derived (`cborHex` shortened):

```json title="build/validators/vesting/validator.plutus.json"
{
  "type": "PlutusScriptV3",
  "purpose": "spending",
  "description": "vesting",
  "cborHex": "590218590215010100323232323232323232322323232323...",
  "hash": "cdf09c382832689b016adac7ef1470488e9ff58b8a474b9086c7a0c3",
  "params": "",
  "sizeBytes": 533
}
```

`abi.json` records how the datum and redeemer are encoded. `VestingDatum` is constructor 0 with `beneficiary` then `deadline` (fields in name order), and `Claim` is constructor 0 with no fields. Off-chain code that locks funds must build the datum in exactly that layout, or the output can never be claimed. [Build and deploy](https://elci-lang.dev/contracts/build-and-deploy/) explains the files and shows how to load the script from Java.

## Recap

- The datum and the redeemer are ordinary Elci types. The compiler decodes them strictly before `validate` runs.
- Time checks reason about the transaction's validity range, never a clock. "After the deadline" means every time in the range is after it: `Interval.isEntirelyAfter`.
- The core `Tx` and `Interval` modules answer the common questions about a transaction without any configuration.
- Scenarios pin down the edge cases. A failing scenario needs a passing twin, or it may fail for the wrong reason.
- A property checks a rule over many generated values, and shrinks a failure to a small counterexample with a seed that reproduces it.

Next, build two cooperating scripts with parameters in [A treasury and its badge policy](https://elci-lang.dev/tutorials/treasury/).

---

# A treasury and its badge policy

> Build two cooperating scripts from an empty directory, a treasury that spends payouts and withdraws staking rewards and a badge minting policy, both parameterized by an admin key.

Source: https://elci-lang.dev/tutorials/treasury/

In this tutorial you build a project with two validators. The first, a treasury, is one script with two purposes: it releases payouts and withdraws its own staking rewards. The second is a separate minting policy for badges. Both take an `admin` key as a deployment parameter. Along the way you share code between scripts, test every purpose, read the minted quantity from the transaction, and apply the parameter for deployment.

You should be comfortable with the [vesting tutorial](https://elci-lang.dev/tutorials/vesting/). The finished project is close to the [treasury example](https://github.com/bloxbean/elci-lang/tree/main/examples/treasury) in the repository; the badge policy here also checks the minted tokens.

## What you'll build

- **`treasury`**, one script with two handlers:
  - `spend`: each locked output holds a `Payout` datum naming a beneficiary and an amount. The redeemer `Release` lets the beneficiary take a payout with a positive amount; `Cancel` lets the admin take it back.
  - `withdraw`: only the admin may withdraw the staking rewards earned by the treasury's stake credential.
- **`badge`**, a separate minting policy: only the admin may mint `BADGE` tokens, and only a positive number of them.

Both scripts are parameterized by the same `admin` key hash, but they are independent scripts with different hashes.

## Create the project

```sh
elci init treasury --validator treasury
cd treasury
rm src/Main.elm tests/MainTest.elm
```

```text
Created Elci project at .../treasury with initial spend handler in validator treasury.
Run: elci check .../treasury
```

## Share the signature check

Both scripts check signatures, so put the check in its own module. Create `src/Auth.elm`:

```elm title="src/Auth.elm"
module Auth exposing (signedBy)

import Julc.Ledger exposing (PubKeyHash, ScriptContext)

signedBy : PubKeyHash -> ScriptContext -> Bool
signedBy key ctx =
    List.any (\signer -> signer == key) ctx.txInfo.signatories
```

A module is plain source. Each script includes only the functions its handlers reach, so sharing a module costs nothing. The core `Tx` module has the same check as `Tx.signedBy`; this project keeps its own to show a shared module.

## Write the spend handler

1. **Configure the treasury.** Replace the validator table in `elci.toml`. The table declares the `admin` parameter and the spend handler:

   ```toml title="elci.toml"
   [project]
   source-directories = ["src"]
   target = "plutus-v3-pv11-uplc-1.1.0"
   julc-version = "0.1.0-pre20-ebaf028-SNAPSHOT"

   [validators.treasury]
   boundary = "julc-strict-v1"
   parameters = ["admin"]
   spend = "Treasury.spend"
   ```

2. **Write the handler.** Create `src/Treasury.elm`:

   ```elm title="src/Treasury.elm"
   module Treasury exposing (Action(..), Payout, spend)

   import Auth exposing (signedBy)
   import Julc.Ledger exposing (PubKeyHash, ScriptContext)

   type alias Payout =
       { beneficiary : PubKeyHash
       , amount : Int
       }

   type Action
       = Release
       | Cancel

   spend : PubKeyHash -> Payout -> Action -> ScriptContext -> Bool
   spend admin payout action ctx =
       case action of
           Release ->
               payout.amount > 0 && signedBy payout.beneficiary ctx

           Cancel ->
               signedBy admin ctx
   ```

   The parameter comes first, then the datum (`Payout`), the redeemer (`Action`) and the context.

3. **Check it.**

   ```sh
   elci check .
   ```

   ```text
   validator treasury (spend): checked; 458 FLAT bytes; plutus-v3-pv11-uplc-1.1.0
   ```

4. **Test it.** Create `tests/TreasuryTest.elm`. The helper `claim` builds a spend of a payout with a given action. Parameters are passed as `Data` in the declared order:

   ```elm title="tests/TreasuryTest.elm"
   module TreasuryTest exposing (adminCancels, adminCannotRelease, beneficiaryReleases)

   import Julc.Data as Data
   import Julc.Ledger exposing (PubKeyHash)
   import Scenario exposing (Scenario)
   import Treasury exposing (Action(..), Payout)

   admin : PubKeyHash
   admin =
       Scenario.key "admin"

   beneficiary : PubKeyHash
   beneficiary =
       Scenario.key "beneficiary"

   payout : Payout
   payout =
       { beneficiary = beneficiary, amount = 50 }

   claim : Action -> Scenario
   claim action =
       Scenario.spend "treasury" (Scenario.outRef "treasury" 0) (Data.encode payout)
           |> Scenario.parameters [ Data.encode admin ]
           |> Scenario.redeemer (Data.encode action)

   beneficiaryReleases : Scenario
   beneficiaryReleases =
       claim Release
           |> Scenario.signedBy beneficiary

   adminCannotRelease : Scenario
   adminCannotRelease =
       claim Release
           |> Scenario.signedBy admin
           |> Scenario.expectFailure

   adminCancels : Scenario
   adminCancels =
       claim Cancel
           |> Scenario.signedBy admin
   ```

   ```sh
   elci test .
   ```

   ```text
   PASS TreasuryTest.beneficiaryReleases (cpu 11698810, mem 46679)
   PASS TreasuryTest.adminCannotRelease (cpu 12077243, mem 48611)
   PASS TreasuryTest.adminCancels (cpu 11310693, mem 45520)
   3 passed, 0 failed
   ```

## Add the withdraw handler

A script's hash can also serve as a stake credential. If the treasury's address uses the script's hash for its staking part too, the staking rewards of the funds it holds accrue to that credential, and withdrawing them runs the script with the `withdraw` purpose. Adding a handler to the same table keeps it **one script**, so the address that holds the payouts and the credential that earns the rewards share one hash.

1. **Add the handler key.**

   ```toml title="elci.toml" ins={6,11}
   [project]
   source-directories = ["src"]
   target = "plutus-v3-pv11-uplc-1.1.0"
   julc-version = "0.1.0-pre20-ebaf028-SNAPSHOT"

   # One script: the treasury address spends payouts and withdraws its staking rewards.
   [validators.treasury]
   boundary = "julc-strict-v1"
   parameters = ["admin"]
   spend = "Treasury.spend"
   withdraw = "Treasury.withdraw"
   ```

2. **Write the handler.** Expose `withdraw` from `src/Treasury.elm` and add it at the end:

   ```elm title="src/Treasury.elm"
   module Treasury exposing (Action(..), Payout, spend, withdraw)
   ```

   ```elm title="src/Treasury.elm (at the end)"
   withdraw : PubKeyHash -> () -> ScriptContext -> Bool
   withdraw admin _ ctx =
       signedBy admin ctx
   ```

   A withdraw handler has no datum: parameters, redeemer, context. It receives the same `admin` parameter as `spend`; every handler of a validator receives all of its parameters.

3. **Check it.** The check line now lists both purposes:

   ```sh
   elci check .
   ```

   ```text
   validator treasury (spend, withdraw): checked; 540 FLAT bytes; plutus-v3-pv11-uplc-1.1.0
   ```

4. **Test it.** Add two scenarios to `tests/TreasuryTest.elm`, and to its `exposing` list. `Scenario.withdraw "treasury"` withdraws rewards from the script's own stake credential:

   ```elm title="tests/TreasuryTest.elm"
   module TreasuryTest exposing (adminCancels, adminCannotRelease, adminWithdrawsRewards, beneficiaryReleases, rewardsNeedTheAdmin)
   ```

   ```elm title="tests/TreasuryTest.elm (at the end)"
   adminWithdrawsRewards : Scenario
   adminWithdrawsRewards =
       Scenario.withdraw "treasury"
           |> Scenario.parameters [ Data.encode admin ]
           |> Scenario.signedBy admin

   rewardsNeedTheAdmin : Scenario
   rewardsNeedTheAdmin =
       Scenario.withdraw "treasury"
           |> Scenario.parameters [ Data.encode admin ]
           |> Scenario.signedBy beneficiary
           |> Scenario.expectFailure
   ```

   ```sh
   elci test .
   ```

   ```text
   PASS TreasuryTest.beneficiaryReleases (cpu 11746810, mem 46979)
   PASS TreasuryTest.adminCannotRelease (cpu 12125243, mem 48911)
   PASS TreasuryTest.adminCancels (cpu 11358693, mem 45820)
   PASS TreasuryTest.adminWithdrawsRewards (cpu 6103274, mem 24333)
   PASS TreasuryTest.rewardsNeedTheAdmin (cpu 6481707, mem 26265)
   5 passed, 0 failed
   ```

   The spend scenarios cost a little more than before: the script now chooses between two purposes before it runs a handler.

## Add the badge policy

The badge policy is a separate script, so it gets its own table. It reads the minted quantity from the transaction's `mint` field. That field is a multi-asset `Value`, which the core [`Value`](https://elci-lang.dev/reference/core-modules/#value) module reads.

:::caution[Don't trust the redeemer for amounts]
The redeemer is whatever the transaction's builder puts there. A policy that only checked a quantity passed in the redeemer would approve a transaction whose redeemer says `3` while it mints a thousand tokens. Read what actually happens from `ctx.txInfo`.
:::

1. **Configure it.** Add the `badge` table:

   ```toml title="elci.toml" ins={13-17}
   [project]
   source-directories = ["src"]
   target = "plutus-v3-pv11-uplc-1.1.0"
   julc-version = "0.1.0-pre20-ebaf028-SNAPSHOT"

   # One script: the treasury address spends payouts and withdraws its staking rewards.
   [validators.treasury]
   boundary = "julc-strict-v1"
   parameters = ["admin"]
   spend = "Treasury.spend"
   withdraw = "Treasury.withdraw"

   # A separate script, and so a separate policy id.
   [validators.badge]
   boundary = "julc-strict-v1"
   parameters = ["admin"]
   mint = "Badge.mint"
   ```

2. **Write the policy.** Create `src/Badge.elm`:

   ```elm title="src/Badge.elm"
   module Badge exposing (mint)

   import Auth
   import Bytes
   import Julc.Ledger exposing (PubKeyHash, ScriptContext, ScriptInfo(..), TokenName(..))
   import Value

   {-| The admin may mint badges. The quantity is read from the transaction's mint field,
   never from the redeemer, which the transaction builder chooses freely.
   -}
   mint : PubKeyHash -> () -> ScriptContext -> Bool
   mint admin _ ctx =
       case ctx.scriptInfo of
           MintingScript policy ->
               (Value.quantityOf policy (TokenName (Bytes.fromString "BADGE")) ctx.txInfo.mint > 0)
                   && Auth.signedBy admin ctx

           _ ->
               False
   ```

   - `ctx.scriptInfo` is `MintingScript policy` when the script runs as a minting policy. `policy` is the script's own policy id.
   - `Value.quantityOf` returns how many tokens of that policy and name the transaction mints (negative for a burn, zero if none). `policy` is already a `PolicyId`, and `TokenName (Bytes.fromString "BADGE")` builds the token name from its bytes.
   - The `_` branch never runs for a script with only a mint handler, but `case` must cover every constructor.

3. **Check both validators.**

   ```sh
   elci check .
   ```

   ```text
   validator badge (mint): checked; 341 FLAT bytes; plutus-v3-pv11-uplc-1.1.0
   validator treasury (spend, withdraw): checked; 540 FLAT bytes; plutus-v3-pv11-uplc-1.1.0
   ```

4. **Test it.** Create `tests/BadgeTest.elm`, with a property that covers every quantity:

   ```elm title="tests/BadgeTest.elm"
   module BadgeTest exposing (adminMintsBadges, badgesNeedAPositiveQuantity, strangersCannotMint)

   import Bytes
   import Julc.Data as Data
   import Julc.Ledger exposing (PubKeyHash)
   import Property exposing (Property)
   import Scenario exposing (Scenario)

   admin : PubKeyHash
   admin =
       Scenario.key "admin"

   badges : Int -> Scenario
   badges quantity =
       Scenario.mint "badge"
           |> Scenario.parameters [ Data.encode admin ]
           |> Scenario.minting (Bytes.fromString "BADGE") quantity

   adminMintsBadges : Scenario
   adminMintsBadges =
       badges 3
           |> Scenario.signedBy admin

   strangersCannotMint : Scenario
   strangersCannotMint =
       badges 3
           |> Scenario.signedBy (Scenario.key "stranger")
           |> Scenario.expectFailure

   badgesNeedAPositiveQuantity : Int -> Property
   badgesNeedAPositiveQuantity quantity =
       let
           signed =
               badges quantity
                   |> Scenario.signedBy admin
       in
       if quantity > 0 then
           Property.scenario signed

       else
           Property.scenario (Scenario.expectFailure signed)
   ```

   `Scenario.minting` mints (or, with a negative quantity, burns) tokens under the validator's own policy. The property runs with generated quantities: positive ones must succeed, and zero and negative ones must be rejected.

## Add a property and a budget to the treasury

Two more checks for the treasury tests. Add `import Property exposing (Property)`, expose `onlyTheBeneficiaryReleases`, give `beneficiaryReleases` a budget, and add the property at the end:

```elm title="tests/TreasuryTest.elm" ins={1,5}
module TreasuryTest exposing (adminCancels, adminCannotRelease, adminWithdrawsRewards, beneficiaryReleases, onlyTheBeneficiaryReleases, rewardsNeedTheAdmin)

import Julc.Data as Data
import Julc.Ledger exposing (PubKeyHash)
import Property exposing (Property)
import Scenario exposing (Scenario)
import Treasury exposing (Action(..), Payout)
```

```elm title="tests/TreasuryTest.elm" ins={5}
beneficiaryReleases : Scenario
beneficiaryReleases =
    claim Release
        |> Scenario.signedBy beneficiary
        |> Scenario.withinBudget 20000000 100000
```

```elm title="tests/TreasuryTest.elm (at the end)"
onlyTheBeneficiaryReleases : PubKeyHash -> Property
onlyTheBeneficiaryReleases signer =
    let
        release =
            claim Release
                |> Scenario.signedBy signer
    in
    if signer == beneficiary then
        Property.scenario release

    else
        Property.scenario (Scenario.expectFailure release)
```

- `Scenario.withinBudget cpu memory` fails the scenario if the script uses more than that budget, so a change that makes releases much more expensive can't slip through.
- The property generates 28-byte key hashes and checks that a release signed by anyone else is rejected. Random keys essentially never equal the beneficiary, so in practice it checks "everyone else is rejected"; `beneficiaryReleases` covers the beneficiary.

Run everything:

```sh
elci test . --seed 42
```

```text
PASS BadgeTest.adminMintsBadges (cpu 10442084, mem 36669)
PASS BadgeTest.strangersCannotMint (cpu 10820517, mem 38601)
PASS BadgeTest.badgesNeedAPositiveQuantity (100 runs, max cpu 10442084, mem 36669)
PASS TreasuryTest.beneficiaryReleases (cpu 11746810, mem 46979)
PASS TreasuryTest.adminCannotRelease (cpu 12125243, mem 48911)
PASS TreasuryTest.adminCancels (cpu 11358693, mem 45820)
PASS TreasuryTest.adminWithdrawsRewards (cpu 6103274, mem 24333)
PASS TreasuryTest.rewardsNeedTheAdmin (cpu 6481707, mem 26265)
PASS TreasuryTest.onlyTheBeneficiaryReleases (100 runs, max cpu 12125243, mem 48911)
9 passed, 0 failed (seed 42)
```

A mint costs about 10 million CPU units, against about 6 million for a withdrawal, which only checks a signature. Most of the difference is `Value.quantityOf` reading the mint value. That's affordable, but the budget is worth watching as a policy grows.

## Build both scripts

```sh
elci build .
```

```text
validator badge (mint): checked; 341 FLAT bytes; plutus-v3-pv11-uplc-1.1.0
validator treasury (spend, withdraw): checked; 540 FLAT bytes; plutus-v3-pv11-uplc-1.1.0
```

- treasury/
  - elci.toml
  - src/
    - Auth.elm
    - Badge.elm
    - Treasury.elm
  - tests/
    - BadgeTest.elm
    - TreasuryTest.elm
  - build/
    - validators/
      - elci-outputs.json
      - badge/
        - abi.json
        - validator.flat
        - validator.plutus
        - validator.plutus.json
      - treasury/
        - abi.json
        - validator.flat
        - validator.plutus
        - validator.plutus.json

To rebuild only one script, select it: `elci build . --validator badge`. The treasury's artifact records its two purposes as `multi` and its pending parameter (`cborHex` shortened):

```json title="build/validators/treasury/validator.plutus.json"
{
  "type": "PlutusScriptV3",
  "purpose": "multi",
  "description": "treasury",
  "cborHex": "...",
  "hash": "",
  "params": "admin:PubKeyHash",
  "sizeBytes": 540
}
```

## Apply the admin key

Both scripts need the admin's key hash before they can be deployed. Keep it in a file, as Plutus Data JSON:

```json title="params/admin.json"
{"bytes": "887d8fbb82ce756a9dac9210c3d1235e9d3ff2457a667d311d318142"}
```

Apply it to each script. `@params/admin.json` is read relative to the project directory:

```sh
elci apply . --validator treasury --param admin=@params/admin.json
elci apply . --validator badge --param admin=@params/admin.json
```

```text
validator treasury: applied 1 parameter; hash 16a075885ca1a8102d56e474815e720bf5d7c342f4bd2e225a87441e; wrote .../treasury/build/validators/treasury/applied.plutus.json
validator badge: applied 1 parameter; hash 94e8ac9685e836de2886ca6411c97a1328aea45ac669f3fd05ae4949; wrote .../treasury/build/validators/badge/applied.plutus.json
```

The same admin gives two different hashes, because the scripts are different:

- The **treasury** hash is the payment credential of the treasury's address, and the stake credential whose rewards `withdraw` guards.
- The **badge** hash is the badge policy id.

`elci apply` checked that the value is a well-formed `PubKeyHash` before applying it. Replace the example key with the real admin's key hash, and note that the next `elci build` removes both `applied.plutus.json` files; use `--output` to keep them elsewhere. See [Parameterized validators](https://elci-lang.dev/contracts/parameters/) and [Build and deploy](https://elci-lang.dev/contracts/build-and-deploy/).

## Recap and next steps

- One `[validators.<name>]` table is one script. Several handler keys make one script serve several purposes with one hash.
- Separate tables make independent scripts. They can share modules and parameters but have their own hashes.
- Every handler receives all of its validator's parameters, first and in the declared order.
- Read amounts from the transaction, not from the redeemer.

The treasury trusts the beneficiary to take the payout: `Release` checks the signature and that the amount is positive, not where the funds go. As an exercise, require that the transaction pays `payout.amount` lovelace to the beneficiary, using the output checks in [Reading the transaction](https://elci-lang.dev/contracts/reading-the-transaction/), and add scenarios with `Scenario.output`.

Next, write a minting policy that can only ever run once in [A one-shot minting policy](https://elci-lang.dev/tutorials/one-shot-policy/).

---

# A one-shot minting policy

> Build a minting policy that can mint only once, by tying it to a seed output that the minting transaction must spend, and prove the accept and reject cases with scenarios and properties.

Source: https://elci-lang.dev/tutorials/one-shot-policy/

In this tutorial you build a **one-shot** minting policy: a policy under which one token can be minted once, and never again. It is the standard way to make a true NFT. You take a ledger type as a deployment parameter, check the transaction's inputs, inspect what it mints, and prove every rule with scenarios and properties.

You should have finished the [vesting tutorial](https://elci-lang.dev/tutorials/vesting/). [Reading the transaction](https://elci-lang.dev/contracts/reading-the-transaction/) explains the ledger types used here.

## How a one-shot policy works

A minting policy's id is its script hash, and a parameter is part of the script. So if the policy takes an output reference, a `TxOutRef`, as a parameter, every choice of that **seed** output gives a different policy id.

Now require that minting spends the seed. An output can be spent only once, so only one transaction can ever satisfy the policy. After it, no transaction can mint under this policy id again.

The policy you'll build has two parameters, `seed : TxOutRef` and `tokenName : TokenName`, and these rules:

1. Minting succeeds only in a transaction that spends the seed output.
2. That transaction must mint exactly one `tokenName` token under this policy, and nothing else.
3. Burning that one token is always allowed.

## Create the project

```sh
elci init one-shot --validator nft --purpose mint
cd one-shot
rm src/Main.elm tests/MainTest.elm
```

```text
Created Elci project at .../one-shot with initial mint handler in validator nft.
Run: elci check .../one-shot
```

`--purpose mint` starts from a minting-policy template, which you've just removed; `--validator nft` names the validator.

## Require the seed

1. **Configure the policy** with a single parameter for now:

   ```toml title="elci.toml"
   [project]
   source-directories = ["src"]
   target = "plutus-v3-pv11-uplc-1.1.0"
   julc-version = "0.1.0-pre20-ebaf028-SNAPSHOT"

   [validators.nft]
   boundary = "julc-strict-v1"
   parameters = ["seed"]
   mint = "OneShot.mint"
   ```

2. **Write the check.** Create `src/OneShot.elm`:

   ```elm title="src/OneShot.elm"
   module OneShot exposing (mint)

   import Julc.Ledger exposing (ScriptContext, TxOutRef)

   {-| Minting is allowed only in the transaction that spends the seed output.
   -}
   mint : TxOutRef -> () -> ScriptContext -> Bool
   mint seed _ ctx =
       List.any (\input -> input.outRef == seed) ctx.txInfo.inputs
   ```

   A mint handler has the shape parameters, redeemer, context. `TxOutRef` is a ledger type that can cross the Data boundary, so it can be a parameter; `==` compares two references. Each entry of `ctx.txInfo.inputs` is a `TxInInfo`, whose `outRef` says which output it spends. The core `Tx` module has this check as `Tx.spends seed ctx`; this tutorial writes it out to show what it does.

   ```sh
   elci check .
   ```

   ```text
   validator nft (mint): checked; 208 FLAT bytes; plutus-v3-pv11-uplc-1.1.0
   ```

3. **Test both sides.** A minting scenario doesn't spend anything by default, so add the seed as an input with `Scenario.input`. An input needs an output to spend: here, 5 ADA at a wallet address built from a test key. Create `tests/OneShotTest.elm`:

   ```elm title="tests/OneShotTest.elm"
   module OneShotTest exposing (mintingWithTheSeedSucceeds, mintingWithoutTheSeedFails)

   import Bytes
   import Julc.Data as Data
   import Julc.Ledger as Ledger exposing (Address, TxOutRef)
   import Scenario exposing (Scenario)

   seed : TxOutRef
   seed =
       Scenario.outRef "seed" 0

   wallet : Address
   wallet =
       Ledger.Address (Ledger.PubKeyCredential (Scenario.key "minter")) (Data.toOptional Nothing)

   mintOne : Scenario
   mintOne =
       Scenario.mint "nft"
           |> Scenario.parameters [ Data.encode seed ]
   ```
