`geq` subtracts, then checks every quantity of the difference, so it costs more again when the difference
holds many tokens. `Value.sum` converts each value once: summing five small values cost about 20 million
CPU, against 22 million for folding them with `Value.add`. Read ada with `lovelaceOf`, and prefer
`quantityOf` or `==` to building a filtered value.

## Traces

`Debug.trace` costs budget and bytes even when the script succeeds. One trace of a 19-character message
added about 140,000 CPU and 26 bytes. Remove traces from validators you deploy, or keep them only on
failure paths.

## Practical tips

- Measure before and after a change: `elci test` for validators, `elci eval` for helper functions.
- Order `&&` chains from cheap to expensive, and avoid naming expensive checks in a `let` you might not need.
- Keep purpose-specific work inside its handler. Turn expensive top-level values into functions.
- Traverse lists once. Over 100 elements, `List.filter` followed by `List.foldl` cost about 127 million CPU;
  one `List.foldl` with an `if` inside cost about 96 million.
- Convert to an `Array` once when you read many positions; never rebuild an array to change it.
- Avoid sorting on-chain. When the transaction can provide sorted data, check the order in one pass.
- Build keyed data with `Dict.fromList` rather than `Map.fromList`, which is quadratic. Keep maps and
  dictionaries small: every lookup scans.
- Read ada with `Value.lovelaceOf`, whose cost is fixed. Other `Value` operations grow with the number of
  assets in the value.
- Use each generic helper at as few types as you can, and drop `Debug.trace` from deployed scripts.
- Library functions are compiled Java code, not builtins: `Julc.ByteString.toHex` over 32 bytes cost
  about 73 million CPU. Check the cost of a library call before using it in a loop.

For how strictness and specialization come from the compiler's design, see
[how Elci compiles](https://elci-lang.dev/advanced/how-it-works/).

---

# How Elci compiles

> The path from .elm source to a Plutus V3 script — Elci's frontend stages, the boundary with Julc's backend, strict data boundaries and the native executable.

Source: https://elci-lang.dev/advanced/how-it-works/

This page follows your source through the compiler, from `.elm` text to the bytes in
`validator.plutus.json`. Knowing the stages helps you read error messages, predict costs and understand
what Elci guarantees and what it does not.

## The pipeline

Elci is a **frontend** over Julc's backend. It does not translate your code to Java, and it does not
have its own UPLC optimizer. It turns source into typed Plutus IR (PIR), and Julc does the rest:

```text
  .elm sources + elci.toml
          |
          v
  lexer and layout-aware parser        ELCI1xxx
          |
          v
  module and name resolution            ELCI21xx
          |
          v
  type inference and checks             ELCI20xx
          |
          v
  specialization and PIR lowering       ELCI3xxx
          |
  ======= | ======= Julc backend boundary ==========
          v
  validator wrapper, PIR verifier       ELCI4002, ELCI4003
          |
          v
  UPLC optimization and FLAT encoding
          |
          v
  build/validators/<name>/validator.plutus.json, abi.json, ...
```

The diagnostic codes on the right show where each class of error comes from; see
[diagnostics](https://elci-lang.dev/reference/diagnostics/).

## Frontend stages

### Lexing and parsing

The lexer turns text into tokens and records the line and column of each one. It rejects what Elci does
not support at the character level: tabs, `Float` literals such as `1.5`, character literals and
unknown escapes.

The parser is a hand-written, layout-aware recursive-descent parser. Like Elm, it uses indentation:
top-level declarations start in column 1, `let` declarations align with each other, and `case` branches
align with each other. Operators are parsed by precedence, as listed in the
[language reference](https://elci-lang.dev/reference/language/). Features outside Elci's profile, such as extensible records
or refutable patterns in function arguments, fail here with a message that names the feature.

### Modules and names

Module resolution builds the module graph. Each module `A.B` must live at `A/B.elm` under one source
directory, every module has one owner, and import cycles are rejected. The core modules (`Basics`,
`List`, `Maybe`, `Result`, `Tuple`, `String`, `Map`, `Dict`, `Array`, `Value`, `Interval` and `Tx`) are
ordinary Elci source, bundled with the compiler and compiled with your code. Every project and test module gets Elm's default imports of
`Basics`, `List`, `Maybe`, `Result`, `String`, `Tuple` and `Debug`; the core modules themselves import
what they need explicitly, as in Elm. `Bytes`, `Debug` and `Julc.Data` are compiler intrinsics, as are
`not`, `modBy` and `remainderBy`, which `Basics` exposes. Modules listed in `[java-modules]` are resolved
to Julc library classes.

Every name is then qualified with the module that owns it. A name is visible only if its module exposes
it and your module imports it. A module's own declarations shadow its imports, and two imports never
silently shadow each other: a name both expose is an error where it is used.

### Type inference and checks

Elci infers types with Hindley-Milner inference restricted to rank-1 types, then checks them against your
signatures. Every top-level declaration needs a signature. The checker also:

- groups recursive definitions and rejects eager value cycles (recursion must go through functions);
- keeps recursive calls monomorphic, so polymorphic recursion is rejected;
- allows limited local polymorphism: simple local functions and values may be used at several types;
- checks that `==`, ordering and `++` are used only at types that support them, and that a signature
  names such requirements with Elm's `comparable` and `appendable` type variables;
- accepts type variables that nothing determines, as Elm does: no value of such a type can exist, so any
  representation serves;
- proves every `case` exhaustive and every branch reachable;
- requires validator handlers and entrypoints to have concrete types that match their configuration.

### Specialization and lowering

Plutus has no runtime type information, so generic code cannot run as-is. The lowering stage
**specializes** every generic function reachable from your handlers: `List.map` used at `Int` and at
`Bool` becomes two separate functions. Each concrete use of a generic Java method is compiled by Julc in
the same way. A compiler limit of 256 specializations stops runaway growth.

Lowering then produces typed PIR while keeping Elci's evaluation rules:

- **Strict calls.** Arguments and captured variables are evaluated once, before use, from left to right.
  `let` values are evaluated in dependency order, with source order breaking ties, and an unused `let`
  value is still evaluated.
- **Selective branches.** `if`, `case`, `&&` and `||` evaluate only the branch they take.
- **Explicit representations.** Lists are Julc's native `List<Data>`, with each element encoded and
  decoded explicitly. Records, tuples and custom types become Plutus Data constructors.
- **Ordering.** `Int` and byte strings compare with the Plutus builtins, and `String` compares its UTF-8
  bytes. Lists and tuples compare with a function generated once per concrete type, like any other
  specialization.

Nothing is erased to an untyped `Data` value behind your back: a type Elci cannot represent faithfully is
a compile error.

## The Julc backend boundary

Elci hands Julc one of two kinds of program.

**Function programs.** An `[entrypoint]` function, run by `elci eval`, and each `elci test` program is a
closed, fully specialized function. Library exports are inlined at each use. Julc checks that the term is
closed and valid for the target, then compiles it without a validator wrapper.

**Validator programs.** Each `[validators.<name>]` table becomes one validator program with:

- **imports:** every library function the handlers need, linked once per script;
- **definitions:** the specialized top-level definitions reachable from any handler, with their PIR types;
- **handlers:** one reference per configured purpose;
- **parameters:** the deployment parameters, in the order listed in `parameters`;
- **named types:** your records and custom types.

Before compiling, Elci checks that the backend supports every capability the validator needs
(`ELCI4003` otherwise). Julc then runs a structural **PIR verifier** over Elci's definitions and handlers,
checking bindings, types and data-constructor agreement. A rejection is reported at the Elci declaration
it names (`ELCI4002`). If you ever see one, it is a compiler bug worth reporting.

Julc wraps the program in its shared multi-validator wrapper. The deployed script:

1. takes the deployment parameters, then **one** argument: the ledger's script context;
2. dispatches on the script purpose, rejecting purposes without a handler;
3. decodes the selected handler's datum and redeemer strictly;
4. calls the handler and turns `True` into success and `False` into a script failure.

Elci never builds its own dispatcher. Its one addition is a small adapter for `spend-datum = "optional"`:
Julc's optional datum and Elci's `Maybe` use different constructor tags, so the adapter re-tags the value.

Finally, Julc's UPLC pipeline optimizes the program and encodes it as FLAT bytes, and the CLI writes the
artifacts.

### Library imports

Java on-chain libraries reach Elci through a **provider**. The provider parses each library's Java
source (bundled with the compiler, or read from your `library-jars`), compiles the exports you use to
closed PIR with their transitive dependencies, and describes their types. Generic methods are described
as schemes and compiled once per concrete type. Elci never calls library code on the JVM. See
[Java libraries](https://elci-lang.dev/advanced/java-libraries/).

## Strict data boundaries

Everything that enters a validator from outside is `Data`, and Elci decodes it **strictly** before your
code runs. The wrapper checks constructor tags, field counts and nested field kinds of the datum and
redeemer, even the parts your handler ignores. Malformed data fails the transaction; it never becomes a
`Nothing` or a default value. Only the selected handler's datum and redeemer are decoded, so each
handler may use its own redeemer type.

Deployment parameters are decoded once when they are applied to the script but, as with Julc's Java
validators, not validated on-chain. `elci apply` therefore checks each parameter off-chain with the same
strict decoder before applying it. See [parameterized validators](https://elci-lang.dev/contracts/parameters/).

The encoding is deterministic:

| Elci value | Plutus Data |
| --- | --- |
| `Int` | integer |
| `Bytes`, ledger hashes | byte string |
| `String` | byte string holding its UTF-8 encoding |
| `Bool` | `False` is constructor 0, `True` is constructor 1, no fields |
| `()` | constructor 0, no fields |
| record | constructor 0, fields sorted by **name** |
| tuple | constructor 0, fields in position order |
| custom type | constructor tag = declaration order of the variant, fields in order |
| `Maybe a` | `Nothing` is constructor 0, `Just x` is constructor 1 with one field |
| `Result e a` | `Ok x` is constructor 0, `Err e` is constructor 1, each with one field |
| `List a` | list |
| `Map k v` | map |

Each build writes these choices to `abi.json`. Pin that file with `expected-abi` and the build fails if a
change to your types would change the on-chain format. The ledger's own context is decoded by Julc's
existing ledger-context convention, not by a new general decoder.

## What the verifier does and does not prove

Elci owns source typing, name hygiene, specialization and data representation. Julc's verifier checks
that the PIR it receives is well-formed and well-typed; it is not a proof that your contract is correct.
Your tests are. Compilation also has resource guards, such as the specialization limit, that are
separate from Cardano's execution budget.

## The native executable

The `elci` command is built twice from the same code: as a JVM application and as a GraalVM native
executable. The native executable:

- bundles the Elci core modules, Julc's standard-library sources and the JavaParser metadata needed to
  compile Java library source, so it needs no JDK at run time;
- reads your library JARs as source files, exactly like the JVM build;
- produces byte-identical artifacts. Building the `vesting` example with both gave the same file hashes;
- starts fast: that build took about 0.05 seconds natively and about 0.5 seconds on the JVM.

The compiler keeps no global mutable state between compilations, and builds are deterministic: building
twice gives the same bytes.

## What Elci does not do

- It does not run your code on the JVM to compute on-chain results.
- It does not generate Java, and it has no second UPLC pipeline.
- It does not fall back to untyped `Data` when a type is unsupported; it reports an error.
- It does not produce CIP-57 blueprints yet; the ABI manifest is Elci's own format.

To see how these stages show up in practice, read [costs and performance](https://elci-lang.dev/advanced/costs/) and the
[language reference](https://elci-lang.dev/reference/language/).

---

# CLI

> Every elci command and option — init, check, build, eval, test, apply and explain — with outputs, exit codes and error formats.

Source: https://elci-lang.dev/reference/cli/

This page documents every `elci` command and option, what each one prints and writes, and how it
reports errors. The examples use the native executable; the JVM launcher accepts exactly the same
arguments.

## Synopsis

```text
$ elci --help
Elci 0.1.0-dev — Elm-syntax compiler powered by Julc
Usage: elci <check|build> [project-directory] [--validator <name>]...
       elci eval [project-directory] [--builtins]
       elci test [project-directory] [--match <substring>] [--seed <n>] [--fuzz <runs>]
       elci apply [project-directory] --validator <name> --param <name>=<plutus-data-json|@file> [--output <file>]
       elci init <project-directory> [--validator <name>] [--purpose spend|mint|withdraw|certify|vote|propose|function]
       elci explain [code]
       elci --version
check, build, eval and test take --report=json to print each compile error as a JSON object on its own line,
and --color=auto|always|never for coloured errors (auto: on a terminal, unless NO_COLOR is set)
A build writes build/validators/<name>/validator.flat, validator.plutus, validator.plutus.json (Julc format) and abi.json (Elci schema)
for each [validators.<name>] group; an [entrypoint] function project writes build/validator.flat, validator.plutus and abi.json.
```

`elci`, `elci help`, `elci --help` and `--help` after any command (such as `elci eval --help`) print this
text and exit with status 0.

```text
$ elci --version
elci 0.1.0-dev / julc 0.1.0-pre20-ebaf028-SNAPSHOT
```

The second version is the Julc build the compiler is pinned to. A project's `julc-version` in
[`elci.toml`](https://elci-lang.dev/reference/configuration/) must match it exactly.

## Common behavior

**Project directory.** Every command except `init` and `explain` takes an optional project directory: the directory
that holds `elci.toml`. It defaults to the current directory. Giving two directories is an error.

**Two kinds of project.** A project configures either `[validators.<name>]` tables or one `[entrypoint]`
function. `check`, `build` and `test` work with both; `eval` needs an `[entrypoint]`; `apply` and
`--validator` need validators.

**Output streams.** Results go to standard output, including test results and a failed `eval` run.
Compile, configuration and command-line errors go to standard error.

**Exit status.**

| Status | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `0` | The command succeeded. |
| `1` | Any error: invalid arguments or configuration, a compile error, an `eval` that failed at run time, a failing test, or no tests found. |

**Error format.** A compile error starts with a line that names the source location and the code. The
source line follows, with carets under the reported code, and then any hints. The report ends with the
command that explains the code:

```text
my-project/src/Main.elm:6:5: ELCI2005: Unknown name 'lenght'

6|     lenght [ 1, 2 ]
       ^^^^^^
Hint: did you mean `List.length`?

For more on ELCI2005, run `elci explain ELCI2005`.
```

The first line always has the form `path:line:column: code: message`. A problem inside a bundled module
such as `List` is reported where your code uses it, or otherwise as `<bundled>/List.elm`, without an
excerpt. For a validator, the `elci.toml` table follows the diagnostic, on its own line:

```text
my-project/src/Main.elm:6:1: ELCI2014: Handler Main.spend does not have the spend signature datum -> redeemer -> ScriptContext -> Bool that [validators.main] needs (0 parameters); its type is () -> ScriptContext -> Bool; it has `Bool` where the configuration needs `ScriptContext -> Bool`

6| spend : () -> ScriptContext -> Bool
   ^^^^^

In my-project/elci.toml:6: [validators.main]

For more on ELCI2014, run `elci explain ELCI2014`.
```

Configuration and command-line errors start with `elci:` and carry the code `ELCI4001`, apart from the
few listed under [errors without a code](https://elci-lang.dev/reference/diagnostics/#errors-without-a-code):

```text
elci: ELCI4001: unknown validator 'treasury'; configured: main
```

**Several errors.** A run reports every compile error it finds, in source order and separated by blank
lines, followed by a count such as `3 errors`. It shows at most 20, then a line such as `... and 3 more`.
Each top-level declaration reports its first error, and type errors are reported only when there are no
syntax, import or qualified-name errors. Code generation, configuration and command-line errors stop the run at the first.
The [diagnostics](https://elci-lang.dev/reference/diagnostics/#several-errors-in-one-run) page explains how to read them and
lists every code.

**Colour.** On a terminal, compile errors are in colour, unless the `NO_COLOR` environment variable is
set. Every command takes `--color=auto`, `--color=always` or `--color=never` to choose; `auto` is the
default. Any other value is an `ELCI4001` error. JSON reports are never coloured.

**JSON reports.** `check`, `build`, `eval` and `test` take `--report=json`. With it, each error is printed on
standard error as one JSON object on its own line (JSON Lines), instead of the text above. A run with one
error prints one line; a run with several prints one line for each. Here one is formatted with `jq`:

```text
$ elci check my-project --report=json 2>&1 | jq
{
  "code": "ELCI2005",
  "path": "my-project/src/Main.elm",
  "line": 6,
  "column": 5,
  "message": "Unknown name 'lenght'",
  "hints": [
    "did you mean `List.length`?"
  ],
  "excerpt": "6|     lenght [ 1, 2 ]\n       ^^^^^^",
  "context": null
}
```

| Field | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `code` | The `ELCI` code, or null for an error without one |
| `path`, `line`, `column` | The location, or null for an error without one |
| `message` | The message, without the path and code |
| `hints` | The hints, as an array of strings; empty when there are none |
| `excerpt` | The source lines and their caret lines, separated by newlines, or null |
| `context` | The `elci.toml` line and table of a failing validator, such as `my-project/elci.toml:6: [validators.main]`, or null |

The JSON report has no count line and no `elci explain` line. A configuration or command-line error keeps
the same fields, with null location fields:

```text
{"code":"ELCI4001","path":null,"line":null,"column":null,"message":"unknown validator 'treasury'; configured: main","hints":[],"excerpt":null,"context":null}
```

The exit status doesn't change. Results stay text on standard output: the `check` and `build` lines, the
value, budget or `evaluation failed:` line of `eval`, and test results, including failing tests. `init`,
`apply` and `explain` reject the option:

```text
$ elci apply --report=json
{"code":"ELCI4001","path":null,"line":null,"column":null,"message":"--report=json applies to check, build, eval and test","hints":[],"excerpt":null,"context":null}
```

## `elci init`

Creates a new project in an empty or missing directory.

```text
elci init <project-directory> [--validator <name>] [--purpose <purpose>]
```

| Option | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--purpose` | `spend` | The first handler's purpose: `spend`, `mint`, `withdraw`, `certify`, `vote` or `propose`. `function` creates an `[entrypoint]` project for `elci eval` instead. |
| `--validator` | `main` | The validator's name: lowercase letters, digits, `-` or `_`, starting with a letter. Not allowed with `--purpose function`. |

```text
$ elci init my-project
Created Elci project at /path/to/my-project with initial spend handler in validator main.
Run: elci check /path/to/my-project
```

A validator project gets `elci.toml`, `src/Main.elm`, `tests/MainTest.elm`, `README.md` and a
`.gitignore` that ignores `build/`. The starter handler accepts transactions signed by an `owner`
deployment parameter, and the two tests check that the owner passes and anyone else is rejected. A
`--purpose function` project gets `elci.toml`, `src/Main.elm` (returning `42`), `README.md` and
`.gitignore`, and no tests.

Errors are `ELCI4001`, such as `ELCI4001: Project directory is not empty: ...`,
`ELCI4001: Unsupported purpose: lend; expected spend, mint, withdraw, certify, vote, propose or function` and
`ELCI4001: Invalid validator name '9bad'; use lowercase letters, digits, '-' or '_', starting with a letter`.

## `elci check`

Compiles the project and reports each result without writing files.

```text
elci check [project-directory] [--validator <name>]... [--report=json]
```

| Option | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `--validator <name>` | Check only this validator. Repeat it to select several. Validator projects only. |
| `--report=json` | Print each error as one JSON object on its own line on standard error (see [JSON reports](#common-behavior)). |

For a validator project, it prints one line per validator, sorted by name, with the purposes it
handles and its size in FLAT bytes:

```text
$ elci check
validator badge (mint): checked; 198 FLAT bytes; plutus-v3-pv11-uplc-1.1.0
validator treasury (spend, withdraw): checked; 540 FLAT bytes; plutus-v3-pv11-uplc-1.1.0
```

For an `[entrypoint]` project it prints the function instead:

```text
$ elci check
Main.main: checked; 6 FLAT bytes; plutus-v3-pv11-uplc-1.1.0
```

`check` compiles the source directories only; test modules are compiled by `elci test`. When `expected-abi` is set,
`check` also compares the ABI and fails on drift, exactly like `build`.

## `elci build`

Compiles the project and writes its artifacts under `build/`. It prints the same lines as `check`.

```text
elci build [project-directory] [--validator <name>]... [--report=json]
```

It takes the same options as `check`.

For each validator it writes `build/validators/<name>/`:

| File | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `validator.flat` | the script's FLAT bytes |
| `validator.plutus` | a `PlutusScriptV3` text envelope with the CBOR hex |
| `validator.plutus.json` | Julc's artifact: type, purpose, CBOR hex, script hash, parameters and `sizeBytes` |
| `abi.json` | Elci's ABI manifest: handlers, datum and redeemer schemas, parameters |

`build/validators/elci-outputs.json` records which files Elci owns. The `hash` in
`validator.plutus.json` is empty for a validator with parameters, because applying parameters changes
the hash. Its `purpose` is `multi` when the validator has several handlers.

Publishing is all-or-nothing: every selected validator is compiled and ABI-checked before any file is
written, and files are replaced atomically. A build of all validators also removes the output
directories of validators you deleted from `elci.toml`. A build with `--validator` touches only the
selected validators. Rebuilding a validator removes the `applied.plutus.json` that `elci apply` left in
its directory, since it belonged to the previous script.

An `[entrypoint]` project writes `build/validator.flat`, `build/validator.plutus` and `build/abi.json`.

See [build and deploy](https://elci-lang.dev/contracts/build-and-deploy/) for using these files.

## `elci eval`

Runs an `[entrypoint]` project's function on Julc's evaluator and prints the result.

```text
elci eval [project-directory] [--builtins] [--report=json]
```

| Option | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `--builtins` | Also print the builtin calls of the run, one per line, with arguments and result. The log keeps the last 20 calls. |
| `--report=json` | Print each compile error, or a configuration error, as one JSON object on its own line. A failed evaluation still prints `evaluation failed:` as text. |

The first line is the value, written in Elci syntax. The second is the CPU and memory consumed. Each
`Debug.trace` message follows on its own line:

```elm title="src/Main.elm"
module Main exposing (main)

type alias Quote =
    { price : Int, approved : Bool }

main : Quote
main =
    Debug.trace "pricing" { price = 25 * 1000000, approved = True }
```

```text
$ elci eval --builtins
{ approved = True, price = 25000000 }
cpu 1026458, mem 4557
trace: pricing
builtin: IfThenElse(True, <Delay>, <Delay>) → <Delay>
builtin: MkNilData(()) → [0 elems]
builtin: ConstrData(1, [0 elems]) → <Data>
builtin: IData(25000000) → <Data>
builtin: MkNilData(()) → [0 elems]
builtin: MkCons(<Data>, [0 elems]) → [1 elems]
builtin: MkCons(<Data>, [1 elems]) → [2 elems]
builtin: ConstrData(0, [2 elems]) → <Data>
builtin: Trace("pricing", <Data>) → <Data>
```

Values print as you would write them: `True`, `"text"`, `[1, -2]`, `Just 5`, `( 1, "a" )`, records with
their fields in name order, byte strings as `#474f4c44` (and `#(empty)`), maps as `Map.fromList [...]`,
dictionaries as `Dict.fromList [...]`, arrays as `Array.fromList [...]` and values as
`Value.fromList [( #policy, #token, quantity )]`, where ada's policy and token name are `#(empty)`. `eval` passes no arguments, so an entrypoint of function type
prints `<function>`. If evaluation fails, it prints `evaluation failed:` with the reason, then the
budget, and exits with status 1:

```text
$ elci eval
evaluation failed: QuotientInteger: division by zero
cpu 276441, mem 1001
```

`eval` rejects validator projects and the `--validator` option; test validators with `elci test`.

## `elci test`

Runs the tests in the project's test directories (`tests/` by default) and reports each with its budget.

```text
elci test [project-directory] [--match <substring>] [--seed <n>] [--fuzz <runs>] [--report=json]
```

| Option | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--match <substring>` | all tests | Run tests whose full name (`Module.test`) contains the substring, ignoring case. |
| `--seed <n>` | random | Seed for property tests. The seed used is printed, so any run can be repeated. |
| `--fuzz <runs>` | `100` | Number of runs for each property test. Must be positive. |
| `--report=json` | text | Print each compile error, such as one in a test module, or a configuration error as one JSON object on its own line. Test results stay text. |

```text
$ elci test --match deadline --seed 42
PASS VestingTest.claimsAfterTheDeadline (cpu 16763911, mem 61637)
PASS VestingTest.claimsAtTheDeadlineFail (cpu 13950292, mem 52228)
PASS VestingTest.claimsSucceedExactlyAfterTheDeadline (100 runs, max cpu 16763911, mem 61637)
3 passed, 0 failed (seed 42)
```

A failing test prints its details and traces, indented, and the command exits with status 1:

```text
$ elci test
FAIL FeeTest.feeIsRounded (cpu 2130706, mem 8398)
    Expect.equal
        expected: 30
        actual:   31
    trace: computing fee
PASS FeeTest.halves (cpu 424774, mem 1602)
PASS MainTest.ownerSigns (cpu 7675163, mem 29990)
PASS MainTest.othersAreRejected (cpu 8053596, mem 31922)
3 passed, 1 failed
```

The `(seed ...)` suffix appears only when a property test ran. If nothing runs, `elci test` prints
`No tests found in tests` or `No tests match '<substring>'` and exits with status 1, so it is safe as a
CI gate. What counts as a test is described in [unit tests](https://elci-lang.dev/testing/unit-tests/).

## `elci apply`

Applies deployment parameters to a validator and writes the applied script.

```text
elci apply [project-directory] --validator <name> --param <name>=<value> [--param ...] [--output <file>]
```

| Option | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `--validator <name>` | Required. Exactly one validator. |
| `--param <name>=<value>` | Required once for every name in the validator's `parameters`, and only for those. |
| `--output <file>` | Where to write the applied script. Default: `build/validators/<name>/applied.plutus.json`. |

Each value is Plutus Data in the detailed JSON schema that cardano-cli uses:

| JSON | Data |
| --- | --- |
| `{"int": 5}` | integer |
| `{"bytes": "a2c2..."}` | byte string, in hex |
| `{"list": [ ... ]}` | list |
| `{"map": [{"k": ..., "v": ...}]}` | map |
| `{"constructor": 0, "fields": [ ... ]}` | constructor |

Write `@path` instead of JSON to read the value from a file. That path is relative to the project
directory, while `--output` is relative to the current directory. JSON strings may not contain escapes.

```text
$ elci apply --validator main --param 'owner={"bytes": "a2c20c77887ace1cd986193e4e75babd8993cfd56995cd5cfce609c2"}'
validator main: applied 1 parameter; hash f050dee3352fb4863e471b360e9d9a1121d81e6705580d1cbc3b831f; wrote /path/to/my-project/build/validators/main/applied.plutus.json
```

`apply` compiles the validator, checks its ABI when `expected-abi` is set, and checks every value
off-chain with the strict decoder for the parameter's type, because the script itself does not validate
parameters. A value of the wrong shape is rejected before anything is written:

```text
$ elci apply --validator main --param 'owner={"int": 5}'
elci: ELCI4001: parameter owner is not a well-formed org.julclang.ledger.PubKeyHash value
```

Other errors name the problem: `missing --param owner=<plutus-data-json>`, `parameter owner is given more
than once`, `validator main has no parameter 'nope'; declared: owner`, and
`validator main declares no parameters`. See [parameterized validators](https://elci-lang.dev/contracts/parameters/).

## `elci explain`

Prints the long-form entry for a diagnostic code.

```text
elci explain [code]
```

The code may be written `ELCI2002`, `elci2002` or `2002`. An entry says what the code means and its
common causes, shows a failing example with its exact output, and gives the fix and the pages to read.
Code blocks are indented by four spaces. Without a code, `explain` lists every code with its title:

```text
$ elci explain
Run elci explain <code> for one of these:

  ELCI1001: Invalid character or literal
  ELCI1002: Malformed or unsupported syntax
  ELCI2001: Invalid expression or pattern
  ELCI2002: Type mismatch
```

The list goes on with every other code. An unknown code, or more than one, is an error:

```text
$ elci explain ELCI9999
elci: ELCI4001: ELCI9999 is not an Elci error code; run elci explain to list them
```

The entries are part of the compiler, so they match its version. The
[diagnostics](https://elci-lang.dev/reference/diagnostics/#elci-explain) page shows a whole entry.

---

# elci.toml

> Every table and key of elci.toml — project settings, validators, entrypoints, Java modules and tests — with the rules the parser enforces and complete examples.

Source: https://elci-lang.dev/reference/configuration/

Every Elci project has an `elci.toml` file at its root. This page lists every table and key, the values
each one accepts and the rules the compiler enforces. Unknown tables and keys are errors, so a typo
never goes unnoticed.

## Format

`elci.toml` uses a small, strict subset of TOML:

- A table header is a line like `[project]` or `[validators.treasury]`. Each table may appear once.
- Each setting is `key = value` on **one line**. A key may be quoted, as in `"Julc.Math" = "..."`.
- A value is either a quoted string, such as `"src"`, or an array of quoted strings on the same line,
  such as `["src", "lib"]`.
- Strings cannot contain escapes (`\`) or embedded quotes.
- Comments are whole lines starting with `#`. A comment after a value is an error.
- A key may appear only once per table.

## Project kinds

A project configures **either** one or more `[validators.<name>]` tables **or** one `[entrypoint]`
function, never both:

- **Validator projects** produce deployable scripts. Use `elci check`, `build`, `test` and `apply`.
- **Function projects** have an `[entrypoint]` for `elci eval`, which runs a function and prints its
  value and cost. They are for experiments and helper code, not for deployment.

## `[project]`

Required in every project.

| Key | Required | Value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `source-directories` | yes | Array of directories holding source modules, relative to the project. At least one; each must exist. |
| `target` | yes | Must be `"plutus-v3-pv11-uplc-1.1.0"`, the only supported target. |
| `julc-version` | yes | Must equal the Julc version the compiler is pinned to, currently `"0.1.0-pre20-ebaf028-SNAPSHOT"`. `elci --version` prints it. |
| `library-jars` | no | Array of JAR paths, relative to the project, that contain on-chain Java library sources. See [Java libraries](https://elci-lang.dev/advanced/java-libraries/). |
| `expected-abi` | no | Path of a committed `abi.json` to compare with the build. **Function projects only**; validators set it in their own table. |

A module `A.B` must live at `A/B.elm` inside exactly one source directory. Two files defining the same
module are an error.

## `[validators.<name>]`

One table per deployed script. The name becomes the output directory `build/validators/<name>/` and the
name you use in `elci apply --validator`, in tests and in `--validator` options. It must be 1 to 64
characters: lowercase letters, digits, `-` or `_`, starting with a letter.

| Key | Required | Value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `boundary` | yes | Must be `"julc-strict-v1"`, the strict data boundary. |
| `spend` | at least one handler | Handler for spending, as `"Module.function"`. |
| `mint` | | Handler for minting. |
| `withdraw` | | Handler for reward withdrawals. |
| `certify` | | Handler for certificates. |
| `vote` | | Handler for governance votes. |
| `propose` | | Handler for governance proposals. |
| `parameters` | no | Array of deployment parameter names, in application order. |
| `spend-datum` | no | `"required"` (default), `"optional"` or `"absent"`. Needs a `spend` handler. |
| `expected-abi` | no | Path of a committed `abi.json`; `check`, `build` and `apply` fail if the new ABI differs. |

Rules:

- **Handlers** name an exposed function as `"Module.function"`, for example `"Treasury.spend"`. Each
  handler key adds a purpose to the **same** script, so one table is always one script hash.
- **Parameter names** start with a lowercase letter, followed by letters, digits or `_`, and must be
  unique. Every handler receives all parameters as its leading arguments, in this order, so their types
  must agree across handlers.
- **Handler signatures** depend on the purpose and `spend-datum`:

| Handler | Required type |
| --- | --- |
| `spend` | `parameters -> datum -> redeemer -> ScriptContext -> Bool` |
| `spend` with `spend-datum = "optional"` | `parameters -> Maybe datum -> redeemer -> ScriptContext -> Bool` |
| `spend` with `spend-datum = "absent"` | `parameters -> redeemer -> ScriptContext -> Bool` |
| `mint`, `withdraw`, `certify`, `vote`, `propose` | `parameters -> redeemer -> ScriptContext -> Bool` |

Adding, removing or changing a handler changes the script and its hash. See
[validators and purposes](https://elci-lang.dev/contracts/validators/) and [datums and redeemers](https://elci-lang.dev/contracts/datums-and-redeemers/).

## `[entrypoint]`

The single function of a function project.

| Key | Required | Value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `module` | yes | The module name, such as `"Main"`. |
| `function` | yes | An exposed top-level function or value with a concrete type, such as `"main"`. |
| `purpose` | no | Only `"function"`, the default. |
| `boundary` | no | Only `"julc-strict-v1"`. |

Validator purposes in `[entrypoint]` were removed. `purpose = "spend"` fails with a message telling you to
move the handler into a `[validators.<name>]` table.

## `[java-modules]`

Maps Elm-style module names to on-chain Java library classes:

```toml
[java-modules]
"Julc.Math" = "org.julclang.stdlib.lib.MathLib"
"Acme.Pricing" = "acme.Pricing"
```

The key is the module name you import; the value is the fully qualified class name. A mapping is only
read when a module imports it. A module name cannot be both a source module and a Java module.
`Julc.TypedMap` and `Julc.TypedArray` are reserved by the core `Map` and `Array` modules and cannot be
remapped. The core module names `Basics`, `List`, `Maybe`, `Result`, `String`, `Tuple`, `Map`, `Dict`,
`Array`, `Value`, `Interval` and `Tx`, the reserved names `Set` and `Elci`, and names starting with `Elci.`
cannot be keys. See
[standard library](https://elci-lang.dev/advanced/standard-library/) for the bundled classes.

## `[tests]`

| Key | Required | Value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `source-directories` | no | Array of directories holding test modules. Default `["tests"]`. |

A missing default `tests` directory simply means there are no tests. Test modules are never part of
`check`, `build` or the deployed scripts. See [unit tests](https://elci-lang.dev/testing/unit-tests/).

## Complete examples

### A validator project

This project uses every validator setting: two scripts, a shared parameter, an optional datum, a pinned
ABI, a Java library JAR, a second source directory and a custom test directory.

```toml title="elci.toml"
# Settings for the whole project.
[project]
source-directories = ["src", "lib"]
target = "plutus-v3-pv11-uplc-1.1.0"
julc-version = "0.1.0-pre20-ebaf028-SNAPSHOT"
library-jars = ["libs/pricing.jar"]

# One script with two purposes and a deployment parameter.
[validators.treasury]
boundary = "julc-strict-v1"
parameters = ["admin"]
spend = "Treasury.spend"
withdraw = "Treasury.withdraw"
spend-datum = "optional"
expected-abi = "abi/treasury.json"

# A second, independent script.
[validators.badge]
boundary = "julc-strict-v1"
parameters = ["admin"]
mint = "Badge.mint"

[java-modules]
"Julc.Math" = "org.julclang.stdlib.lib.MathLib"
"Acme.Pricing" = "acme.Pricing"

[tests]
source-directories = ["spec"]
```

```text
$ elci check
validator badge (mint): checked; 229 FLAT bytes; plutus-v3-pv11-uplc-1.1.0
validator treasury (spend, withdraw): checked; 603 FLAT bytes; plutus-v3-pv11-uplc-1.1.0
```

With `spend-datum = "optional"`, the spend handler's datum is a `Maybe`:

```elm title="src/Treasury.elm"
spend : PubKeyHash -> Maybe Int -> () -> ScriptContext -> Bool
spend admin datum _ ctx =
    case datum of
        Just limit ->
            ctx.txInfo.fee <= Math.max limit (Pricing.fee limit 100)

        Nothing ->
            signedBy admin ctx
```

### A function project

This is what `elci init my-project --purpose function` creates:

```toml title="elci.toml"
[project]
source-directories = ["src"]
target = "plutus-v3-pv11-uplc-1.1.0"
julc-version = "0.1.0-pre20-ebaf028-SNAPSHOT"

[entrypoint]
module = "Main"
function = "main"
purpose = "function"
```

## Common errors

| Mistake | Message |
| --- | --- |
| Wrong `julc-version` | `ELCI4001: Julc version does not match this compiler; expected julc-version = "0.1.0-pre20-ebaf028-SNAPSHOT"` |
| Wrong `target` | `ELCI4001: Unsupported target; expected plutus-v3-pv11-uplc-1.1.0` |
| Misspelled key | `ELCI4001: Unknown configuration key: [project] name` |
| Unknown table | `ELCI4001: elci.toml:6: unknown configuration section: dependencies` |
| Missing `boundary` | `ELCI4001: Missing configuration key: [validators.main] boundary` |
| Bad validator name | `ELCI4001: elci.toml:6: invalid validator name 'Main'; use lowercase letters, digits, '-' or '_', starting with a letter (at most 64 characters)` |
| No handler | `ELCI4001: elci.toml:6: [validators.main] configures no handler; add one of mint, spend, withdraw, certify, vote, propose` |
| Handler without module | `ELCI4001: elci.toml:9: [validators.main] spend = "spend" must name an exposed function as "Module.function"` |
| `spend-datum` without `spend` | `ELCI4001: elci.toml:6: [validators.main] spend-datum requires a spend handler` |
| Both project kinds | `ELCI4001: elci.toml mixes [entrypoint] with [validators.*]; use one form` |
| Neither project kind | `ELCI4001: elci.toml must configure at least one [validators.<name>], or an [entrypoint] function` |
| `expected-abi` in `[project]` of a validator project | `ELCI4001: [project] expected-abi applies to [entrypoint] projects; set expected-abi in each [validators.<name>] table` |
| Unquoted value | `ELCI4001: Expected a quoted string without escapes: julc-strict-v1` |
| Comment after a value | `ELCI4001: Expected a quoted string without escapes: "0.1.0-pre20-ebaf028-SNAPSHOT" # pinned` |
| Multi-line array | `ELCI4001: elci.toml:3: expected key = value` |
| Missing source directory | `ELCI4001: Source directory not found: my-project/lib` |
| Remapping a core library | `ELCI4001: my-project/elci.toml:6: [validators.main]: [java-modules] may not remap Julc.TypedMap, which the Elci core library uses for org.julclang.stdlib.lib.TypedMapLib` |
| Mapping a core module name | `ELCI4001: my-project/elci.toml:6: [validators.main]: [java-modules] may not map Value, a module name of Elci's core library` |
| ABI changed | `ELCI4001: my-project/elci.toml:9: [validators.main]: ABI drift from abi/main.json; compare constructor tags, field order, handler roles and parameters` |

Each message is printed after `elci: ` and the command exits with status 1.

---

# Core modules

> Exact signatures and semantics of Elci's core library, imported by default as in Elm, and of the Dict, Map, Array, Value, Interval, Tx, Bytes, Julc.Data and Debug modules.

Source: https://elci-lang.dev/reference/core-modules/

This page lists every function the compiler provides without configuration: the `Basics` prelude, the
`List`, `Maybe`, `Result`, `Tuple` and `String` modules that every module imports, and the `Dict`, `Map`,
`Array`, `Value`, `Interval`, `Tx`, `Bytes`, `Julc.Data` and `Debug` modules. Signatures are exact; the notes
describe behavior, failure cases and cost. Names, argument orders and edge cases follow Elm 0.19's core library; the few differences
are listed [at the end](#differences-from-elm).

## Default imports

As in Elm, every source and test module starts with these imports, which you don't write:

```elm
import Basics exposing (..)
import List
import Maybe exposing (Maybe(..))
import Result exposing (Result(..))
import String
import Tuple
import Debug
```

So `max`, `compare`, `Just` and `Ok` work unqualified, and `List.map`, `String.fromInt` and `Debug.trace`
work qualified. Writing one of these imports yourself is allowed; an `exposing` list then adds names, as
in `import List exposing (head)`.

`Bytes`, `Dict`, `Map`, `Array`, `Value`, `Interval`, `Tx` and `Julc.Data` need an explicit import, as `Dict`
and `Array` do in Elm. Using one without it names the import to add:

```text
src/Main.elm:6:5: ELCI2104: Bytes.fromString needs the Bytes module; add `import Bytes`
```

**Name precedence** follows Elm, with one addition:

- A module's own declarations shadow every import. If your module defines `max`, it uses its own;
  `Basics.max` still reaches the prelude's.
- Two imports that expose different things under one name make that name ambiguous. The error is
  reported where you use the name, and lists the qualified alternatives. A default import counts, so an
  `import Utils exposing (..)` whose `max` differs from `Basics.max` gives:

  ```text
  src/Main.elm:8:5: ELCI2102: max is ambiguous: it could be Basics.max or Utils.max. Write the one you mean, like Basics.max, or stop exposing the other
  ```

- *Addition:* a name you list explicitly, as in `import Utils exposing (max)`, takes precedence over a
  default import.
- Qualified names always work: `Basics.max`, `Maybe.withDefault`, `Result.Ok`.
- An import can't use a default module's name as its alias. `import Utils as String` gives
  `ELCI2104: The alias String names a core module that every module imports; choose another alias for Utils`.
- Nor can it use the name of any other core module or of a module in the project, since the
  two modules' names would merge. `import Julc.Interval as Interval` gives
  `ELCI2104: The alias Interval names Elci's core module Interval; choose another alias for Julc.Interval`.

The core modules are compiled with your code. A function you don't use is never compiled into the
script, so the default imports cost nothing.

### Built-in types

| Type | Values |
| --- | --- |
| `Int` | arbitrary-precision integers |
| `Bool` | `True`, `False` |
| `String` | UTF-8 text; `++` appends; functions in [`String`](#string) |
| `()` | the unit value `()` |
| `Bytes` | byte strings; functions in [`Bytes`](#bytes) |
| `Data` | Plutus Data; `==` compares structure; convert with [`Julc.Data`](#julcdata) |
| `List a` | linked lists; functions in [`List`](#list) |
| `Maybe a` | `Nothing`, `Just a`; functions in [`Maybe`](#maybe) |
| `Result error value` | `Ok value`, `Err error`; functions in [`Result`](#result) |
| `Order` | `LT`, `EQ`, `GT`, the result of `compare` |
| `Dict k v` | dictionaries with comparable keys, kept sorted; functions in [`Dict`](#dict) |
| `Map k v` | the ledger's association maps; functions in [`Map`](#map) |
| `Array a` | constant-time indexed arrays; functions in [`Array`](#array) |
| `Value` | the ledger's multi-asset values: lovelace and native tokens; functions in [`Value`](#value) |
| `JulcOptional a` | Julc's optional, returned by some Java library functions |

Tuples of two or three elements, closed records and your own custom types complete the picture; see the
[language reference](https://elci-lang.dev/reference/language/). `Dict`, `Map` and `Array` are type names you can use without
importing their modules. You may also write them as in Elm, with `import Dict exposing (Dict)` or
qualified as `Dict.Dict`, and likewise for `Map` and `Array`. The compiler's own modules qualify their types
the same way: `Bytes.Bytes` after `import Bytes`, and `Data.Data` after `import Julc.Data as Data`. `Value`
is not an Elm type, so its name needs an import: `import Value exposing (Value)`, or `Value.Value` after
`import Value`. Reading `out.value` needs no import. The same holds for `Interval`: name it after
`import Interval exposing (Interval)`, but read `ctx.txInfo.validRange` without one.

`Maybe`, `Just` and `Nothing` are built into the compiler. A module can't declare constructors named
`Just`, `Nothing`, `True` or `False` (`ELCI2011: Nothing is a constructor of the built-in Maybe type;
choose another name`), or types named `Int`, `Bool`, `String`, `Bytes`, `Data`, `List`, `Maybe`, `Dict`,
`Map`, `Array` or `Float` (`ELCI2011: Bytes is a built-in type; choose another name`).

## Comparable types

`<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, `compare`, `min`, `max`, `List.sort`, `List.sortBy`, `List.maximum` and
`List.minimum` work on **comparable** types. Both operands have the same type.

| Type | Order |
| --- | --- |
| `Int` | numeric |
| `String` | by its UTF-8 bytes, which is Unicode code point order: `"Zebra" < "apple"` |
| `Bytes` | lexicographic by unsigned byte; a proper prefix comes first |
| ledger byte strings: `PubKeyHash`, `ScriptHash`, `PolicyId`, `TokenName`, `TxId`, `DatumHash` and the other hashes | as `Bytes` |
| lists of a comparable type | lexicographic; a proper prefix comes first |
| tuples of comparable types | component by component |

`Bool`, `()`, records, custom types, `Maybe`, `Result`, `Dict`, `Map`, `Array`, `Value`, `Data`, functions
and ledger records such as `TxOutRef` are not comparable. Sort them by a comparable key with `List.sortBy`, or with
your own order and `List.sortWith`. Every order is total and agrees with `==`: `compare x y == EQ` exactly
when `x == y`. The arithmetic operators remain `Int`-only.

The error names the operation and the part of the type that isn't comparable:

```text
src/Main.elm:6:17: ELCI2003: The operator < needs comparable values, but Bool, in ( Int, Bool ), is not comparable. Comparable types are Int, String, Bytes, byte-string ledger types such as PubKeyHash, and lists and tuples of comparable types
```

A generic function that compares its arguments names its type variable `comparable`, as in Elm; see
[constrained type variables](https://elci-lang.dev/reference/language/#constrained-type-variables). The keys of a
[`Dict`](#dict) are comparable too.

## `Basics`

The prelude. Every module imports it with `exposing (..)`, so these names need no qualifier.

| Function | Type | Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `negate` | `Int -> Int` | `negate 42` is `-42` |
| `abs` | `Int -> Int` | `abs -4` is `4` |
| `min` | `comparable -> comparable -> comparable` | the smaller: `min 3 7` is `3` |
| `max` | `comparable -> comparable -> comparable` | the larger: `max "pear" "apple"` is `"pear"` |
| `clamp` | `Int -> Int -> Int -> Int` | `clamp low high x`: `clamp 0 100 150` is `100` |
| `compare` | `comparable -> comparable -> Order` | `compare 3 7` is `LT` |
| `identity` | `a -> a` | returns its argument |
| `always` | `a -> b -> a` | `always x` ignores its argument: `List.map (always 0) [ 1, 2 ]` is `[ 0, 0 ]` |
| `xor` | `Bool -> Bool -> Bool` | `True` when exactly one argument is `True` |
| `not` | `Bool -> Bool` | Boolean negation |
| `modBy` | `Int -> Int -> Int` | `modBy divisor value`: the result has the divisor's sign |
| `remainderBy` | `Int -> Int -> Int` | `remainderBy divisor value`: the result has the value's sign |

`type Order = LT | EQ | GT` is also part of `Basics`.

The operator `^` raises an `Int` to a power: `2 ^ 10` is `1024`. It binds tighter than `*` and groups to
the right, so `2 * 3 ^ 2` is `18` and `2 ^ 3 ^ 2` is `512`. A negative exponent fails the script, because
there is no `Float` for `2 ^ -1`.

| Expression | Result |
| --- | ---: |
| `modBy 3 7` | `1` |
| `modBy 3 -7` | `2` |
| `modBy -3 7` | `-2` |
| `remainderBy 3 7` | `1` |
| `remainderBy 3 -7` | `-1` |
| `remainderBy -3 7` | `1` |
| `-7 // 2` | `-3` |

A zero divisor fails the script. `//` truncates towards zero. There is no `/`, `Float`, `toFloat`,
`round` or other floating-point function.

```elm title="src/Main.elm"
module Main exposing (main)

main : ( List Int, ( String, String ), List Order )
main =
    ( [ negate 42, abs -4, min 3 7, clamp 0 100 150, 2 ^ 10, always 1 2 ]
    , ( max "pear" "apple", min "Zebra" "apple" )
    , [ compare 3 7, compare [ 1, 2 ] [ 1, 2 ], compare ( 2, "a" ) ( 1, "z" ) ]
    )
```

```text
$ elci eval
( [-42, 4, 3, 100, 1024, 1], ( "pear", "Zebra" ), [LT, EQ, GT] )
cpu 23660515, mem 86721
```

## `List`

Every module imports `List`; call its functions as `List.map` and so on, or expose them with
`import List exposing (foldl)`. The module is ordinary Elci source, compiled with your code.

| Function | Type | Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `singleton` | `a -> List a` | a list of one element |
| `repeat` | `Int -> a -> List a` | `n` copies; empty when `n <= 0` |
| `range` | `Int -> Int -> List Int` | `range 1 4` is `[ 1, 2, 3, 4 ]`; empty when the first is larger |
| `map` | `(a -> b) -> List a -> List b` | |
| `indexedMap` | `(Int -> a -> b) -> List a -> List b` | the index counts from 0 |
| `filter` | `(a -> Bool) -> List a -> List a` | |
| `filterMap` | `(a -> Maybe b) -> List a -> List b` | keeps the `Just` results |
| `foldl` | `(a -> b -> b) -> b -> List a -> b` | from the first element |
| `foldr` | `(a -> b -> b) -> b -> List a -> b` | from the last element |
| `concat` | `List (List a) -> List a` | |
| `concatMap` | `(a -> List b) -> List a -> List b` | |
| `intersperse` | `a -> List a -> List a` | `intersperse 0 [ 1, 2, 3 ]` is `[ 1, 0, 2, 0, 3 ]` |
| `map2` | `(a -> b -> result) -> List a -> List b -> List result` | stops at the shorter list |
| `map3` | `(a -> b -> c -> result) -> List a -> List b -> List c -> List result` | stops at the shortest list |
| `length` | `List a -> Int` | walks the whole list |
| `reverse` | `List a -> List a` | |
| `member` | `a -> List a -> Bool` | uses `==` |
| `all` | `(a -> Bool) -> List a -> Bool` | `True` for `[]` |
| `any` | `(a -> Bool) -> List a -> Bool` | `False` for `[]` |
| `maximum` | `List comparable -> Maybe comparable` | `Nothing` for `[]` |
| `minimum` | `List comparable -> Maybe comparable` | `Nothing` for `[]` |
| `sum` | `List Int -> Int` | `0` for `[]` |
| `product` | `List Int -> Int` | `1` for `[]` |
| `append` | `List a -> List a -> List a` | `append a b` is `a ++ b` |
| `isEmpty` | `List a -> Bool` | |
| `head` | `List a -> Maybe a` | `Nothing` for `[]` |
| `tail` | `List a -> Maybe (List a)` | `Nothing` for `[]` |
| `take` | `Int -> List a -> List a` | the first `n`; empty when `n <= 0` |
| `drop` | `Int -> List a -> List a` | all but the first `n`; the whole list when `n <= 0` |
| `partition` | `(a -> Bool) -> List a -> ( List a, List a )` | `( passing, failing )`, both in input order |
| `unzip` | `List ( a, b ) -> ( List a, List b )` | |
| `sort` | `List comparable -> List comparable` | smallest first |
| `sortBy` | `(a -> comparable) -> List a -> List a` | by a key |
| `sortWith` | `(a -> a -> Order) -> List a -> List a` | by a comparison function |

Semantics:

- `foldl` combines from the first element and `foldr` from the last. Both callbacks receive the
  **element first** and the accumulator second: `List.foldl (\v acc -> acc * 10 + v) 0 [ 1, 2, 3 ]` is
  `123`, and the same with `foldr` is `321`.
- `all` stops at the first `False` and `any` at the first `True`.
- `map2` and `map3` drop the extra elements of longer lists, as in Elm. On-chain, check lengths first when
  extras matter: pairing outputs with expected payouts would silently ignore an extra output.
- The sorts are stable merge sorts, O(n log n): equal elements keep their order. `sortBy` computes the
  key at each comparison, so keep keys cheap.
- Every other function is a traversal, O(n) in the list's length.

```elm title="src/Main.elm"
module Main exposing (main)

main : ( List Int, Maybe Int, ( List Int, List Int ) )
main =
    let
        amounts =
            [ 30, 5, 12, 5, 40 ]
    in
    ( List.sort amounts
    , List.maximum amounts
    , List.partition (\amount -> amount >= 10) amounts
    )
```

```text
$ elci eval
( [5, 5, 12, 30, 40], Just 40, ( [30, 12, 40], [5, 5] ) )
cpu 48378577, mem 228938
```

Records and custom types are not comparable. Sort them by a key, or with a comparison:

```elm title="src/Main.elm"
module Main exposing (main)

type alias Bid =
    { bidder : String
    , amount : Int
    }

bids : List Bid
bids =
    [ Bid "carol" 30, Bid "alice" 50, Bid "bob" 30 ]

main : ( List String, List String, String )
main =
    ( List.map (\bid -> bid.bidder) (List.sortBy (\bid -> bid.amount) bids)
    , List.map (\bid -> bid.bidder) (List.sortWith (\a b -> compare b.amount a.amount) bids)
    , String.join ", " (List.map (\bid -> String.fromInt bid.amount) bids)
    )
```

```text
$ elci eval
( ["carol", "bob", "alice"], ["alice", "carol", "bob"], "30, 50, 30" )
cpu 60322206, mem 262554
```

The constructors `[]` and `::`, list literals `[ 1, 2 ]`, `++` and list patterns are part of the
language. Sorting on-chain is not cheap; see [costs and performance](https://elci-lang.dev/advanced/costs/#sorting-and-comparing).

## `Maybe`

`Maybe a` is built in. Every module imports the `Maybe` module with `exposing (Maybe(..))`, so `Just` and
`Nothing` need no qualifier.

| Function | Type | Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `withDefault` | `a -> Maybe a -> a` | the value inside a `Just`, or the default |
| `map` | `(a -> b) -> Maybe a -> Maybe b` | transforms the value inside a `Just` |
| `map2` | `(a -> b -> value) -> Maybe a -> Maybe b -> Maybe value` | `Just` when both are present |
| `map3` | `(a -> b -> c -> value) -> Maybe a -> Maybe b -> Maybe c -> Maybe value` | `Just` when all are present |
| `andThen` | `(a -> Maybe b) -> Maybe a -> Maybe b` | chains computations that may produce nothing |

Arguments are evaluated before a call, as in Elm, so `Maybe.withDefault default m` always evaluates
`default`, even when `m` is a `Just`. On-chain that costs budget, and a failing default fails the script.
Keep an expensive or failing default in a `case` branch.

`Nothing` is constructor 0 and `Just` is constructor 1 in Plutus Data.

## `Result`

`type Result error value = Ok value | Err error`. Every module imports the `Result` module with
`exposing (Result(..))`.

| Function | Type | Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `map` | `(a -> value) -> Result x a -> Result x value` | transforms an `Ok` value |
| `map2` | `(a -> b -> value) -> Result x a -> Result x b -> Result x value` | the first `Err` wins |
| `map3` | `(a -> b -> c -> value) -> Result x a -> Result x b -> Result x c -> Result x value` | the first `Err` wins |
| `andThen` | `(a -> Result x b) -> Result x a -> Result x b` | chains computations that may fail |
| `withDefault` | `a -> Result x a -> a` | the `Ok` value, or the default |
| `toMaybe` | `Result x a -> Maybe a` | `Just` the `Ok` value, or `Nothing` |
| `fromMaybe` | `x -> Maybe a -> Result x a` | `Ok` with the value of a `Just`, or `Err` with the given error |
| `mapError` | `(x -> y) -> Result x a -> Result y a` | transforms an `Err` error |

In Plutus Data, `Ok` is constructor 0 and `Err` is constructor 1, following the declaration order. This
is the reverse of PlutusTx's `Either` (`Left` 0, `Right` 1): a datum written as an `Either` does not read
as a `Result`, because decoding would swap success and failure.

```elm title="src/Main.elm"
module Main exposing (main)

positive : Int -> Result String Int
positive amount =
    if amount > 0 then
        Ok amount

    else
        Err "not positive"

main : ( ( Int, Maybe Int, Maybe Int ), ( Result String Int, Result String Int, Int ) )
main =
    ( ( Maybe.withDefault 0 (List.head [])
      , Maybe.map (\n -> n * 2) (List.head [ 4, 5 ])
      , Maybe.andThen List.head (List.tail [ 1, 2, 3 ])
      )
    , ( Result.map2 (+) (positive 5) (positive 7)
      , Result.map2 (+) (positive -1) (positive 0)
      , Result.withDefault 0 (Result.andThen positive (Ok 3))
      )
    )
```

```text
$ elci eval
( ( 0, Just 8, Just 2 ), ( Ok 12, Err "not positive", 3 ) )
cpu 19297460, mem 75445
```

## `Tuple`

Every module imports `Tuple`. The functions work on pairs; take a triple apart with a pattern such as
`( a, b, c )`.

| Function | Type | Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `pair` | `a -> b -> ( a, b )` | `pair 1 "one"` is `( 1, "one" )` |
| `first` | `( a, b ) -> a` | |
| `second` | `( a, b ) -> b` | |
| `mapFirst` | `(a -> x) -> ( a, b ) -> ( x, b )` | |
| `mapSecond` | `(b -> y) -> ( a, b ) -> ( a, y )` | |
| `mapBoth` | `(a -> x) -> (b -> y) -> ( a, b ) -> ( x, y )` | |

## `String`

Every module imports `String`. A `String` is Plutus text: UTF-8, compared by its bytes.

| Function | Type | Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `fromInt` | `Int -> String` | the decimal form: `fromInt -42` is `"-42"` |
| `isEmpty` | `String -> Bool` | |
| `append` | `String -> String -> String` | the same as `++` |
| `concat` | `List String -> String` | `concat [ "ab", "cd" ]` is `"abcd"` |
| `join` | `String -> List String -> String` | `join ", " [ "a", "b" ]` is `"a, b"` |

There is no `length`, `toInt`, `split`, `slice` or `fromFloat`. `Bytes.fromString` and `Bytes.toString`
convert to and from the UTF-8 bytes, and `Bytes.length (Bytes.fromString s)` is the byte length. Asking
for a missing function lists what the module has:

```text
src/Main.elm:6:5: ELCI2104: Elci's String module has no toInt. It has append, concat, fromInt, isEmpty, join
```

## `Dict`

`import Dict exposing (Dict)`. A `Dict k v` is Elm's dictionary, with Elm's functions, argument orders and
results. It is stored as a Plutus map whose keys are strictly ascending in the
[comparable order](#comparable-types), so every dictionary has exactly one representation. Keys are
comparable types: `Int`, `String`, `Bytes`, ledger hashes such as `PubKeyHash`, and lists and tuples of
these. Values may be any type with a Data encoding.

| Function | Type | Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `empty` | `Dict k v` | |
| `singleton` | `comparable -> v -> Dict comparable v` | |
| `insert` | `comparable -> v -> Dict comparable v -> Dict comparable v` | replaces an existing binding |
| `update` | `comparable -> (Maybe v -> Maybe v) -> Dict comparable v -> Dict comparable v` | `Nothing` removes the key, `Just v` sets it |
| `remove` | `comparable -> Dict comparable v -> Dict comparable v` | |
| `isEmpty` | `Dict k v -> Bool` | |
| `member` | `comparable -> Dict comparable v -> Bool` | |
| `get` | `comparable -> Dict comparable v -> Maybe v` | `Nothing` when the key is absent |
| `size` | `Dict k v -> Int` | |
| `keys` | `Dict k v -> List k` | in ascending order |
| `values` | `Dict k v -> List v` | in ascending key order |
| `toList` | `Dict k v -> List ( k, v )` | in ascending key order |
| `fromList` | `List ( comparable, v ) -> Dict comparable v` | for a repeated key, the last pair wins |
| `map` | `(k -> a -> b) -> Dict k a -> Dict k b` | |
| `foldl` | `(k -> v -> b -> b) -> b -> Dict k v -> b` | from the smallest key |
| `foldr` | `(k -> v -> b -> b) -> b -> Dict k v -> b` | from the largest key |
| `filter` | `(comparable -> v -> Bool) -> Dict comparable v -> Dict comparable v` | |
| `partition` | `(comparable -> v -> Bool) -> Dict comparable v -> ( Dict comparable v, Dict comparable v )` | `( passing, failing )` |
| `union` | `Dict comparable v -> Dict comparable v -> Dict comparable v` | for a key in both, the left value wins |
| `intersect` | `Dict comparable v -> Dict comparable v -> Dict comparable v` | the left bindings whose keys the right has |
| `diff` | `Dict comparable a -> Dict comparable b -> Dict comparable a` | the left bindings whose keys the right lacks |
| `merge` | `(comparable -> a -> result -> result) -> (comparable -> a -> b -> result -> result) -> (comparable -> b -> result -> result) -> Dict comparable a -> Dict comparable b -> result -> result` | see below |

```elm title="src/Main.elm"
module Main exposing (main)

import Dict exposing (Dict)

stock : Dict String Int
stock =
    Dict.fromList [ ( "pear", 5 ), ( "apple", 3 ), ( "fig", 0 ), ( "apple", 4 ) ]

main : ( List ( String, Int ), ( Maybe Int, Bool ), List String )
main =
    ( Dict.toList (Dict.insert "kiwi" 2 stock)
    , ( Dict.get "apple" stock, Dict.member "plum" stock )
    , Dict.keys (Dict.filter (\_ count -> count > 0) stock)
    )
```

```text
$ elci eval
( [( "apple", 4 ), ( "fig", 0 ), ( "kiwi", 2 ), ( "pear", 5 )], ( Just 4, False ), ["apple", "pear"] )
cpu 77921806, mem 309819
```

The bindings come out in key order, whatever order they went in, and the second `"apple"` replaced the
first. Combining two dictionaries follows Elm too. `merge` folds over both in ascending key order, with one
step for keys only in the left dictionary, one for keys in both and one for keys only in the right:

```elm title="src/Main.elm"
module Main exposing (main)

import Dict exposing (Dict)

left : Dict Int String
left =
    Dict.fromList [ ( 1, "a" ), ( 2, "b" ) ]

right : Dict Int String
right =
    Dict.fromList [ ( 2, "x" ), ( 3, "y" ) ]

main : ( ( List ( Int, String ), List Int, List Int ), ( List String, Bool ) )
main =
    ( ( Dict.toList (Dict.union left right)
      , Dict.keys (Dict.intersect left right)
      , Dict.keys (Dict.diff left right)
      )
    , ( Dict.merge
            (\key _ result -> result ++ [ "only left " ++ String.fromInt key ])
            (\key _ _ result -> result ++ [ "both " ++ String.fromInt key ])
            (\key _ result -> result ++ [ "only right " ++ String.fromInt key ])
            left
            right
            []
      , Dict.insert 2 "b" (Dict.singleton 1 "a") == left
      )
    )
```

```text
$ elci eval
( ( [( 1, "a" ), ( 2, "b" ), ( 3, "y" )], [2], [1] ), ( ["only left 1", "both 2", "only right 3"], True ) )
cpu 116952501, mem 457650
```

**Equality.** `==` compares bindings: two dictionaries are equal when they have the same keys with equal
values, however they were built. The values need equality themselves, so a `Dict Int (Map Int Int)` can't
be compared (`ELCI2003`). Dictionaries are not comparable.

**Cost.** A `Dict` is a list of pairs, not a tree as in Elm:

- `get`, `member`, `insert`, `remove` and `update` walk from the smallest key and stop at the first key
  that isn't smaller than the one they look for. They are O(n), at about 1.1 million CPU units per key
  passed. Small keys are found fastest, and a missing key costs half a scan on average.
- `fromList` is a stable merge sort: O(n log n), and O(n) when the pairs are already in key order. For 50
  entries it cost about 0.28 billion CPU units with sorted input and 0.66 billion with shuffled input,
  against 1.5 billion for `Map.fromList`.
- `size`, `keys`, `values`, `toList`, the folds, `map`, `filter` and `partition` are single passes.
  `union`, `intersect`, `diff` and `merge` walk both dictionaries once: O(n + m).

**In Data.** A `Dict` encodes as a Plutus map with its keys in ascending order. Decoding checks the order:
a map whose keys are not strictly ascending, because they are out of order or repeated, fails to decode.
The check applies to datums, redeemers, parameters, `Julc.Data.decode` and property-test arguments, and to
every `Dict` inside them: in records, tuples, custom types, `Maybe`, `Result`, Julc optionals, lists and
map values. It costs about 1.1 million CPU units per entry. Without it, a datum could place a key after a
larger one, where `member` and `get` stop before reaching it;
[datums and redeemers](https://elci-lang.dev/contracts/datums-and-redeemers/#dictionaries-in-data) shows the attack.
`elci apply` rejects such a parameter:

```text
elci: ELCI4001: parameter caps has a Dict whose keys are not strictly ascending; write its keys sorted and without repeats
```

Two rules keep every decoded `Dict` checked. Checking the order needs comparable keys, so a `Dict` with
other keys can't be decoded from Data:

```text
src/Main.elm:9:5: ELCI2003: A Dict decoded from Data needs comparable keys, to check that they are in order; Bool is not comparable. Use a Map instead
```

And a Java library's generic function can't be used at a type that contains a `Dict`, because the library
could build one without the check:

```text
src/Main.elm:14:18: ELCI3003: Type argument a = Dict Int Int of filter contains a Dict, which a Java library cannot keep sorted; pass a Map or a List and build the Dict with Dict.fromList
```

**`Dict` or `Map`?** Use a `Dict` for data you build or look up by a comparable key, including datums. Use a
[`Map`](#map) for the ledger's own maps, such as `txInfo.withdrawals` and `txInfo.redeemers`, and for keys
that are not comparable.

## `Map`

`import Map`. A `Map k v` is the ledger's map representation: a list of key/value pairs, compared by the
keys' Data encoding. The transaction's maps, such as `txInfo.withdrawals`, `txInfo.redeemers` and
`txInfo.datums`, are `Map`s. Keys and values may be any type with a Data encoding, including records,
custom types and ledger types; keys need not be comparable.

| Function | Type | Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `empty` | `Map k v` | |
| `singleton` | `k -> v -> Map k v` | |
| `get` | `k -> Map k v -> Maybe v` | `Nothing` when the key is absent |
| `member` | `k -> Map k v -> Bool` | |
| `insert` | `k -> v -> Map k v -> Map k v` | replaces an existing binding |
| `remove` | `k -> Map k v -> Map k v` | |
| `update` | `k -> (Maybe v -> Maybe v) -> Map k v -> Map k v` | `Nothing` removes the key, `Just v` sets it |
| `size` | `Map k v -> Int` | |
| `isEmpty` | `Map k v -> Bool` | |
| `keys` | `Map k v -> List k` | in map order |
| `values` | `Map k v -> List v` | in map order |
| `toList` | `Map k v -> List ( k, v )` | in map order |
| `fromList` | `List ( k, v ) -> Map k v` | inserts the pairs in list order |
| `foldl` | `(k -> v -> b -> b) -> b -> Map k v -> b` | in map order |
| `foldr` | `(k -> v -> b -> b) -> b -> Map k v -> b` | in reverse map order |
| `filter` | `(k -> v -> Bool) -> Map k v -> Map k v` | keeps map order |
| `map` | `(k -> a -> b) -> Map k a -> Map k b` | keeps map order |

**Map order.** `insert` puts the binding at the front, and a replaced key moves to the front. So
`Map.keys (Map.fromList [ ( 1, 10 ), ( 2, 20 ), ( 3, 30 ) ])` is `[ 3, 2, 1 ]`. `filter` and `map` keep
the order of the map they are given:

```elm title="src/Main.elm"
module Main exposing (main)

import Map exposing (Map)

prices : Map String Int
prices =
    Map.fromList [ ( "apple", 3 ), ( "pear", 5 ) ]

main : ( Map String Int, Map String Int, Maybe Int )
main =
    ( Map.insert "fig" 7 prices
    , Map.filter (\_ price -> price > 3) (Map.insert "fig" 7 prices)
    , Map.get "pear" prices
    )
```

```text
$ elci eval
( Map.fromList [( "fig", 7 ), ( "pear", 5 ), ( "apple", 3 )], Map.fromList [( "fig", 7 ), ( "pear", 5 )], Just 5 )
cpu 36520840, mem 151709
```

Avoid making results depend on map order. To process the bindings in key order, sort them,
`List.sortBy Tuple.first (Map.toList prices)`, or keep them in a [`Dict`](#dict).

**No equality.** `==` on maps is rejected (`ELCI2003`): two maps with the same bindings may hold them in
different orders. For the same reason `Data.encode` of two such maps may differ. Compare the lookups you
care about, or their `toList` after sorting, or use a `Dict`.

**Repeated keys.** A map built in Elci never repeats a key, but a map decoded from Data can, because
decoding doesn't check a `Map`'s keys. In such a map, `get` returns the first binding of the key, `remove`
and `insert` remove every binding of it, and `map` and `filter` keep every binding.

**Cost.** `get`, `member`, `insert`, `remove` and `update` scan the pairs from the front: O(n), at about 1.1
million CPU units per key passed. `size`, `keys`, `values`, `toList`, the folds, `filter` and `map` are
single passes. `fromList` checks each key against the pairs before it, so it is O(n²): building a 50-entry
map cost about 1.5 billion CPU units. With comparable keys, `Dict.fromList` is much cheaper. See
[costs and performance](https://elci-lang.dev/advanced/costs/#maps-and-dictionaries).

A map or dictionary whose key and value types nothing determines can't be compiled, because the
operations are specialized for them. `Map.size Map.empty` on its own fails at the call:

```text
src/Main.elm:8:5: ELCI3001: `Map.size` is used here at a type that is not known (Map a b -> Int); add a type annotation, for example to a let binding
```

Give the map a type, for example with a local definition `noPrices : Map String Int`.

## `Array`

`import Array`. An `Array a` works like Elm's `Array`. It is a Plutus V3 array: built once from a list,
then read in constant time.

| Function | Type | Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `empty` | `Array a` | |
| `fromList` | `List a -> Array a` | O(n) |
| `toList` | `Array a -> List a` | O(n) |
| `toIndexedList` | `Array a -> List ( Int, a )` | pairs of index and element |
| `length` | `Array a -> Int` | O(1) |
| `isEmpty` | `Array a -> Bool` | O(1) |
| `get` | `Int -> Array a -> Maybe a` | O(1); `Nothing` for an index below 0 or at least `length` |
| `initialize` | `Int -> (Int -> a) -> Array a` | `initialize 4 (\i -> i * i)` is `[ 0, 1, 4, 9 ]` |
| `repeat` | `Int -> a -> Array a` | `repeat 3 7` is `[ 7, 7, 7 ]` |
| `foldl` | `(a -> b -> b) -> b -> Array a -> b` | from the first element |
| `foldr` | `(a -> b -> b) -> b -> Array a -> b` | from the last element |
| `map` | `(a -> b) -> Array a -> Array b` | O(n) |
| `indexedMap` | `(Int -> a -> b) -> Array a -> Array b` | O(n) |
| `filter` | `(a -> Bool) -> Array a -> Array a` | O(n) |
| `slice` | `Int -> Int -> Array a -> Array a` | from `start` up to, not including, `end` |

`slice` counts a negative index from the end and clamps to the array. For `[ 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 ]`,
`slice 1 3` is `[ 20, 30 ]`, `slice 0 -1` is `[ 10, 20, 30, 40 ]` and `slice -2 10` is `[ 40, 50 ]`.

Arrays are immutable and there is no `set` or `push`. Build a list, then convert it once.

**No Data encoding.** An array cannot be a datum, redeemer, parameter or property-test argument, nor a
field of a record, custom type, tuple, list or map. Storing one there fails with `ELCI2013: Arrays have no
Data encoding and cannot be stored in data; keep a List and convert it with Array.fromList`, and
`Julc.Data.encode` on an array is rejected with `ELCI3003`. Keep lists in your data and call
`Array.fromList` in the handler. An `[entrypoint]` may return an array on its own; `elci eval` prints it
as `Array.fromList [40, 50]`.

## `Value`

`import Value exposing (Value)`. A `Value` is the ledger's multi-asset value: an amount of lovelace and
quantities of native tokens. `out.value` and `ctx.txInfo.mint` are `Value`s, and so is everything this
module builds. A token is named by a policy id and a token name, the ledger types `PolicyId` and
`TokenName`; build them from bytes with `import Julc.Ledger exposing (PolicyId(..), TokenName(..))`, as in
`PolicyId bytes`. Ada is the empty token name under the empty policy, and `lovelace` and `lovelaceOf` cover
it; a token with another name under the empty policy is not lovelace. Functions take the value last, as in
Elm.

| Function | Type | Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `zero` | `Value` | the empty value |
| `lovelace` | `Int -> Value` | an amount of lovelace |
| `singleton` | `PolicyId -> TokenName -> Int -> Value` | a quantity of one token |
| `insert` | `PolicyId -> TokenName -> Int -> Value -> Value` | sets the quantity of one token, replacing what the value held; `0` removes the token |
| `fromList` | `List ( PolicyId, TokenName, Int ) -> Value` | the listed quantities; a repeated token adds up |
| `lovelaceOf` | `Value -> Int` | the lovelace: the quantity of ada's token; `0` when there is none, as in a minted value |
| `quantityOf` | `PolicyId -> TokenName -> Value -> Int` | the quantity of one token; `0` when there is none |
| `isZero` | `Value -> Bool` | whether the value holds nothing |
| `policies` | `Value -> List PolicyId` | in ascending order; ada's is the empty policy |
| `tokens` | `PolicyId -> Value -> Dict TokenName Int` | the tokens of one policy and their quantities |
| `toList` | `Value -> List ( PolicyId, TokenName, Int )` | every token, in ascending order |
| `add` | `Value -> Value -> Value` | the sum |
| `subtract` | `Value -> Value -> Value` | the first value minus the second |
| `negate` | `Value -> Value` | every quantity negated |
| `scale` | `Int -> Value -> Value` | every quantity multiplied |
| `sum` | `List Value -> Value` | the sum of the list |
| `geq` | `Value -> Value -> Bool` | `geq a b`: `a` holds at least as much of every token as `b` |
| `leq` | `Value -> Value -> Bool` | `leq a b`: `a` holds at most as much of every token as `b` |
| `withoutLovelace` | `Value -> Value` | the value without its lovelace |
| `restrictedTo` | `List PolicyId -> Value -> Value` | only the tokens of the listed policies |
| `positive` | `Value -> Value` | only the positive quantities: in a minted value, what is minted |
| `negative` | `Value -> Value` | only the negative quantities, still negative: in a minted value, what is burned |

```elm title="src/Main.elm"
module Main exposing (main)

import Bytes
import Julc.Ledger exposing (PolicyId(..), TokenName(..))
import Value exposing (Value)

gold : PolicyId
gold =
    PolicyId (Bytes.fromString "gold")

coin : TokenName
coin =
    TokenName (Bytes.fromString "coin")

payment : Value
payment =
    Value.add (Value.lovelace 2000000) (Value.fromList [ ( gold, coin, 3 ), ( gold, coin, 2 ) ])

main : ( Value, ( Int, Int ), ( Bool, Bool ) )
main =
    ( payment
    , ( Value.lovelaceOf payment, Value.quantityOf gold coin payment )
    , ( Value.geq payment (Value.lovelace 1500000)
      , payment == Value.insert gold coin 5 (Value.lovelace 2000000)
      )
    )
```

```text
$ elci eval
( Value.fromList [( #(empty), #(empty), 2000000 ), ( #676f6c64, #636f696e, 5 )], ( 2000000, 5 ), ( True, True ) )
cpu 29654521, mem 85992
```

`elci eval` prints a value as the `Value.fromList` that builds it, one `( policy, token name, quantity )`
per token; `#(empty)` is ada's policy and token name. The two `coin` entries added up to 5.

**Canonical form and equality.** Every `Value` is canonical: policies ascend by their bytes, compared as
unsigned, token names ascend within each policy, and no quantity is zero. The ledger's values are canonical,
the functions above keep them so, and decoding a `Value` from Data rejects any other form. So two values are
equal exactly when they hold the same quantities, whatever order the tokens were added in: `==` works on
values, and on your records, tuples and lists that contain them. Values are not
[comparable](#comparable-types); compare them with `geq` and `leq`.

**Negative quantities.** A value may hold negative quantities. The transaction's `mint` field holds the
tokens it burns as negative quantities. `geq` and `leq` handle them: `geq a b` subtracts `b` from `a` and
checks that no quantity is below zero, so a burn counts as less than none. `positive` and `negative` split
a mint into what it mints and what it burns:

```elm title="src/Main.elm"
module Main exposing (main)

import Bytes
import Dict
import Julc.Ledger exposing (PolicyId(..), TokenName(..))
import Value exposing (Value)

gold : PolicyId
gold =
    PolicyId (Bytes.fromString "gold")

{-| A mint that creates 3 new coins and burns 2 old ones.
-}
minted : Value
minted =
    Value.fromList
        [ ( gold, TokenName (Bytes.fromString "new"), 3 )
        , ( gold, TokenName (Bytes.fromString "old"), -2 )
        ]

main : ( ( Value, Value ), ( Bool, Bool ), List ( TokenName, Int ) )
main =
    ( ( Value.positive minted, Value.negate (Value.negative minted) )
    , ( Value.geq minted Value.zero, Value.geq (Value.positive minted) Value.zero )
    , Dict.toList (Value.tokens gold minted)
    )
```

```text
$ elci eval
( ( Value.fromList [( #676f6c64, #6e6577, 3 )], Value.fromList [( #676f6c64, #6f6c64, 2 )] ), ( False, True ), [( #6e6577, 3 ), ( #6f6c64, -2 )] )
cpu 45778556, mem 170124
```

`Value.negate (Value.negative minted)` gives the burned amounts as positive quantities.

**Failures.** A policy id or token name longer than 32 bytes, and a quantity outside the signed 128-bit
range, fail the script: `evaluation failed: InsertCoin: tokenName too long: 33 bytes (max 32)`.

**In Data.** A `Value` is stored as the ledger stores it, a Plutus map from policy ids to maps from token
names to quantities, so `Julc.Data.encode` of a value costs nothing. `Julc.Data.decode` accepts only the
canonical form. Unsorted or repeated policies or token names fail with
`UnValueData: currencies not strictly ordered or duplicate`, a zero quantity with
`UnValueData: zero quantity`, and a policy without tokens or an id longer than 32 bytes fail too.

Both conversions work on a `Value` itself. A type that contains one can't be decoded yet, and a list or tuple
