of values can't be encoded either (`ELCI3003`). A `Value` can't be a datum, redeemer or parameter yet, nor
part of one:

```text
src/Main.elm:7:1: ELCI2013: org.julclang.ledger.Value has no approved strict Data boundary (BOUNDARY); for example records containing the map-encoded Value cannot be checked
```

Store a `List ( PolicyId, TokenName, Int )` instead, and rebuild the value with `Value.fromList`.

**Cost.** `lovelaceOf`, `isZero`, `policies`, `tokens` and `toList` read the value's Data directly, and
`positive`, `negative`, `restrictedTo` and `withoutLovelace` filter it entry by entry, keeping it canonical.
The other functions convert it to the protocol's native value (CIP-153 builtins) and back, which costs about a
million CPU units for a value of a few assets; `sum` converts each value once. These small programs, which
include building their values, cost:

| Program | CPU |
| --- | ---: |
| `Value.add` of `Value.lovelace` and `Value.singleton` | 3.5 million |
| `Value.lovelaceOf (Value.lovelace 5000000)` | 2.7 million |
| `Value.quantityOf` of a `Value.singleton` | 2.5 million |
| `Value.geq` of two `Value.lovelace` values | 6.3 million |
| `Value.sum` of five `Value.lovelace` values | 20 million |

Most functions grow with the number of assets; [costs and performance](https://elci-lang.dev/advanced/costs/#values) has figures
for larger values.

**Java libraries.** A Java library builds values in its own order, as Julc's `ValuesLib` does, so no Java
library may hand Elci a `Value`. An export whose result can hold one, directly or in a field of a record or
union, is rejected:

```text
src/Main.elm:9:5: ELCI2105: org.julclang.stdlib.lib.ValuesLib.add: returns a Value, which Java libraries do not keep in the ledger's canonical order; use the core Value module
```

A generic Java function can't be used at a type that holds a `Value` either:

```text
src/Main.elm:9:5: ELCI3003: Type argument a = Value of filter contains a Value, which a Java library does not keep in the ledger's canonical order; build it with the Value module
```

Julc's `ContextsLib` and `OutputLib` are exempt: they only pass along the ledger's own values, as
`ContextsLib.valuePaid` does. Exports that only read a value, such as `ValuesLib.assetOf`, still work, but
this module covers them. A value has no constructors or patterns of its own:
`import Julc.Ledger exposing (Value(..))` gives
`ELCI2104: Value has no approved constructors or patterns; its values come from the Value module`.

## `Interval`

`import Interval`. An `Interval` is the ledger's time range, such as the transaction's validity range
`ctx.txInfo.validRange`. Times are POSIX milliseconds. A range has a start, `range.from`, and an end,
`range.to`. Each bound is `NegInf`, `Finite time` or `PosInf`, and is inclusive or exclusive.

A script can't read the clock. The ledger accepts a transaction only inside its validity range, so a time
check asks where the whole range lies: `isEntirelyAfter deadline ctx.txInfo.validRange` holds only when
the transaction cannot run at or before the deadline.

| Function | Type | Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `isEntirelyAfter` | `Int -> Interval -> Bool` | `isEntirelyAfter t range`: the range has a finite start, and every time in it is after `t` |
| `isEntirelyBefore` | `Int -> Interval -> Bool` | `isEntirelyBefore t range`: the range has a finite end, and every time in it is before `t` |
| `contains` | `Int -> Interval -> Bool` | `contains t range`: `t` is in the range |
| `start` | `Interval -> Maybe Int` | the finite start, or `Nothing` |
| `end` | `Interval -> Maybe Int` | the finite end, or `Nothing` |
| `after` | `Int -> Interval` | from `t` on, inclusive |
| `before` | `Int -> Interval` | up to `t`, inclusive |
| `between` | `Int -> Int -> Interval` | `between low high`: from `low` to `high`, both inclusive |
| `everything` | `Interval` | all time |

"After" and "before" are strict: no time in the range may equal `t`. The checks honor each bound's
inclusiveness. A scenario's `Scenario.validFrom t` gives the range an inclusive start, and
`Scenario.validBefore t` an exclusive end, so:

- `isEntirelyAfter deadline` holds for a range valid from `deadline + 1` on, not from `deadline`. To
  accept a transaction valid from the deadline itself, check `isEntirelyAfter (deadline - 1)`.
- `isEntirelyBefore deadline` holds for a range valid before `deadline`: the exclusive end may equal it.

```elm title="src/Main.elm"
module Main exposing (main)

import Interval exposing (Interval)
import Julc.Ledger exposing (Interval(..), IntervalBound(..), IntervalBoundType(..))

{-| A validity range from 1000, inclusive, to 2000, exclusive.
-}
window : Interval
window =
    Interval (IntervalBound (Finite 1000) True) (IntervalBound (Finite 2000) False)

main : ( ( Bool, Bool, Bool ), ( Bool, Bool, Bool ), ( Bool, Bool, Maybe Int ) )
main =
    ( ( Interval.isEntirelyAfter 999 window, Interval.isEntirelyAfter 1000 window, Interval.contains 1000 window )
    , ( Interval.isEntirelyBefore 2000 window, Interval.isEntirelyBefore 1999 window, Interval.contains 2000 window )
    , ( Interval.isEntirelyAfter 0 (Interval.before 5), Interval.isEntirelyBefore 10 (Interval.after 5), Interval.end (Interval.after 5) )
    )
```

```text
$ elci eval
( ( True, False, True ), ( True, False, False ), ( False, False, Nothing ) )
cpu 44424561, mem 167367
```

The window starts at 1000, inclusive: it is entirely after 999 but not after 1000, and it contains 1000.
It ends at 2000, exclusive: it is entirely before 2000 but not before 1999, and it doesn't contain 2000.

**Unbounded ranges.** The two deadline checks never hold on an infinite bound. `isEntirelyAfter` needs a
finite start and `isEntirelyBefore` a finite end, so a transaction that sets no validity range passes
neither check, and `Interval.before 5` is not entirely after any time. A `PosInf` start or a `NegInf` end,
which only an empty range has, fails the check that reads it, as in Aiken's stdlib v2; Aiken v3 lets such
an empty range pass both checks. `start` and `end` return `Nothing` for an infinite bound, never a sentinel
time. They return the bound's time whether or not it is inclusive; read `range.from.isInclusive` when that
matters, or use the checks, which account for it.

The constructors `Interval`, `IntervalBound`, `Finite`, `NegInf` and `PosInf` come from `Julc.Ledger`, as in
the example. The `Interval` type is the ledger's, so `import Julc.Ledger exposing (Interval)` names the
same type.

**Cost.** Each check reads one or two bounds and compares integers. `isEntirelyAfter` and
`isEntirelyBefore` cost about 2.8 million CPU units, `contains` about 5.5 million.

## `Tx`

`import Tx`. Questions about the transaction a script validates. Every function takes the `ScriptContext`
last, so a check reads `Tx.signedBy owner ctx`.

| Function | Type | Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `signedBy` | `PubKeyHash -> ScriptContext -> Bool` | the key is among the transaction's signatories |
| `spends` | `TxOutRef -> ScriptContext -> Bool` | the transaction spends the output; reference inputs don't count |
| `findInput` | `TxOutRef -> ScriptContext -> Maybe TxInInfo` | the spent output with that reference, with its address, value and datum |
| `ownRef` | `ScriptContext -> Maybe TxOutRef` | when spending, the reference of the output being validated |
| `ownInput` | `ScriptContext -> Maybe TxInInfo` | when spending, the output being validated |
| `ownPolicy` | `ScriptContext -> Maybe PolicyId` | when minting, the script's own policy id |
| `outputsTo` | `Credential -> ScriptContext -> List TxOut` | the outputs whose payment credential is the credential, in order |
| `valuePaidTo` | `Credential -> ScriptContext -> Value` | the total value of those outputs |
| `continuingOutputs` | `ScriptContext -> List TxOut` | when spending, the outputs to the spent output's address |
| `valueSpent` | `ScriptContext -> Value` | the total value of the spent outputs |
| `valueProduced` | `ScriptContext -> Value` | the total value of the outputs |
| `mintedOf` | `PolicyId -> ScriptContext -> Dict TokenName Int` | the tokens the policy mints; a burn is a negative quantity |
| `inlineDatum` | `TxOut -> Maybe Data` | the output's inline datum |
| `datumOf` | `TxOut -> ScriptContext -> Maybe Data` | the output's datum: inline, or by its hash from the datums the transaction supplies |

- **Purposes.** `ownRef`, `ownInput` and `continuingOutputs` describe the output a spend handler
  validates, and `ownPolicy` the policy a mint handler validates. For any other purpose they return
  `Nothing` or `[]`. Match the `Nothing` case and return `False`.
- **Credentials, not addresses.** `outputsTo` and `valuePaidTo` match an output's payment credential
  (`output.address.credential`) and ignore its staking part. Whoever builds the transaction chooses the
  payee's staking part: a payment to the seller's key counts whatever staking credential its address
  carries. When the staking part matters, store the payee's full `Address` and compare `output.address`. `continuingOutputs` compares whole addresses, staking part included.
- **Payments must be tagged.** "Some output pays the seller" is true for two script inputs spent in one
  transaction when one output pays for both. This is the double-satisfaction attack, and an untagged
  `valuePaidTo` check has it. Require each payment to carry the spent output's reference as its inline
  datum, as below, or allow one script input per transaction.
  [Reading the transaction](https://elci-lang.dev/contracts/reading-the-transaction/#one-payment-per-input) explains both
  defences.
- **Datums stay `Data`.** `inlineDatum` returns `Nothing` for an output with a datum hash or no datum.
  `datumOf` also finds a datum by its hash in `txInfo.datums`, and returns `Nothing` when the transaction
  doesn't supply it. Decode a datum with an annotated `Data.decode`, which fails the script on a malformed
  datum, or compare it with an expected encoding: `==` on `Data` compares structure.
- **Values.** `valueSpent` sums the spent outputs, not the reference inputs. `valueProduced` sums the
  outputs; the fee and the minted tokens are separate fields, `txInfo.fee` and `txInfo.mint`. `mintedOf`
  is `Value.tokens policy ctx.txInfo.mint`: an empty `Dict` when the policy mints nothing.

A payment check that pays for this input only:

```elm title="src/Sale.elm"
module Sale exposing (paidFor)

import Julc.Data as Data
import Julc.Ledger exposing (Credential(..), PubKeyHash, ScriptContext)
import Tx
import Value

{-| An output pays the seller at least `price` lovelace and carries this input's
reference as its inline datum.
-}
paidFor : PubKeyHash -> Int -> ScriptContext -> Bool
paidFor seller price ctx =
    case Tx.ownRef ctx of
        Just ref ->
            List.any
                (\output ->
                    (Value.lovelaceOf output.value >= price)
                        && (Tx.inlineDatum output == Just (Data.encode ref))
                )
                (Tx.outputsTo (PubKeyCredential seller) ctx)

        Nothing ->
            False
```

**Cost.** The functions walk the transaction's lists. Measured per element, in CPU units:

| Function | Cost |
| --- | --- |
| `signedBy` | about 0.7 million per signatory before the key |
| `spends`, `findInput`, `ownInput` | about 2.5 million per input before the match; `spends` walks every input when the output isn't spent |
| `outputsTo` | about 2.8 million per output |
| `valuePaidTo` | as `outputsTo`, plus about 2.9 million per matching output to add its value |
| `continuingOutputs` | `ownInput`, then about 3.6 million per output |
| `valueSpent`, `valueProduced` | about 3.3 million per input and 2.8 million per output |
| `ownRef`, `ownPolicy`, `inlineDatum` | a few field reads, whatever the transaction's size |

When a branch needs a result twice, bind it once in a `let` inside that branch.

## `Bytes`

`import Bytes`. Each function is a direct Plutus builtin call, with the byte string last.
[Bytes, hashes and bits](https://elci-lang.dev/advanced/bytes-and-crypto/) explains each group with examples.

| Function | Type | Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `empty` | `Bytes` | |
| `fromString` | `String -> Bytes` | UTF-8 encoding |
| `toString` | `Bytes -> String` | UTF-8 decoding; fails on invalid UTF-8 |
| `length` | `Bytes -> Int` | |
| `append` | `Bytes -> Bytes -> Bytes` | `append a b` is `a` followed by `b` |
| `slice` | `Int -> Int -> Bytes -> Bytes` | `slice start count bytes`; clamps |
| `take` | `Int -> Bytes -> Bytes` | clamps |
| `drop` | `Int -> Bytes -> Bytes` | clamps |
| `at` | `Int -> Bytes -> Int` | the byte at an index, 0–255; fails outside the string |
| `cons` | `Int -> Bytes -> Bytes` | prepends a byte; fails outside 0–255 |
| `replicate` | `Int -> Int -> Bytes` | `replicate count byte`; at most 8,192 bytes |
| `fromIntBigEndian` | `Int -> Int -> Bytes` | `fromIntBigEndian width n`; width `0` is minimal; fails for negative `n` or if it does not fit |
| `fromIntLittleEndian` | `Int -> Int -> Bytes` | as above, little-endian |
| `toIntBigEndian` | `Bytes -> Int` | unsigned |
| `toIntLittleEndian` | `Bytes -> Int` | unsigned |
| `and` | `Bytes -> Bytes -> Bytes` | truncates to the shorter operand |
| `or` | `Bytes -> Bytes -> Bytes` | truncates to the shorter operand |
| `xor` | `Bytes -> Bytes -> Bytes` | truncates to the shorter operand |
| `complement` | `Bytes -> Bytes` | flips every bit |
| `shift` | `Int -> Bytes -> Bytes` | positive shifts towards the front, negative towards the end; same length |
| `rotate` | `Int -> Bytes -> Bytes` | like `shift`, wrapping bits around |
| `testBit` | `Int -> Bytes -> Bool` | bit 0 is the lowest bit of the last byte |
| `countSetBits` | `Bytes -> Int` | |
| `findFirstSetBit` | `Bytes -> Int` | lowest set bit, or `-1` if none |
| `blake2b224` | `Bytes -> Bytes` | 28-byte digest |
| `blake2b256` | `Bytes -> Bytes` | 32-byte digest |
| `sha256` | `Bytes -> Bytes` | 32-byte digest |
| `sha3_256` | `Bytes -> Bytes` | 32-byte digest |
| `keccak256` | `Bytes -> Bytes` | 32-byte digest |
| `ripemd160` | `Bytes -> Bytes` | 20-byte digest |

`==` and `/=` compare byte strings. `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` and `compare` order them lexicographically, a
proper prefix first, with the Plutus builtins `lessThanByteString` and `lessThanEqualsByteString`. There
is no `Bytes.lessThan`: `ELCI2104: Elci has no Bytes.lessThan; bytes are comparable: write a < b`. Ledger
hashes such as `PubKeyHash` are distinct types that compare and order like bytes; read their bytes with
`.hash`.

## `Julc.Data`

`import Julc.Data as Data`. Explicit conversions between Elci values and Plutus Data.

| Function | Type | Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `decode` | `Data -> a` | Julc's strict decoder for `a`. Malformed Data fails the script. |
| `encode` | `a -> Data` | The Data encoding of `a`. |
| `fromOptional` | `JulcOptional a -> Maybe a` | Re-tags a Julc optional as a `Maybe`. |
| `toOptional` | `Maybe a -> JulcOptional a` | The reverse. |

```elm
import Julc.Data as Data
import Julc.Ledger exposing (OutputDatum(..))

inlineAmount : OutputDatum -> Maybe Int
inlineAmount datum =
    case datum of
        OutputDatumInline raw ->
            Just (Data.decode raw)

        _ ->
            Nothing
```

- **Supported types.** `Int`, `Bool`, `String`, `Bytes`, `Data`, your records and custom types, tuples,
  `Maybe`, `Result`, `Order`, lists, dictionaries, maps and optionals of these, a [`Value`](#value), and
  imported types whose provider approves decoding or encoding (for example `PubKeyHash` or `TxOutRef`). The
  rest are rejected with `ELCI3003`: `()`, functions, `Array`, and ledger types without a checkable layout,
  such as `TxOut` for `decode`. A type that contains a `Value` can't be decoded yet.
- **Known types for decoding.** `decode` must know the type it creates where it is used. If inference
  cannot tell, annotate the binding (local definitions accept signatures). Otherwise the call fails with
  `ELCI3001: Cannot determine the type converted by Julc.Data.decode; add a type annotation`. `encode`
  and the optional adapters don't need to know it: `Data.encode Nothing` is `Constr 0`.
- **Strict decoding.** `decode` never returns a `Maybe` for malformed input. A value of the wrong shape,
  such as an integer where a record is expected, fails with an error like `UnConstrData: not ConstrData`.
  A `Dict` whose keys are not strictly ascending fails too, and so does a `Value` that is not canonical.
- **Optionals.** Julc's optional tags `Some` as 0 and `None` as 1, the reverse of `Maybe`. The adapters
  swap the tags without decoding the payload.
- **Equality.** `==` and `/=` on `Data` compare structure exactly, with the `equalsData` builtin. Elci's
  encodings are deterministic, so `Data.encode a == Data.encode b` exactly when `a == b` for your records,
  custom types, lists and dictionaries. That makes a datum check one comparison:
  `Tx.inlineDatum output == Just (Data.encode expected)`. A `Map` has no `==`: two maps with the same
  bindings may hold them in different orders, so their encodings may differ too. Compare their `toList`
  after sorting, or use a `Dict`. `Data` is not comparable: `<` and sorting reject it.

```elm title="src/Main.elm"
module Main exposing (main)

import Dict
import Julc.Data as Data
import Map

type alias Payout =
    { beneficiary : Int
    , amount : Int
    }

main : ( Bool, Bool, ( Bool, Bool ) )
main =
    ( Data.encode (Payout 1 2) == Data.encode { amount = 2, beneficiary = 1 }
    , Data.encode (Just 5) == Data.encode 5
    , ( Data.encode (Dict.fromList [ ( 1, 10 ), ( 2, 20 ) ]) == Data.encode (Dict.fromList [ ( 2, 20 ), ( 1, 10 ) ])
      , Data.encode (Map.fromList [ ( 1, 10 ), ( 2, 20 ) ]) == Data.encode (Map.fromList [ ( 2, 20 ), ( 1, 10 ) ])
      )
    )
```

```text
$ elci eval
( True, False, ( True, False ) )
cpu 62954744, mem 240991
```

The record and the record literal with the same fields encode alike; `Just 5` and `5` do not. The two
dictionaries hold the same bindings, so their encodings are equal; the two maps hold them in different
orders, so theirs are not.

The encoding rules are in the [language reference](https://elci-lang.dev/reference/language/#data-encoding).

## `Debug`

Every module imports `Debug`.

| Function | Type | Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `trace` | `String -> a -> a` | Emits the message as a Plutus trace and returns the second argument. |

There is no `Debug.log`, `Debug.todo` or `Debug.toString`; the error says what to use instead, such as
`ELCI2104: Elci has no Debug.log; use Debug.trace message value, which returns value`.

Both arguments are evaluated first, because Elci is strict. The message is emitted only after the value
has been computed, so `Debug.trace "about to divide" (10 // 0)` fails without tracing. To trace before
something that may fail, trace in a `let`:

```elm
main : Int
main =
    let
        _ =
            Debug.trace "about to divide" ()
    in
    10 // 0
```

```text
$ elci eval
evaluation failed: QuotientInteger: division by zero
cpu 431939, mem 1633
trace: about to divide
```

Traces cost CPU and script bytes in deployed validators. `elci test` prints the traces of failing
tests. See [debugging and budgets](https://elci-lang.dev/testing/debugging/).

## `Julc.Ledger`

`Julc.Ledger` provides the ledger types (`ScriptContext`, `TxInfo`, `PubKeyHash`, `TxOutRef`,
`Credential` and more) rather than functions. See
[reading the transaction](https://elci-lang.dev/contracts/reading-the-transaction/). Its `Value` is the type of the
[`Value`](#value) module and its `Interval` the type of the [`Interval`](#interval) module, so
`import Julc.Ledger exposing (Value)` names the same type. The [`Tx`](#tx) module answers the common
questions about a `ScriptContext`.

## Differences from Elm

| Elm | Elci | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `String` ordered by UTF-16 code units | ordered by UTF-8 bytes, which is code point order | Plutus strings are UTF-8. The orders differ only for a character outside the Basic Multilingual Plane against one from U+E000 to U+FFFF |
| `2 ^ -1 == 0.5` | fails the script | no `Float` |
| `x // 0 == 0`; `modBy 0 x` crashes | both fail the script | Plutus division by zero |
| `number`, `Float` | `Int` only | no floating point on-chain |
| Bytes are not comparable | `Bytes` and ledger hashes are comparable | they are the natural keys on Cardano |
| two imports exposing one name are ambiguous | a name listed in `exposing (...)` takes precedence over a default import | the intent is explicit |
| `Dict` is a balanced tree: `get` and `insert` are O(log n) | `Dict` is a Plutus map with sorted keys: `get` and `insert` are O(n), `fromList` O(n log n) | a tree would not encode as a Plutus map, and rebalancing it on-chain costs more than scanning the small maps contracts use |
| `Debug.log`, `Debug.todo`, `Debug.toString` | `Debug.trace message value` | traces are the on-chain log |
| `Result` has no fixed encoding | `Ok` is constructor 0, `Err` constructor 1 | values cross the script boundary as Data |

Elm's `Set` and `Char` modules and most of `String` are not available. [Coming from
Elm](https://elci-lang.dev/learn/coming-from-elm/) lists every other difference.

---

# Test library

> Complete API of the Expect, Scenario and Property modules that elci test provides to test modules.

Source: https://elci-lang.dev/reference/test-library/

`elci test` provides three modules, written in Elci, to your test modules: `Expect` for expectations, `Scenario` for transactions against your validators, and `Property` for property-based tests. This page lists every type and function they expose. For a guided introduction, start with [Unit tests](https://elci-lang.dev/testing/unit-tests/).

Only test modules can import these modules. An import from a source module is an error at the import, `ELCI2101`: `elci test` reports `Only test modules can import Expect; it is part of the test library, not available to elci build`. A test module cannot be named `Expect`, `Scenario` or `Property`.

## Test discovery

A test is an exposed, top-level declaration of a test module that is either:

- a zero-argument value of type `Bool`, `Expect.Expectation`, `Scenario.Scenario` or `Property.Property`; or
- a function whose result type is `Property.Property`, which runs as a property with generated arguments.

Every other declaration is a helper. Modules run in alphabetical order and the tests of a module in source order.

| `elci test` option | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `--match <substring>` | runs only the tests whose `Module.name` contains the substring, ignoring case |
| `--seed <n>` | runs properties with seed `n`; without it, a random seed is used and printed |
| `--fuzz <runs>` | runs each property `runs` times (default 100; must be positive) |

The command exits with status 1 when a test fails or when no test is found or matches. See also the [CLI reference](https://elci-lang.dev/reference/cli/).

## Expect

```elm
import Expect exposing (Expectation)
```

### Types

```elm
type Expectation
    = Pass
    | Fail String (List Data)
```

A failure carries a message and the Data encodings of the values involved, which the test runner prints. The constructors are exposed, so a helper can match on an expectation with `import Expect exposing (Expectation(..))`.

### Functions

| Function | Signature | Passes when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `pass` | `Expectation` | always |
| `fail` | `String -> Expectation` | never |
| `equal` | `a -> a -> Expectation` | `expected == actual`, for `equal expected actual` |
| `notEqual` | `a -> a -> Expectation` | `unexpected /= actual`, for `notEqual unexpected actual` |
| `atMost` | `comparable -> comparable -> Expectation` | `actual <= bound`, for `atMost bound actual` |
| `atLeast` | `comparable -> comparable -> Expectation` | `actual >= bound`, for `atLeast bound actual` |
| `lessThan` | `comparable -> comparable -> Expectation` | `actual < bound`, for `lessThan bound actual` |
| `greaterThan` | `comparable -> comparable -> Expectation` | `actual > bound`, for `greaterThan bound actual` |
| `every` | `List Expectation -> Expectation` | every expectation in the list passes; otherwise the first failure is the result |
| `onFail` | `String -> Expectation -> Expectation` | the expectation passes; otherwise its message is replaced, keeping its values |

`equal` and `notEqual` require the same structural equality as `==`. Types without it, such as `Map`, functions and imported types without approved equality, are rejected at compile time with `ELCI2003`. `Data` has it: `Expect.equal (Data.encode expected) datum` compares structure. `atMost`, `atLeast`, `lessThan` and `greaterThan` take any [comparable type](https://elci-lang.dev/reference/core-modules/#comparable-types), as in elm-test: integers, strings, bytes, ledger hashes, and lists and tuples of these.

### Failure reports

Values are printed as their Plutus Data encoding: integers as numbers, bytes and strings as `#hex`, lists as `[...]`, and records, tuples, `Bool`, `Maybe` and custom types as `Constr tag [fields]`.

| Expectation | Report |
| --- | --- |
| `equal` | `Expect.equal`, then `expected:` and `actual:` |
| `notEqual` | `Expect.notEqual`, then `values:` with the actual value |
| `atMost`, `atLeast`, `lessThan`, `greaterThan` | the function name, then `values:` with the bound and the actual value |
| `fail message` | the message |
| `onFail message e` | the message, then the values of `e`, if any |

## Scenario

```elm
import Scenario exposing (Scenario)
```

A scenario is data describing one transaction against a validator of the project. The runner compiles the named validator as `elci build` does, applies the scenario's parameters, builds the complete ledger context with julc-testkit and runs the deployed script. The validator's own address, minting policy and staking credential are derived from the applied script's hash. See [Transaction scenarios](https://elci-lang.dev/testing/scenarios/).

### Types

```elm
type Scenario
    = Scenario Spec

type alias Spec =
    { validator : String
    , purpose : Purpose
    , redeemer : Data
    , parameters : List Data
    , signers : List PubKeyHash
    , inputs : List Input
    , referenceInputs : List Input
    , outputs : List Output
    , minted : List Token
    , fee : Int
    , validFrom : Maybe Int
    , validBefore : Maybe Int
    , ownLovelace : Int
    , expectSuccess : Bool
    , budget : Maybe ( Int, Int )
    }

type Purpose
    = Spend TxOutRef (Maybe Data)
    | Mint
    | Withdraw
    | Certify Int TxCert
    | Vote Voter
    | Propose Int ProposalProcedure

type Policy
    = Own
    | Policy Bytes

type alias Token =
    { policy : Policy
    , name : Bytes
    , quantity : Int
    }

type Destination
    = ToScript
    | ToAddress Address
    | ToStakedScript StakingCredential

type alias Output =
    { destination : Destination
    , lovelace : Int
    , tokens : List Token
    , datum : OutputDatum
    , hashedDatum : Maybe Data
    }

type alias Input =
    { ref : TxOutRef
    , output : Output
    }
```

`Policy` is the policy of a token: `Own` is the validator's own script hash, `Policy bytes` any other policy id. `Destination` is where an output is paid: the validator's own address, any address, or the validator's own payment credential with a staking part. An output's `datum` is its inline datum or none; `hashedDatum` holds a datum by hash, which the runner turns into the datum's hash on the output and the datum among the transaction's witnesses. The ledger types `TxOutRef`, `TxCert`, `Voter`, `ProposalProcedure`, `Address`, `StakingCredential`, `OutputDatum` and `PubKeyHash` come from `Julc.Ledger`. Build scenarios with the functions below rather than the `Spec` record.

### Start a scenario

The first argument is the name of a `[validators.<name>]` table.

| Function | Signature | Transaction |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `spend` | `String -> TxOutRef -> Data -> Scenario` | spends the output at `ref`, held at the validator's address with an inline datum |
| `spendWithoutDatum` | `String -> TxOutRef -> Scenario` | spends the output at `ref`, held at the validator's address without a datum |
| `mint` | `String -> Scenario` | mints or burns under the validator's own policy; add tokens with `minting` |
| `withdraw` | `String -> Scenario` | withdraws from the validator's own staking credential |
| `certify` | `String -> Int -> TxCert -> Scenario` | publishes a certificate at an index |
| `vote` | `String -> Voter -> Scenario` | votes as the given voter |
| `propose` | `String -> Int -> ProposalProcedure -> Scenario` | submits a proposal at an index |

A new scenario has these defaults:

| Field | Default |
| --- | --- |
| redeemer | `unit`, the Data of `()` |
| parameters, signers, inputs, reference inputs, outputs, minted tokens | none |
| fee | 200000 lovelace |
| validity range | unbounded on both sides |
| lovelace in the spent output | 2000000 |
| expectation | the validator accepts; no budget limit |

### Describe the transaction

Each function takes the scenario last, so they chain with `|>`. Functions that set a value replace any earlier value; functions that add to a list append in call order.

| Function | Signature | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `redeemer` | `Data -> Scenario -> Scenario` | sets the redeemer |
| `parameters` | `List Data -> Scenario -> Scenario` | sets the deployment parameters, in the validator's declared order; all of them are required |
| `signedBy` | `PubKeyHash -> Scenario -> Scenario` | adds a required signer |
| `input` | `TxOutRef -> Output -> Scenario -> Scenario` | adds an input; an input at the spent reference replaces the default spent output, and must hold the datum the spend gives |
| `referenceInput` | `TxOutRef -> Output -> Scenario -> Scenario` | adds a reference input |
| `output` | `Output -> Scenario -> Scenario` | adds an output |
| `minting` | `Bytes -> Int -> Scenario -> Scenario` | mints (positive quantity) or burns (negative) a token under the own policy |
| `fee` | `Int -> Scenario -> Scenario` | sets the fee in lovelace |
| `validFrom` | `Int -> Scenario -> Scenario` | sets the inclusive lower bound of the validity range, in POSIX time |
| `validBefore` | `Int -> Scenario -> Scenario` | sets the exclusive upper bound of the validity range, in POSIX time |
| `worth` | `Int -> Scenario -> Scenario` | sets the lovelace held by the default spent output |

### Set the expectation

| Function | Signature | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `expectFailure` | `Scenario -> Scenario` | the validator must reject the transaction |
| `withinBudget` | `Int -> Int -> Scenario -> Scenario` | the execution must cost at most this many CPU steps and memory units, whether it succeeds or fails |

### Build outputs

| Function | Signature | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `toScript` | `Int -> Output` | an output of this many lovelace to the validator's own address |
| `toStakedScript` | `StakingCredential -> Int -> Output` | an output of this many lovelace to the validator's own payment credential with a staking part, an address other than `toScript`'s |
| `toAddress` | `Address -> Int -> Output` | an output of this many lovelace to an address |
| `toKey` | `PubKeyHash -> Int -> Output` | an output of this many lovelace to the key's address, without a staking part |
| `withDatum` | `Data -> Output -> Output` | the output with an inline datum; replaces a datum set before |
| `withDatumHash` | `Data -> Output -> Output` | the output with the datum's hash, and the datum among the transaction's witnesses, where `Tx.datumOf` finds it; replaces a datum set before |
| `withToken` | `Policy -> Bytes -> Int -> Output -> Output` | the output with an added token: policy, name and quantity |

### Test data

| Function | Signature | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `key` | `String -> PubKeyHash` | the BLAKE2b-224 hash of the name's UTF-8 bytes: a deterministic 28-byte test key |
| `outRef` | `String -> Int -> TxOutRef` | an output reference whose transaction id is the BLAKE2b-256 hash of the name's UTF-8 bytes |
| `unit` | `Data` | the Data of `()`, `Constr 0 []` |

### Scenario failure reports

| Report | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `validator <name> rejected the transaction: <error>` | the validator failed, and the scenario expected success |
| `validator <name> accepted a transaction expected to fail` | the validator succeeded after `expectFailure` |
| `Budget exceeded: ...` | the execution went over the `withinBudget` limits |
| `cannot prepare validator '<name>': ...` | the validator does not exist, or the scenario does not give all of its parameters; the scenario fails before it runs, even with `expectFailure` |
| `cannot build the transaction: ...` | the ledger could not produce the scenario's transaction, such as one with a token name longer than 32 bytes, or a listed spent output whose datum differs from the one `spend` gives; the scenario fails before it runs, even with `expectFailure` |

## Property

```elm
import Property exposing (Property)
```

### Types

```elm
type Property
```

`Property` is opaque: build it with the functions below.

### Functions

| Function | Signature | The property holds when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `holds` | `Bool -> Property` | the condition is `True`; otherwise it fails with `the property does not hold` |
| `expect` | `Expectation -> Property` | the expectation passes; otherwise it fails with the expectation's report |
| `scenario` | `Scenario -> Property` | the scenario has its expected outcome: accepted, or rejected after `Scenario.expectFailure` |

### Property reports

A passing property reports its number of runs and the budget of its costliest run, as `(100 runs, max cpu ..., mem ...)`. A failing property reports the runs until the failure and the shrunk counterexample, printed as a call in Elci syntax, followed by the failure of that run:

```text
FAIL PricingProperties.quotesNeverLoseValue (15 runs, cpu 5409589, mem 21823)
    counterexample after 15 runs, shrunk 4 times:
        quotesNeverLoseValue (-334)
    the property does not hold
```

A property's parameters must be concrete, Data-encodable types. Functions, arrays, `ScriptContext` and type variables are rejected with `ELCI2009`. [Property-based tests](https://elci-lang.dev/testing/properties/) describes the generated values for each type.

---

# Language reference

> Elci's feature matrix, syntax, imports and reserved names, operators and precedence, equality and ordering, constrained type variables, evaluation order and Plutus Data encoding rules.

Source: https://elci-lang.dev/reference/language/

This page is the compact reference for the Elci language: what is supported, how the syntax looks, how
names resolve, how operators bind, which types compare, in which order things are evaluated and how values
are encoded as Plutus Data. For a
gentle introduction, start with [values, functions and types](https://elci-lang.dev/learn/basics/).

Elci uses Elm 0.19 syntax for a functional core, with its own on-chain semantics. It is a development
preview: the profile below is implemented and tested, and everything outside it is rejected with an error.
The [grammar](https://elci-lang.dev/reference/grammar/) defines the syntax exactly.

## Feature matrix

| Feature | Support |
| --- | --- |
| Modules and imports | Source modules, `as` aliases, explicit `exposing`, `exposing (..)` for source modules, `Type(..)` for constructors, and Elm's default imports. Import cycles are rejected. |
| Functions | Top-level and local functions, lambdas with several arguments, curried and partial application, operators as functions such as `(+)`. |
| Type signatures | Required on every top-level declaration; allowed on local ones. |
| Generics | Rank-1 type variables, specialized to each concrete use. Elm's constrained variables `comparable`, `appendable` and `compappend`. |
| Local polymorphism | Simple local functions and values can be used at several types; calls, conditionals and matches stay monomorphic. |
| Recursion | Self-recursion and mutually recursive functions, top-level or local. Polymorphic recursion and recursive values are rejected. |
| Basic types | `Int` (arbitrary precision), `Bool`, `String`, `()`, `Bytes`, `Data`. |
| Core library | The `Basics` prelude and the `List`, `Maybe`, `Result`, `Tuple` and `String` modules, imported by default. See [core modules](https://elci-lang.dev/reference/core-modules/). |
| Lists | `List a`, literals, `::`, `++` and list patterns. |
| Tuples | Pairs and triples, with patterns and destructuring. |
| Records | Closed records, generic aliases with constructors, field access, accessor functions such as `.name`, update, destructuring. |
| Custom types | Generic and recursive unions; `Maybe` is built in, and `Result` and `Order` come from the core library. |
| Patterns | Nested constructors, lists, cons, tuples, record fields, `as`, `_`, unit, and `Bool`, `Int` and `String` literals. Exhaustiveness and reachability are checked. |
| Equality and order | Structural `==` and `/=` for equality-capable types, and `<`, `compare` and sorting for comparable types (below). |
| Dictionaries, maps and arrays | `Dict k v` (Elm's `Dict`, stored as a sorted Plutus map), `Map k v` (the ledger's association map) and `Array a` (constant-time `get`). |
| Values | `Value`, the ledger's multi-asset value, with the core `Value` module: arithmetic, comparison and exact `==` on the CIP-153 builtins. |
| Bytes | The `Bytes` module: every byte-string builtin. |
| Ledger access | Typed views of the script context, nominal hash types, approved constructors, patterns and equality. The core `Tx` and `Interval` modules answer common questions about the transaction and its validity range. |
| Data conversions | `Julc.Data.decode` and `encode`, optional adapters, and structural `==` on `Data`. |
| Java libraries | Julc's on-chain Java libraries and your own library JARs, including generic methods. |
| Validators | `[validators.<name>]` scripts with spend, mint, withdraw, certify, vote and propose handlers, parameters and datum profiles. |
| Tests | `elci test` with unit tests, transaction scenarios and property tests. |

**Not supported:** `Float`, `/` and `number`, typeclasses and user-defined constraints, extensible
records and row polymorphism, higher-rank types, polymorphic recursion, ports and effects, Elm's `Set` and
`Char` modules and most of `String`, character literals, hexadecimal literals, `%`, tuples of four or
more, and Elm packages.

## Syntax summary

This module uses most of the syntax:

```elm title="src/Main.elm"
module Main exposing (main)

{-| A tour of the syntax. Block comments {- can {- nest -} -}.
-}

type Shape
    = Circle Int
    | Rect Int Int

type alias Point =
    { x : Int, y : Int }

type alias Pair a =
    ( a, a )

area : Shape -> Int
area shape =
    case shape of
        Circle radius ->
            3 * radius * radius

        Rect width height ->
            width * height

describe : List Int -> String
describe values =
    case values of
        [] ->
            "empty"

        [ _ ] ->
            "one"

        0 :: _ ->
            "starts with zero"

        first :: _ ->
            if first < 0 then
                "starts negative"

            else
                "many"

norm : Point -> Int
norm { x, y } =
    x * x + y * y

swap : Pair a -> Pair a
swap ( first, second ) =
    ( second, first )

main : Int
main =
    let
        origin =
            Point 0 0

        moved =
            { origin | x = 3, y = 4 }

        ( a, b ) =
            swap ( 1, 2 )

        total : Int
        total =
            [ Circle 1, Rect 2 3 ]
                |> List.map area
                |> List.foldl (\value sum -> value + sum) 0
    in
    if describe [ 0, 1 ] == "starts with zero" && not (a == b) then
        norm moved + total

    else
        -1
```

| Construct | Syntax |
| --- | --- |
| Module header | `module A.B exposing (f, T, U(..))` or `exposing (..)` |
| Import | `import A.B as B exposing (f, T(..))` |
| Signature and definition | `f : Int -> Int` then `f x = x + 1` |
| Lambda | `\x y -> x + y`, `\( a, b ) -> a + b` |
| Local definitions | `let` ... `in`, with optional signatures and tuple/record destructuring |
| Conditional | `if c then a else b` (the `else` is required) |
| Match | `case e of` followed by aligned `pattern ->` branches |
| Custom type | `type T a = A a \| B` |
| Type alias | `type alias R = { x : Int }`; a record alias is also a constructor `R 1` |
| Record | `{ x = 1, y = 2 }`, `r.x`, `{ r \| x = 3 }` |
| Accessor function | `.x`, which is `\r -> r.x`: `List.map .x points` |
| Field of a qualified value | `Config.settings.x` |
| Tuple | `( 1, True )`, `( 1, 2, 3 )` |
| List | `[ 1, 2 ]`, `1 :: rest`, `xs ++ ys` |
| Operator as a function | `(+)`, `(::)`, `(<)`: `List.foldl (+) 0 xs` |
| Unit | `()` as a value, type and pattern |

Function and lambda parameters, and local destructuring, accept only **irrefutable** patterns: names,
`_`, `()`, tuples and record fields. Anything that can fail to match belongs in `case`.

### Layout

Indentation is significant, as in Elm. Top-level declarations start in column 1. The declarations of a
`let` align with each other, and so do the branches of a `case`. A signature must directly precede its
definition. Tabs are rejected. The grammar gives the [exact layout rules](https://elci-lang.dev/reference/grammar/#layout).

### Lexical rules

- **Names.** Values and functions start with a lowercase letter; types, constructors and module segments
  start with an uppercase letter. Letters, digits and `_` may follow.
- **Reserved words.** `if`, `then`, `else`, `case`, `of`, `let`, `in`, `module`, `import`, `exposing`,
  `as`, `type` and `port`. `alias` is only special after `type`. Don't use them as names: the parser
  doesn't yet reject every such use, as the grammar's [parser details](https://elci-lang.dev/reference/grammar/#parser-details-that-differ-from-elm)
  describe.
- **Integers.** Decimal digits only, arbitrarily large. `1.5` is rejected (`Float is unsupported`), and so
  are `0xFF` and `1_000`. elm-format 0.8.8 corrupts literals that do not fit in 64 bits, so check large
  constants after formatting.
- **Strings.** Double-quoted, on one line. The escapes are `\n`, `\r`, `\t`, `\"` and `\\`. There are no
  triple-quoted strings, Unicode escapes or character literals.
- **Comments.** `--` to the end of the line, and `{- ... -}` blocks, which nest. `{-| ... -}` doc comments
  are ordinary block comments.

## Imports and names

Every module has Elm's default imports, which you don't write:

```elm
import Basics exposing (..)
import List
import Maybe exposing (Maybe(..))
import Result exposing (Result(..))
import String
import Tuple
import Debug
```

`Bytes`, `Dict`, `Map`, `Array`, `Value`, `Interval`, `Tx`, `Julc.Data` and Java library modules are
imported explicitly.
Names resolve as in Elm, with one addition:

- A module's own declarations shadow every import.
- Two imports that expose different things under one name make it ambiguous where it is used
  (`ELCI2102`). The message lists the qualified alternatives.
- *Addition:* a name listed explicitly, as in `import Utils exposing (clamp)`, takes precedence over a
  default import.
- Qualified names such as `Basics.max` and `Result.Ok` always work. A qualified name is written without
  spaces and ends at its first lowercase part, so `Config.settings.fee` is the field `fee` of the value
  `Config.settings`.
- A qualified name that doesn't resolve is `ELCI2104`, with one of three messages: the module doesn't
  expose the name, the module isn't imported (with the import to add), or no imported module has that
  name. See [diagnostics](https://elci-lang.dev/reference/diagnostics/#elci2101-elci2102-and-elci2104).
- An import can't be aliased to the name of another module, core or in the project:
  `import Utils as String` and `import Julc.Interval as Interval` are `ELCI2104`.

[Core modules](https://elci-lang.dev/reference/core-modules/#default-imports) has the details and the messages.

### Reserved names

- **Module names.** `Basics`, `List`, `Maybe`, `Result`, `String`, `Tuple`, `Map`, `Dict`, `Array`,
  `Value`, `Interval` and `Tx` are core modules, and `Set` and `Elci` are reserved for the core library. Neither a project module
  nor a `[java-modules]` key can use these names, or a name that starts with `Elci.`:

  ```text
  src/String.elm:1:1: ELCI2104: The module name String is taken by Elci's core library; rename this module
  src/Value.elm:1:1: ELCI2104: The module name Value is taken by Elci's core library; rename this module
  src/Tx.elm:1:1: ELCI2104: The module name Tx is taken by Elci's core library; rename this module
  src/Set.elm:1:1: ELCI2104: The module name Set is reserved for Elci's core library; rename this module
  src/Elci/Tools.elm:1:1: ELCI2104: The module name Elci.Tools is reserved for Elci's core library; rename this module
  elci: ELCI4001: [java-modules] may not map Value, a module name of Elci's core library
  ```

  `Bytes`, `Debug` and `Julc.Data` belong to the compiler as well.
- **Constructors and types.** A module can't declare constructors named `Just`, `Nothing`, `True` or
  `False`, or types named `Int`, `Bool`, `String`, `Bytes`, `Data`, `List`, `Maybe`, `Dict`, `Map`, `Array`
  or `Float`:

  ```text
  src/Main.elm:4:6: ELCI2011: Nothing is a constructor of the built-in Maybe type; choose another name
  src/Main.elm:4:6: ELCI2011: Bytes is a built-in type; choose another name
  ```

  Other prelude names, such as `Ok`, `Order` or `max`, can be declared; your declaration shadows the
  prelude's in your module.
- **Type names.** Tuples are written `( a, b )` and unit `()`. `Tuple Int Int` gives
  `ELCI2012: Write tuple types as ( a, b ) or ( a, b, c )`, and `Unit` gives
  `ELCI2012: Write the unit type as ()`.

## Operators

From the tightest binding to the loosest:

| Precedence | Operators | Associativity | Meaning |
| ---: | --- | --- | --- |
| highest | `record.field` | | field access, written without spaces |
| 10 | `f x` | left | function application |
| 9 | `>>`, `<<` | `>>` right, `<<` left | function composition |
| 8 | `^` | right | integer power |
| 7 | `*`, `//` | left | multiplication, integer division truncating towards zero |
| 6 | `+`, `-` | left | addition, subtraction |
| 5 | `::`, `++` | right | list cons; append lists or strings |
| 4 | `==`, `/=`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=` | none | comparisons; chaining is an error |
| 3 | `&&` | right | and, short-circuit |
| 2 | `\|\|` | right | or, short-circuit |
| 0 | `\|>`, `<\|` | `\|>` left, `<\|` right | pipelines |

Operators of one precedence that group in opposite directions can't be mixed without parentheses, as in
Elm: `f <| x |> g` is `ELCI1002: Mixing (<|) and (|>) needs parentheses: they associate in opposite
directions, as in Elm`, and the same holds for `>>` with `<<`.

- `+`, `-`, `*`, `//` and `^` work on `Int`. `2 ^ 10` is `1024`, `2 * 3 ^ 2` is `18`, and a negative
  exponent fails the script.
- `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=` compare two values of the same [comparable type](#ordering).
- `==` and `/=` work on equality-capable types (below).
- `/` is rejected; use `//` for the integer quotient, and `modBy` or `remainderBy` for the rest. `%`
  does not exist.
- `a < b < c` is rejected: write `a < b && b < c`.

### Operators as functions

Every binary operator can be used as a function by writing it in parentheses, as in Elm: `(+)`, `(*)`,
`(::)`, `(++)`, `(<)`, `(^)`, `(|>)`. `(op)` is the function `\a b -> a op b`, so `(-) 10` subtracts
from 10. `(/)` is rejected, like `/`. As functions, `(&&)` and `(||)` evaluate both arguments, like any
other call.

```elm title="src/Main.elm"
module Main exposing (main)

main : ( Int, List Int, List Bool )
main =
    ( List.foldl (+) 0 [ 1, 2, 3 ]
    , List.foldr (::) [] [ 4, 5 ] ++ List.map ((-) 10) [ 1, 2 ]
    , List.map2 (<) [ 1, 5 ] [ 2, 2 ]
    )
```

```text
$ elci eval
( 6, [4, 5, 9, 8], [True, False] )
cpu 16223362, mem 77496
```

### Unary minus

Negation follows Elm 0.19. A `-` written directly before its operand, after a space or an opening
bracket, negates it: `f -1` passes `-1` to `f`, and `scale -x 10` passes `-x`. With a space after it, or
with no space before it, `-` subtracts: `x - 1` and `x-1` are both subtractions. A leading `-` negates the
whole function application that follows, so `-(scale x 2)` and `-f x` are negations of the result.

```elm title="src/Main.elm"
module Main exposing (main)

scale : Int -> Int -> Int
scale value factor =
    value * factor

main : List Int
main =
    let
        x =
            4
    in
    [ scale -x 10
    , modBy 3 -7
    , x - 1
    , -x * 2
    , -(scale x 2)
    , 2 * -3
    ]
```

```text
$ elci eval
[-40, 2, 3, -8, -8, -6]
cpu 2719341, mem 9131
```

This is also how elm-format writes negative arguments, so formatted code keeps its meaning. As in Elm,
`x -1` is an application of `x` to `-1`, not a subtraction.

## Equality

`==` and `/=` work on `Int`, `Bool`, `String`, `()`, `Bytes`, ledger hashes of the same type, `Value`,
`Data`, and lists, tuples, records, `Maybe`, `Dict` and custom types whose contents are all
equality-capable. Two dictionaries are equal when they have the same bindings, and two values when they
hold the same quantities: every `Value` is kept in one canonical form, so `==` compares their encodings.
`Data` compares structure exactly, so `Tx.inlineDatum output == Just (Data.encode expected)` checks a datum
without decoding it. Imported types use the equality their provider approves (Java `equals`). Both operands
are evaluated once, left to right.

Rejected with `ELCI2003`: functions, `Map`, `Array`, imported types without approved equality, and the
ledger records that contain a `Value` (`TxOut`, `TxInInfo`, `TxInfo`). Two maps with the same bindings may
hold them in different orders, so `Data.encode` of the two may differ: compare their sorted `toList`, or use
a `Dict`. The message names the part that
has no equality:

```text
src/Main.elm:6:21: ELCI2003: The operator == cannot compare List (Int -> Int) values: Int -> Int is part of them, and functions have no equality
```

## Ordering

`<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, `compare`, `min`, `max` and the sorting functions take two values of the same
**comparable** type:

- `Int`, ordered numerically;
- `String`, ordered by its UTF-8 bytes, which is Unicode code point order;
- `Bytes` and the ledger's byte-string types (`PubKeyHash`, `ScriptHash`, `PolicyId`, `TokenName`,
  `TxId` and the other hashes), ordered lexicographically by unsigned byte, a proper prefix first;
- lists of a comparable type, lexicographically, and tuples of comparable types, component by component.

`Bool`, `()`, records, custom types, `Maybe`, `Dict`, `Map`, `Array`, `Value`, `Data`, functions and ledger
records such as `TxOutRef` are not comparable (`ELCI2003`). Every order is total and agrees with `==`. Comparing `Int`
values uses the integer builtins; byte strings use `lessThanByteString` and `lessThanEqualsByteString`;
`String` encodes both sides to UTF-8 and compares the bytes; lists and tuples use a comparison function
generated once per type.

## Constrained type variables

As in Elm, a type variable in a signature is unconstrained unless its name says otherwise:

| Name | Values must support | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `comparable`, or a name starting with it (`comparable2`, `comparableKey`) | `<`, `compare` and sorting | `max : comparable -> comparable -> comparable` |
| `appendable…` | `++` (strings and lists) | `twice : appendable -> appendable` |
| `compappend…` | both | |

The name is also a requirement on callers: each use is checked at its concrete type.

```elm title="src/Main.elm"
module Main exposing (main)

largest : comparable -> List comparable -> comparable
largest first rest =
    List.foldl max first rest

twice : appendable -> appendable
twice value =
    value ++ value

main : ( String, List Int )
main =
    ( twice (largest "fig" [ "apple", "pear" ]), twice [ largest 3 [ 9, 4 ] ] )
```

```text
$ elci eval
( "pearpear", [9, 9] )
cpu 8891872, mem 43250
```

Comparing or appending values of a plain variable is an error that suggests the rename:

```text
src/Main.elm:6:10: ELCI2003: The operator > compares values of type `a`, but the annotation of `larger` says `a` can be any type. Rename it `comparable` (as in Elm) to require comparable values
```

A requirement that no type can meet, such as `x < y` on values of type `Maybe comparable`, is reported at
the definition. A caller that passes the wrong type is reported at the call, and Elm's `number` gets its
own message, because Elci has one number type:

```text
src/Main.elm:11:5: ELCI2003: `twice` appends String or List values, not Int
src/Main.elm:4:1: ELCI2003: The annotation of `total` uses `number`, Elm's type variable for Int or Float. Elci has one number type: write Int
```

Equality needs no special name, as in Elm: `List.member : a -> List a -> Bool` uses `==`, and each use is
checked at its type. Type and alias parameters are never constrained, and a definition without a
signature, such as a local helper, infers its requirements.

## Ambiguous types

A type variable that nothing in a program determines, such as the element type of `[] == []` or the error
type of `Ok 5`, is *ambiguous*. As in Elm, such programs compile without annotations: no value of that
type can exist, so any representation serves. `List.length []` is `0`,
`Result.withDefault 0 (Ok 5)` is `5`, and `Julc.Data.encode Nothing` is `Constr 0`.

Creating a value of the type still needs to know it. `Julc.Data.decode` and generic Java library
functions report `ELCI3001` and ask for an annotation:

```elm
import Julc.Data as Data

main : Int
main =
    List.length (Data.decode (Data.encode [ 1, 2 ]))
```

```text
src/Main.elm:8:18: ELCI3001: Cannot determine the type converted by Julc.Data.decode; add a type annotation
```

Annotating the decoded value, as in a local `amounts : List Int`, fixes it.

## Evaluation order

Elci is strict. These rules are part of the language, because they decide which failures and costs
happen:

1. **Application.** The function, then its arguments from left to right. A partial application
   evaluates the arguments it has immediately.
2. **`let`.** Every binding is evaluated, even if unused, before the body. Bindings run in dependency
   order; independent ones run in source order.
3. **Literals and constructors.** List elements, tuple components, record fields and constructor
   arguments are evaluated from left to right, in source order. Record order does not follow the
   field names.
4. **Record update.** The base record first, then the new field values in source order.
5. **Selective forms.** `if` evaluates the condition and one branch. `case` evaluates the scrutinee once
   and one branch. `&&` and `||` evaluate the right operand only when needed.
6. **Composition.** `f >> g` evaluates `f` and `g` when the composition is built.
7. **Validators.** Top-level values reachable from any handler are evaluated once per script run,
   before the purpose is dispatched.

This program traces every step:

```elm title="src/Main.elm"
module Main exposing (main)

type alias Order =
    { price : Int, amount : Int }

add : Int -> Int -> Int
add left right =
    left + right

main : Int
main =
    let
        total =
            Debug.trace "total" (subtotal + 1)

        subtotal =
            Debug.trace "subtotal" 10

        unrelated =
            Debug.trace "unrelated" 0

        order =
            { price = Debug.trace "price" 5, amount = Debug.trace "amount" 2 }

        sum =
            add (Debug.trace "left" 1) (Debug.trace "right" 2)

        same =
            Debug.trace "eq-left" 1 == Debug.trace "eq-right" 1
    in
    if same then
        total + order.price + sum

    else
        0
```

```text
$ elci eval
19
cpu 3661600, mem 13949
trace: subtotal
trace: total
trace: unrelated
trace: price
trace: amount
trace: left
trace: right
trace: eq-left
trace: eq-right
```

`subtotal` runs before `total` because `total` needs it, and `unrelated` runs although nothing uses it.

## Data encoding

Values that cross the script boundary (datums, redeemers, parameters) or pass through `Julc.Data.encode`
use a fixed encoding:

| Elci value | Plutus Data |
| --- | --- |
| `Int` | integer |
| `Bytes`, ledger hashes | byte string |
| `String` | byte string with the UTF-8 encoding |
| `Bool` | constructor 0 (`False`) or 1 (`True`), no fields |
| `()` | constructor 0, no fields (as a datum or redeemer; `Julc.Data.encode ()` is rejected) |
| record | constructor 0, fields **sorted by field name** |
| tuple | constructor 0, fields in position order |
| custom type | constructor tag = the variant's position in the declaration, from 0; fields in order |
| `Maybe a` | `Nothing` is constructor 0; `Just x` is constructor 1 with one field |
| `Result e a` | `Ok x` is constructor 0 and `Err e` constructor 1, each with one field |
| `Order` | `LT`, `EQ` and `GT` are constructors 0, 1 and 2, no fields |
| `JulcOptional a` | `Some x` is constructor 0 with one field; `None` is constructor 1 |
| `List a` | list |
| `Dict k v` | map with its keys in strictly ascending order |
| `Map k v` | map, in the map's order |
| `Value` | map from policy ids to maps from token names to quantities, both in ascending byte order, without zero quantities |
| imported record or sum | as declared in Java: constructor in declaration order, fields in declaration order |

Functions and arrays have no encoding. A `Value` can't be a datum, redeemer or parameter yet, and a type
that contains one can't be decoded. You can see the encoding of any value with `Julc.Data.encode` and
`elci eval`, which prints Data as `Constr tag [fields]`, lists, `{key: value}` maps, integers and `#bytes`:

```elm title="src/Main.elm"
module Main exposing (main)

import Julc.Data as Data

type Action
    = Buy Int
    | Cancel

type alias Payout =
    { beneficiary : Int, amount : Int }

main : List Data
main =
    [ Data.encode (Just 5)
    , Data.encode Cancel
    , Data.encode (Buy 3)
    , Data.encode { beneficiary = 1, amount = 2 }
    , Data.encode ( 1, True )
    , Data.encode [ 1, 2 ]
    , Data.encode (Data.toOptional (Just 5))
    , Data.encode "hi"
    ]
```

```text
$ elci eval
[Constr 1 [5], Constr 1, Constr 0 [3], Constr 0 [2, 1], Constr 0 [1, Constr 1], [1, 2], Constr 0 [5], #6869]
cpu 5878521, mem 25242
```

The record `{ beneficiary = 1, amount = 2 }` encodes as `Constr 0 [2, 1]`, because `amount` sorts before
`beneficiary`.

Decoding is strict: tags, field counts and nested field kinds are checked, and a mismatch fails the
script. A `Dict`, at any depth, must have strictly ascending keys: a map whose keys are out of order or
repeated fails to decode. A `Value` must be canonical: its policies and token names strictly ascending,
and no quantity zero. Each build records the encoding of its boundary types in `abi.json`; see
[datums and redeemers](https://elci-lang.dev/contracts/datums-and-redeemers/).

## Compiler limits

- A program may create at most 256 specializations of generic functions.
- Tuples have two or three elements.
- The only target is `plutus-v3-pv11-uplc-1.1.0`.

For the error codes these rules produce, see [diagnostics](https://elci-lang.dev/reference/diagnostics/).

---

# Grammar

> Elci's formal grammar in EBNF — the lexical grammar, the exact layout rules, the syntactic grammar, operator precedence, the adjacency rules for `.` and `-`, and the Elm syntax Elci rejects.

Source: https://elci-lang.dev/reference/grammar/

This page is Elci's formal grammar: the lexical grammar, the layout rules and the syntactic grammar. It
describes what the compiler's parser accepts, including the edge cases. For a summary of the syntax, see
the [language reference](https://elci-lang.dev/reference/language/#syntax-summary); for what programs mean, the rest of that
page.

The grammar covers syntax only. A program that matches it can still be rejected later, for example for a
type error, a missing signature or an unknown name.

The same grammar is kept in the repository as
[`docs/GRAMMAR.md`](https://github.com/bloxbean/elci-lang/blob/main/docs/GRAMMAR.md). A test parses every
complete module it shows, and the syntax corpus has a module for each area of the grammar. The repository also has
a [tree-sitter grammar](https://github.com/bloxbean/elci-lang/tree/main/tree-sitter-elci) that follows it,
for highlighting and folding in Neovim, Helix and Zed.

## Notation

The grammar uses the W3C EBNF notation of the XML 1.0 specification (section 6):

| Notation | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `A ::= ...` | defines the symbol `A` |
| `"text"` | the literal text |
| `[abc]`, `[^abc]` | one character from the set, or one not in it |
| `#xN` | the character with hexadecimal code point `N` |
| `A B` | `A` followed by `B` |
| `A \| B` | `A` or `B` |
| `A?`, `A*`, `A+` | `A` optionally, zero or more times, one or more times |
| `A - B` | what `A` matches, except what `B` matches |
| `( ... )` | grouping |
| `/* ... */` | a comment |

Elci's layout needs two additions, used only in the syntactic grammar:

| Notation | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `X<f>` | the symbol `X` read with the *floor* `f`, a column (see [Layout](#layout)); `X<none>` has no floor |
| `CONT<f>` | matches nothing; allowed only when the next token is not a *boundary* for the floor `f` |
| `COL<c>` | matches nothing; allowed only when the next token is in column `c` |

The lexical grammar is over characters. The syntactic grammar is over tokens: a quoted string there
means a token with that text, and the lexer has already removed whitespace and comments.

## Lexical grammar

The lexer reads the source from left to right and produces tokens. Between tokens it skips
whitespace and comments. At each position it tries the rules in this order: whitespace, line
comment, block comment, name, integer, string, symbol.

### Whitespace and positions

```text
Space     ::= /* a character for which Java's Character.isWhitespace is true, except tab */
Tab       ::= #x9
```

- A tab outside a string or comment is an error: `ELCI1001: Tabs are not permitted; use spaces for
  Elm layout`. Tabs inside strings and comments are allowed.
- Every token has a line and a column, both counted from 1. The column counts characters (Java
  `char`s) from the start of the line. A newline is `#xA`; `#xD` is whitespace, so CRLF line endings
  work.

### Comments

```text
LineComment  ::= "--" [^#xA]*
BlockComment ::= "{-" CommentText ( BlockComment CommentText )* "-}"
CommentText  ::= Char* - ( Char* ( "{-" | "-}" ) Char* )
Char         ::= /* any character */
```

- Block comments nest: `{- a {- b -} c -}` is one comment.
- The lexer scans a block comment from left to right: each `{-` opens a nested comment, and each
  `-}` closes one. So `{- a{-}` is unterminated, since its `{-}` opens a comment
  (`ELCI1001: Unterminated block comment`).
- `{-| ... -}`, Elm's doc comment, is an ordinary block comment. The compiler does not read it.
- An unterminated block comment is `ELCI1001: Unterminated block comment`.
- Comments are not tokens. They take no part in layout: a token after a comment is placed by its
  own line and column.

### Names and reserved words

```text
Letter    ::= /* a character for which Character.isLetter is true */
Digit     ::= /* a character for which Character.isDigit is true */
Name      ::= ( Letter | "_" ) ( Letter | Digit | "_" )*
LowerName ::= Name - Reserved   /* whose first character is a lowercase letter */
UpperName ::= Name              /* whose first character is an uppercase letter */
Reserved  ::= "then" | "else" | "in" | "of" | "module" | "import" | "exposing" | "as" | "type"
            | "port"
```

- `_` alone is the wildcard pattern.
- `if`, `case` and `let` are keywords where an expression starts. `alias` is a keyword only after
  `type`. `True` and `False` are the Boolean literals.

### Integers

```text
Int ::= Digit+
```

- An integer is decimal and has no size limit.
- A `.` followed by a digit right after an integer is an error: `ELCI1001: Float is unsupported;
  represent fractional amounts using an explicit integer scale`.
- `0xFF` and `1e3` are not literals: they read as the integer `0` or `1` followed by a name.

### Strings

```text
String     ::= '"' ( StringChar | Escape )* '"'
StringChar ::= Char - ( '"' | "\" | #xA | #xD )
Escape     ::= "\" ( "n" | "r" | "t" | '"' | "\" )
```

- A string is on one line. A raw line break in it is `ELCI1001: Use an escaped newline in a string`.
- Any other escape, such as `\u{0041}`, is `ELCI1001: Unsupported string escape`.
- There are no character literals and no triple-quoted strings.

### Symbols

```text
Symbol ::= "->" | "//" | "==" | "/=" | "<=" | ">=" | "&&" | "||" | "::" | "++" | "|>" | "<|"
         | ">>" | "<<" | ".."
         | "(" | ")" | "[" | "]" | "{" | "}" | "," | ":" | "=" | "|" | "." | "\" | "+" | "-"
         | "*" | "<" | ">" | "/" | "^"
```

- The two-character symbols are tried first, so `a+++b` reads as `a ++ + b`.
- Any other character is `ELCI1001: Unsupported character 'c'`, for example `%`, `'`, `` ` `` and
  `!`.
- `/` is a symbol but not an operator: the parser rejects it (see [Operators](#operators)).

## Layout

Indentation is significant. The parser reads it from token columns; it does not insert layout
tokens. These are the exact rules.

**New line.** A token *starts a new line* when its line is after the line of the token before it.

**Floors and boundaries.** Every expression and type is read with a *floor* `f`, a column. A token
is a *boundary* for the floor `f` when it is the end of the input, or when it starts a new line in
column `f` or less. A boundary ends the expression or type being read. `none` is a floor that no
token reaches: only the end of the input is a boundary for it.

**Where boundaries are checked.** The parser looks for a boundary only at these points, written
`CONT<f>` in the grammar:

- in an expression, before a binary operator, before a function argument (including a negative
  argument such as `-1` in `f -1`) and before a field access `.field`;
- in a type, before each argument of a type application;
- in a custom type, before each argument type of a constructor.

Everything else is read at any column: the first token of an expression; the keywords `then`,
`else`, `of` and `in`; the symbols `->`, `=`, `:`, `|`, `,` and the closing brackets; every token of
a pattern; and the module header, imports and exposing lists.

**Blocks.** Three places start a block whose items align at one column `c`:

| Block | Column `c` | Items | The block ends |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The module | 1 | declarations | at the end of the input |
| `let` | the column of the first token after `let` | declarations | at `in`, in any column |
| `case` | the column of the first token after `of` | branches | at a token not in column `c`, or at `in`, `else` or the end of the input |

- Each item starts in column `c`. After an item, the next token must end the block or be in column
  `c`. Otherwise it is:
  - after a value declaration, `ELCI1002: Unexpected token after declaration`;
  - after a `type`, a `type alias` or a destructuring, `ELCI1002: Declarations must align at
    column c`.
- A declaration's expressions and types have the floor `c`. A branch's body has the floor `c` too.
  So a line that continues a declaration or branch must be indented past `c`.

**Floors elsewhere.**

- The parts of `if`, the body of a lambda, the body after `in` and the scrutinee of `case` keep the
  floor of the expression they are in.
- Inside `( )`, `[ ]` and `{ }` in an expression, and inside a record type, the floor is `none`. A
  `let` or `case` inside brackets still has its own block column.
- Inside `( )` in a type, the floor is kept.

This module shows the rules:

```elm
module Layout exposing (total)

total : List Int -> Int
total values =
    let
        doubled =
            List.map (\value -> value * 2) values

        sum =
            List.foldl (+) 0 doubled
    in
    case doubled of
        [] ->
            0

        first :: _ ->
            sum
                + first
```

`sum` and `doubled` align in column 9. `first :: _` aligns with `[]` in column 9, and
`+ first` continues the branch because column 17 is past 9. `in` ends the `let` block at any
column.

## Syntactic grammar

### Modules and imports

```text
Module       ::= Header Import* ( COL<1> TopDecl )*
Header       ::= "module" ModuleName "exposing" Exposing
ModuleName   ::= UpperName ( "." UpperName )*
Import       ::= "import" ModuleName ( "as" UpperName )? ( "exposing" Exposing )?
Exposing     ::= "(" ( ".." | ( Exposed ( "," Exposed )* )? ) ")"
Exposed      ::= LowerName | UpperName ( "(" ".." ")" )?
```

- There are no `port module` or `effect module` headers.
- An exposing list names values, types, and types with all their constructors (`Shape(..)`). It
  cannot list constructors one by one or name an operator.
- Imports come before the first declaration.

```elm
module Example.Shapes exposing (Shape(..), area, unit)

import Dict exposing (Dict)
import Julc.Data as Data

type Shape
    = Square Int
    | Rect Int Int

area : Shape -> Int
area shape =
    case shape of
        Square side ->
            side * side

        Rect width height ->
            width * height

unit : Data
unit =
    Data.encode (Dict.fromList [ ( 1, area (Square 1) ) ])
```

### Declarations

```text
TopDecl         ::= TypeAlias<1> | CustomType<1> | ValueDecl<1>
LetDecl<c>      ::= TypeAlias<c> | CustomType<c> | ValueDecl<c> | Destructuring<c>

TypeAlias<c>    ::= "type" "alias" UpperName LowerName* "=" Type<c>
CustomType<c>   ::= "type" UpperName LowerName* "=" Constructor<c> ( "|" Constructor<c> )*
Constructor<c>  ::= UpperName ( CONT<c> TypeAtom<c> )*

ValueDecl<c>    ::= Signature<c>? LowerName PatternAtom* "=" Expr<c>
Signature<c>    ::= LowerName ":" Type<c> COL<c>
Destructuring<c> ::= ( PatternAtom - LowerName ) "=" Expr<c>
```

- A signature must be followed directly by the definition of the same name, in the same column.
  When another value declaration follows instead, it is
  `ELCI1002: A signature must precede its matching definition`. When the input ends, or a `type`
  or an uppercase name follows, it is `ELCI1002: Expected name` or `Expected lowercase name`. Every
  top-level value needs a signature, but that is a type-checking rule (`ELCI2004`).
- A function's parameters and a destructuring pattern must be irrefutable: `_`, a name, `()`, a
  tuple of irrefutable patterns, a record pattern, or an irrefutable pattern with `as`. Otherwise:
  `ELCI1002: Function parameters require irrefutable patterns; use case for refutable matching`,
  and likewise for lambda parameters, and `ELCI1002: Local destructuring requires an irrefutable
  tuple or record pattern`.
- Destructuring is only for `let`. At the top level it is `ELCI1002: Top-level declarations require
  a name`.
- A record type alias also declares a constructor function, with the fields in declaration order.

```elm
module Declarations exposing (Pair, Tree(..), main)

type alias Pair a =
    ( a, a )

type Tree a
    = Leaf
    | Node (Tree a) a (Tree a)

type alias Account =
    { owner : String, balance : Int }

main : Int
main =
    let
        ( low, high ) =
            ( 1, 2 )

        { balance } =
            Account "alice" 5

        add : Int -> Int -> Int
        add a b =
            a + b
    in
    add low high + balance
```

### Types

```text
Type<f>       ::= TypeApp<f> ( "->" Type<f> )?
TypeApp<f>    ::= TypeAtom<f> ( CONT<f> TypeAtom<f> )*
TypeAtom<f>   ::= QualifiedType | LowerName
                | "(" ")"
                | "(" Type<f> ")"
                | "(" Type<f> "," Type<f> ( "," Type<f> )* ")"
                | "{" ( FieldType ( "," FieldType )* )? "}"
FieldType     ::= LowerName ":" Type<none>
QualifiedType ::= UpperName ( "." UpperName )*
```

- `->` groups to the right: `a -> b -> c` is `a -> (b -> c)`.
- A lowercase name is a type variable. `comparable`, `appendable` and `compappend` (and names that
  start with them) are constrained, as in Elm.
- Tuples are written `( a, b )` or `( a, b, c )`; a longer tuple is `ELCI2012: Tuples require two
  or three elements`. `()` is the unit type. `Tuple` and `Unit` are not type names: `ELCI2012: Write
  tuple types as ( a, b ) or ( a, b, c )` and `ELCI2012: Write the unit type as ()`.
- Records are closed. `{ r | field : Int }` is `ELCI1002: Extensible records are unsupported; use a
  closed record`.
- `Float` is `ELCI2001: Float is unsupported; use scaled Int`.

### Expressions

```text
Expr<f>        ::= Operand<f> ( CONT<f> BinaryOperator Operand<f> )*   /* grouped by the operator table */

Operand<f>     ::= Head<f> ( CONT<f> Suffix )*
Head<f>        ::= Atom
                 | "-" Operand<f> ( CONT<f> ( ">>" | "<<" ) Operand<f> )*   /* negation */
                 | "if" Expr<f> "then" Expr<f> "else" Expr<f>
                 | "let" LetBlock "in" Expr<f>
                 | "case" Expr<f> "of" CaseBlock
                 | "\" PatternAtom+ "->" Expr<f>
Suffix         ::= FieldAccess | Argument | NegativeArgument
Argument       ::= Atom FieldAccess*
NegativeArgument ::= "-" Atom FieldAccess*     /* see Adjacency rules */
FieldAccess    ::= "." LowerName               /* the "." touches the token before it */

LetBlock       ::= ( COL<c> LetDecl<c> )*      /* c: the column of the first token after "let" */
CaseBlock      ::= Branch<c> ( COL<c> Branch<c> )*   /* c: the column of the first token after "of" */
Branch<c>      ::= Pattern "->" Expr<c>

Atom           ::= QualifiedName
                 | "True" | "False" | Int | String
                 | "(" ")"
                 | "(" Expr<none> ")"
                 | "(" Expr<none> "," Expr<none> ( "," Expr<none> )? ")"
                 | "(" BinaryOperator ")"
                 | "[" ( Expr<none> ( "," Expr<none> )* )? "]"
                 | "{" ( Field ( "," Field )* )? "}"
                 | "{" LowerName "|" Field ( "," Field )* "}"
                 | "." LowerName               /* accessor: see Adjacency rules */
Field          ::= LowerName "=" Expr<none>
QualifiedName  ::= LowerName
                 | UpperName ( "." UpperName )* ( "." LowerName )?   /* no spaces, see Adjacency rules */
BinaryOperator ::= "|>" | "<|" | "||" | "&&" | "==" | "/=" | "<" | ">" | "<=" | ">=" | "::" | "++"
                 | "+" | "-" | "*" | "//" | "^" | ">>" | "<<"
```

- `if` needs its `else`.
- `if`, `let` and a lambda extend as far to the right as they can: `if a then b else c |> f` is
  `if a then b else (c |> f)`. A `case` ends where its block ends, so an operator on a line left of
  its branches applies to the whole `case`.
- A `-` after an operand is either `BinaryOperator` or the start of a `NegativeArgument`; the
  characters around it decide (see [Adjacency rules](#adjacency-rules)).
- A tuple has two or three elements: `ELCI1002: Tuples have two or three elements`.
- `(op)` is the operator as a function of two arguments, for every operator in the table:
  `(+)`, `(::)`, `(|>)`. `(/)` is rejected, like `/`.
- `{ r | x = 1 }` updates the record `r`, which must be a plain lowercase name.
- `.field` is the function `\r -> r.field`.
- An argument can't start with `if`, `let`, `case`, `\` or `-`; put it in parentheses. A minus
  written as in `f -1` is the exception: see [Adjacency rules](#adjacency-rules).

```elm
module Expressions exposing (main)

type alias Point =
    { x : Int, y : Int }

main : ( Int, List Int, Bool )
main =
    let
        origin =
            { x = 0, y = 0 }

        moved =
            { origin | x = 3 }

        points =
            [ moved, Point 1 2 ]
    in
    ( List.foldl (+) 0 (List.map .x points)
    , List.map (\point -> point.y * -1) points
    , if moved.x > origin.x then True else False
    )
```

### Patterns

```text
Pattern      ::= PatternApp ( "::" Pattern )? ( "as" LowerName )?
PatternApp   ::= QualifiedCtor PatternAtom+ | PatternAtom   /* True and False take no arguments */
PatternAtom  ::= "_" | LowerName | QualifiedCtor
               | Int | "-" Int | String
               | "(" ")"
               | "(" Pattern ")"
               | "(" Pattern "," Pattern ( "," Pattern )? ")"
               | "[" ( Pattern ( "," Pattern )* )? "]"
               | "{" ( LowerName ( "," LowerName )* )? "}"
QualifiedCtor ::= UpperName ( "." UpperName )*
```

- `True` and `False` take no arguments: `True x ->` is `ELCI1002: Expected '->', found 'x'`.
- `::` groups to the right: `a :: b :: rest`.
- `as` names the pattern just before it. In `first :: rest as all`, `all` names `rest`, not the whole
  list (Elm names the whole list); write `(first :: rest) as all` for that.
- A tuple pattern has two or three elements: `ELCI1002: Tuple patterns have two or three elements`.
- `[ a, b ]` is the pattern `a :: b :: []`.
- Function and lambda parameters and `let` destructuring take a single `PatternAtom`, which must be
  irrefutable (see [Declarations](#declarations)).

```elm
module Patterns exposing (describe)

describe : List (Maybe Int) -> String
describe values =
    case values of
        [] ->
            "none"

        [ Just 0 ] ->
            "one zero"

        (Just -1) :: _ ->
            "starts at minus one"

        ((Just _) :: _) as all ->
            if List.length all > 2 then
                "many"

            else
                "some"

        Nothing :: _ ->
            "starts empty"
```

## Operators

From the tightest binding to the loosest:

| Precedence | Operators | Associativity |
| ---: | --- | --- |
| | `record.field` | |
| 10 | function application `f x` | left |
| 9 | `>>` | right |
| 9 | `<<` | left |
| | negation `-x`, a `-` where an expression starts | |
| 8 | `^` | right |
| 7 | `*`, `//` | left |
| 6 | `+`, `-` | left |
| 5 | `::`, `++` | right |
| 4 | `==`, `/=`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=` | none |
| 3 | `&&` | right |
| 2 | `\|\|` | right |
| 0 | `\|>` | left |
| 0 | `<\|` | right |

- The precedences are those of Elm 0.19, and of `Parser.PRECEDENCE`. Negation has no number in the
  parser: it reads its operand at precedence 9, so it covers applications and `>>`/`<<` chains and
  stops before `^`. `-x ^ 2` is `(-x) ^ 2`, `-f x` is `-(f x)` and `2 * -3` is `2 * (-3)`.
- Comparisons do not chain: `a < b < c` is `ELCI1002: Comparison operators cannot be chained; use &&
  or explicit parentheses`.
- Operators of one precedence that associate in opposite directions do not mix:
  `f <| x |> g` is `ELCI1002: Mixing (<|) and (|>) needs parentheses: they associate in opposite
  directions, as in Elm`, and the same holds for `>>` and `<<`.
- `/` is `ELCI2001: Float division is unsupported; use // for integer quotient`, and `(/)` is
  `ELCI2001: Float division is unsupported; use (//) for integer quotient`. `%` does not exist: use
  `modBy` or `remainderBy`.

```elm
module Operators exposing (main)

main : List Int
main =
    [ 1 + 2 * 3 ^ 2
    , 2 ^ 3 ^ 2
    , (List.map ((*) 2) >> List.sum) [ 1, 2 ]
    , [ 1, 2 ] |> List.map negate |> List.sum
    , List.sum <| 0 :: [ 1 ] ++ [ 2 ]
    ]
```

## Adjacency rules

Some tokens mean different things depending on whether they *touch*: two tokens touch when no
character, space or comment, separates them.

**Field access and accessors.** A `.` that touches the token before it reads a field of that value.
A `.` that does not touch the token before it, followed by a lowercase name that touches the `.`, is
an accessor function.

| Source | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `r.field` | the field `field` of `r` |
